docs.title: Which of your applications can run in containers?
docs.text:
Containerizer scans your whole application portfolio, rates every application from A (container-ready: a modern stack that moves to containers without code changes) to E (not feasible: stays on Windows), explains each obstacle with a fix and references, and generates hardened Dockerfiles and Kubernetes manifests for everything that can move. Then it proves them by building, running and deploying them in its own sandbox cluster.

Get started How it works GitHub

docs.title: Why Containerizer?
docs.text:
• Rules first, AI last

    A data-driven rule set classifies every component, so results are repeatable, explainable and free. An LLM is asked only about what the rules are unsure of, and its answers are validated first.

    How it works

  • Learns by doing

    When unsure, it builds and runs the container, matches failures, patches the plan and retries. Fixes that work become rule proposals that a person approves, so the next run needs no retries.

    Rule review

  • Secure by default

    Chiseled images, non-root, read-only root filesystem, no capabilities, seccomp, Pod Security restricted, and a gate that scans with Trivy and Grype. Every exception is recorded with its reason.

    Security gate

  • Your whole organization

    Schedule scans of Azure DevOps, GitHub and GitLab organizations. New repositories are found automatically, and the A-rated ones are pushed and committed for Argo CD or Flux.

    Organization scans

  • Proven in a sandbox

    A built-in k3s cluster deploys what was generated and reports "deployed and healthy" or exactly why not, even with a restored copy of the application's development database.

    The sandbox cluster

  • A migration plan, not just a verdict

    Every blocker maps to a Linux replacement: System.Drawing to SkiaSharp, WCF to CoreWCF, Windows Service to a worker service, with packages, steps and checks.

    Migration assistant

  • Refactoring patches, verified

    For a B-rated application the LLM makes the targeted code changes, one file at a time. The patch is applied to the assessed commit, checked with the rules, built and run before you download it.

    Refactoring patches

  • Build pipelines for your CI

    GitHub Actions, GitLab CI/CD or Azure Pipelines, for where the code lives: build every component, SBOM and scan it on pull requests, push and sign from the default branch, as a patch to git am.

    Build pipelines

  • Runs in your network

    One immutable appliance with signed upgrades and roll back, only SSH and HTTPS in, and outgoing traffic blocked except for hosts an admin allows. Use Claude, your own self-hosted LLM, or the appliance's built-in CPU LLM when you have no GPU.

    Appliance · The LLM

  • Built for management and audit

    Single sign-on, admins, product owners and operators, an audit log of every change, an access log, trends over time, and SBOMs with licences and CVEs per package.

    Sign-in and roles

docs.title: Every application, explained
docs.text:
Open an application to see its components, the rating, the main obstacles, and for each finding what to change, why, and where to read more. Everything links back to the rule that decided it.

How it works

docs.title: From blocker to a concrete plan
docs.text:
The migration assistant turns each blocking finding into a Linux-compatible replacement with packages to add and remove, steps and checks. What can't move is marked "keep on Windows" instead of being forced.

Migration assistant

docs.title: Make it A
docs.text:
One order has the LLM fix everything that keeps a B application from A, verifies and repairs the patch, assesses it again and deploys the patched copy to the sandbox beside the original. Every order shows its tokens and time, and needs an administrator's approval until you trust it.

Refactoring patches

docs.title: Watch the portfolio move
docs.text:
Trends show how ratings change over time per business unit and product, so you can see the effect of each fix and each newly learned rule.

Install the appliance

docs.title: Scans that run themselves
docs.text:
Define organization scans on the admin pages, by day and time or on demand. Discover first lists the projects, repositories and latest commits without cloning anything, so deprecated ones can be disabled before the full scan. Every repository shows its last result, and skipped ones are listed with the reason, such as "no source code".

Organization scans

docs.title: A slow LLM never holds up a scan
docs.text:
With a CPU-only or busy LLM, scans can leave the LLM reviews to a queue: uncertain components first, then a second opinion on blockers. Reorder it, limit it to quiet hours or an idle machine, and see how many tokens and hours are left, estimated from the speed it has measured on your LLM.

The LLM queue

docs.title: From finding to a verified patch
docs.text:
For applications that need targeted code changes, an operator orders a refactoring patch. The LLM makes the changes, then Containerizer applies them to the assessed commit, runs the rules again and builds and runs the container. You get a coloured diff, the result per finding and a .patch to apply with git am.

Refactoring patches

docs.title: A person approves what the AI learns
docs.text:
Fixes the learning loop discovers arrive as rule proposals with their evidence. Approve, edit or reject them; approved rules make the next run faster and AI-free.

Rule review

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Scripts and other tools can read the results and maintain the business units, products and application mapping through a JSON API under /api/v1. Callers authenticate with an API key, or with an OAuth access token from the same identity provider as the sign-in. Cookies are never used.

The API is on whenever the admin pages are (with sign-in, or in development mode).

docs.title: API keys
docs.text:
Administrators make keys on Admin → API, which also shows how to call the API from this server with curl and Python. A key (czk_…) has a name, a role and an optional expiry:

Role May Read only GET everything the API offers Full also add, change and remove business units and products, and map applications

The key is shown once, when it is made: only its SHA-256 is stored. The page lists every key with its status, who made it and when, when it expires and when it was last used, and revokes keys. Making and revoking keys, and every change made with a key (as api-key:<prefix>), are in the change history.

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $CZ_API_KEY" https://containerizer.example.com/api/v1/applications

docs.title: Access tokens (OpenID Connect)
docs.text:
To let automation use access tokens from your identity provider instead, add two settings to /etc/containerizer/web.env next to the sign-in ones and restart the web UI:

Variable Meaning CONTAINERIZER_API_AUDIENCE The audience access tokens must be issued for, e.g. api://containerizer (Entra ID: the Application ID URI of the app registration). CONTAINERIZER_API_CLIENTS Automation that may change everything, comma separated: client:<client id> (the token's azp, appid or client_id), or role:, group:, email:, domain:, sub: rules. Optional when the roles are enough.

With Entra ID: set accessTokenAcceptedVersion to 2 in the API app's manifest so its access tokens carry the same v2.0 issuer as the sign-in, define an app role (e.g. Containerizer.Write, allowed member type Applications), grant it to the client app, and set CONTAINERIZER_API_CLIENTS=role:Containerizer.Write.

docs.title: Authentication and authorization
docs.text:
Callers send Authorization: Bearer <API key or access token>. For access tokens: the client-credentials flow for automation, or a user's token. Signature, issuer, audience and expiry are checked; an ID token is refused (its audience is the web app). Cookies are ignored, so there is no CSRF surface.

The roles apply to tokens too: admins and API clients can change everything, product owners only their own products and applications (403 forbidden outside them), operators only read. A token that matches none of these (viewers included) gets 403 insufficient_scope. Changes appear in the change history with Via API and the user's e-mail, or client:<client id> for an application.

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
Bodies are JSON (Content-Type: application/json, up to 64 KiB); unknown fields are refused.

Method and path Does GET /api/v1/business-units · POST list (?name=) · create {"name", "owner", "description"} GET · PATCH · PUT · DELETE /api/v1/business-units/{id} read · change some fields · replace · delete (409 while products are in it) GET /api/v1/products · POST list (?name=, ?businessUnitId=) · create {"name", "businessUnitId", "infoUrl", "owner", "description"} GET · PATCH · PUT · DELETE /api/v1/products/{id} as above (409 while applications are mapped to it) GET /api/v1/applications list with the latest rating (?unmapped=true, ?productId=, ?name=, ?retired=true) GET · PATCH /api/v1/applications/{id} read · set productId, displayName, owner, description, retired (applications themselves come from scans) GET /api/v1/audit the change history (?table=Application, ?rowId=, ?limit= up to 1000) GET /api/v1/applications/{id}/components/{cid}/sbom packages of one component with licence, policy status and CVEs; ?format=cyclonedx for the CycloneDX document GET /api/v1/sbom/packages packages across the portfolio (?businessUnitId=, ?productId=, ?licenseStatus=allowed,warn,denied,unknown, ?vulnerable=true, ?limit= up to 10000) GET /api/v1/sbom/summary the numbers of the Dependencies and licences page (?businessUnitId=, ?productId=)

businessUnitId and productId filters take an id or none (not assigned). Errors are {"error": "...", "message": "..."} with 400 (invalid field), 401 (no or bad token), 403 (not allowed), 404, 405, 409 (name taken, referenced row missing or still in use), 413 or 415.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
# Entra ID client credentials (a second app registration as the client, granted the API's app role)
TOKEN=$(curl -s https://login.microsoftonline.com/$TENANT/oauth2/v2.0/token \
  -d grant_type=client_credentials -d client_id=$CLIENT_ID -d client_secret=$CLIENT_SECRET \
  -d scope=api://containerizer/.default | jq -r .access_token)
API=https://containerizer.example.com/api/v1

# map every unmapped application from one repository to the Billing product
PRODUCT=$(curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "$API/products?name=Billing" | jq '.items[0].id')
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "$API/applications?unmapped=true" \
  | jq -r '.items[] | select(.repositoryUrl == "https://dev.azure.com/contoso/Billing/_git/billing") | .id' \
  | while read id; do
      curl -s -X PATCH -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
        -d "{\"productId\": $PRODUCT}" "$API/applications/$id"
    done

# licences to review or denied in one business unit
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "$API/sbom/packages?businessUnitId=3&licenseStatus=warn,denied"

docs.title: Running the appliance
docs.text: The appliance is an immutable OS image built with the Elemental toolkit (as in Firewall4AI), installed from an ISO or started from a disk image, and upgraded from the admin pages. To install it, see Getting started.

The OS is a read-only snapshot of the container image ghcr.io/olljanat-ai/containerizer-appliance. Everything that has to survive a restart or an upgrade is on the persistent partition: the database, /etc/containerizer (configuration and generated secrets), Docker and k3s data, the registry, clones, learned rules, logs. An upgrade writes the new version as a new snapshot next to the running one; if it does not start properly, the appliance goes back to the previous snapshot by itself.

docs.title: Root password and SSH
docs.text:
root is the only administrator account on the OS. It signs in on the console or over SSH with its password, or over SSH with a key in /root/.ssh/authorized_keys. The password is containerizer and expired on a new appliance, so the first sign-in, on the console or over SSH, asks for a new one (until then PAM may refuse an SSH key as well). /etc is rebuilt at every boot, so the appliance keeps root's password entry in /etc/containerizer/secrets/root-shadow (persistent partition) and puts it back at every start; changes with passwd are saved there by themselves (containerizer-root-password.path).

  • Keys only: after adding your key, passwd -l root locks the password: password sign-in stops working on SSH and the console, keys keep working. passwd -u root unlocks it.
  • Forgotten password: start the recovery system from the GRUB menu (it always starts with the default password, expired), mount the persistent partition (label COS_PERSISTENT) and delete root-shadow from the secrets folder of /etc/containerizer there; the next start of the appliance goes back to the default password.
  • The recovery system does not keep a changed password: each start asks for a new one again.

docs.title: Unattended installs
docs.text:
Pass an Elemental cloud-config with the key, e.g. elemental install --cloud-init my.yaml /dev/sda from the ISO, or put the file into the OEM partition:

stages:
  fs:
    - name: "SSH key of the administrator"
      authorized_keys:
        root:
          - "ssh-ed25519 AAAA... you@example.com"

The root password is the default (containerizer) and expired on unattended installs too.

docs.title: Configuration files
docs.text:
The first boot creates /etc/containerizer/ (mode 700) with:

File What to set appliance.env CZ_HOSTNAME (the name in the HTTPS certificate and the sign-in redirect), CZ_ACME_EMAIL (Let's Encrypt instead of the appliance's own CA), CZ_DNS_SERVERS, CZ_MSSQL_EDITION, CZ_MSSQL_MEMORY, CZ_SQL_* (external database), CZ_LLM_HEAVY (LLM-heavy mode, off by default) web.env Sign-in for the web UI: CONTAINERIZER_OIDC_*, CONTAINERIZER_ADMINS, roles, viewers, API (sign-in and roles) worker.env Push credentials for an external image registry, and extra registry hosts the worker may push to. Scans that push to the appliance's own registry need none; source control tokens are registered on the admin pages (source-control.md) sandbox.env The output repository the sandbox cluster deploys from (the sandbox cluster) grafana.env Optional Grafana settings, e.g. sign-in with your identity provider egress.json The egress allow-list: change it on the Firewall page, not here secrets/ Generated passwords (SQL Server logins, Grafana admin), the root password (root-shadow), sql-owner for an external database and the key pair that seals source control tokens (credential-key for the worker only, credential-key.pub for the web UI): root-only, never shown in the web UI. Keep credential-key when restoring a backup: the registered tokens open only with it network/ Optional systemd-networkd .network files for static addresses (default: DHCP on every NIC)

docs.title: External database
docs.text:
By default the results database runs on the appliance, and you back it up (Backup). To keep it on a SQL Server you already run and back up (SQL Server 2019 or later, or Azure SQL Managed Instance), point the appliance at it in appliance.env. SQL Server then does not run on the appliance, and the database is backed up with your server; the appliance's files still need their backup (Backup).

  1. On your server, create the database and a login that owns it (db_owner). With CZ_SQL_LOGINS=create (the default) the login also needs ALTER ANY LOGIN (e.g. securityadmin): it creates the logins cz_scanner, cz_web and cz_admin with generated passwords. If your DBA creates logins instead, create those three yourself and set CZ_SQL_LOGINS=existing.

  2. In /etc/containerizer/appliance.env:

    CZ_SQL_SERVER=sql01.example.com,1433
CZ_SQL_DATABASE=Containerizer
CZ_SQL_USER=containerizer_owner
CZ_SQL_LOGINS=create
# optional: more connection string options, in quotes
CZ_SQL_OPTIONS="Schema=containerizer"
# optional: the CA of the server's certificate when the system CAs do not cover it
CZ_SQL_CA=/etc/containerizer/sql-ca.pem

  3. Put the passwords in place (root only):

    install -m 0400 /dev/stdin /etc/containerizer/secrets/sql-owner      # the password of CZ_SQL_USER, then Ctrl-D
# only with CZ_SQL_LOGINS=existing: the three logins' passwords, the same way, into
# secrets/cz-scanner, secrets/cz-web and secrets/cz-admin

  4. Reboot.

At every start containerizer-db-init creates or upgrades the schema on that server as CZ_SQL_USER (the same as on the appliance's own SQL Server), so an upgrade of the appliance upgrades the database. The connection is encrypted and the server certificate is checked (the system CAs, or CZ_SQL_CA); TrustServerCertificate=yes in CZ_SQL_OPTIONS turns the check off, for test servers only. The firewall allows the server and port by itself (Firewall page → Always allowed); a DNS name must resolve through the appliance's DNS servers (CZ_DNS_SERVERS). Named instances (host\instance) are not supported: give the port. The login names are fixed, so one SQL Server instance serves one appliance with CZ_SQL_LOGINS=create.

To move the data of an appliance that already ran scans: back up its database (Backup), restore the .bak on your server, then set it up as above: the restored database users cz_scanner, cz_web and cz_admin are mapped to the logins of that server by themselves. The appliance no longer uses /var/lib/containerizer/mssql; keep it until a scan has written to the external database, then delete it. To go back to the appliance's own SQL Server, empty CZ_SQL_SERVER and reboot (it starts with what that folder holds).

If the settings are not valid, the web UI and the scan worker do not start: journalctl -b -u containerizer-firstboot -u containerizer-db-init says why.

docs.title: Firewall
docs.text:
Inbound: only TCP 22 (SSH) and 443 (HTTPS). The k3s API, SQL Server, the registry, Prometheus and Grafana listen on the loopback interface or are not reachable from outside; NodePorts of the sandbox cluster are blocked too (use ssh -L to reach anything else).

Outbound: blocked, except to the names and networks on the allow-list. This holds for the appliance itself, the scan worker, every container Docker builds or runs, and every pod in the sandbox cluster.

How it works: the host, Docker and k3s resolve names only through the appliance's DNS filter (dnsmasq on 169.254.53.53). It answers only names an allow-list rule covers (anything else gets REFUSED), and puts the addresses of the answer into nftables sets of that rule's ports. The firewall lets connections out only to addresses in those sets (and to the networks of network rules), on the rule's ports. A connection to an address nobody resolved through the filter, an address of a name that is not allowed, or another port is dropped and logged.

Admin → Firewall (administrators only):

  • Allow a name (it covers its subdomains: nuget.org also allows api.nuget.org) or a network (10.20.0.0/16), with ports (443, 80,443, udp/123) and a note.
  • Refused names, last 24 hours: what something on the appliance tried to resolve and was refused, with an Allow button. Run a scan, then allow what it needs.
  • Blocked connections: addresses and ports the firewall dropped.
  • Log only mode lets everything out but still lists what would have been refused, to build the list. Turn blocking back on when you are done.
  • Always allowed: what the appliance needs itself (GHCR and Sigstore for upgrades and their signatures, Docker Hub and the Microsoft registry for its own service images). Part of the OS image. While the built-in LLM's model downloads, huggingface.co and hf.co are listed here too.
  • Change history: who changed what, kept on the persistent partition.

The web UI does not change the firewall itself: it asks the system agent (root), which checks the rules again, loads the new ruleset in one transaction (checked with nft -c first, and the previous ruleset is kept if the new one does not load) and restarts the DNS filter. On the console: /usr/lib/containerizer/venv/bin/python -m containerizer.sysagent firewall show.

docs.title: Local registry and the sandbox cluster
docs.text:
The registry at localhost:5000 is for images of the sandbox: in an organization scan, set the registry to localhost:5000/<path> and turn pushing on; the scan worker pushes there without credentials, and k3s pulls from it (/etc/rancher/k3s/registries.yaml) without pull secrets. It is not reachable from outside the appliance. Deleted tags free their space after a garbage collection: docker exec cz-registry registry garbage-collect --delete-untagged /etc/distribution/config.yml (stop the worker first).

k3s also runs External Secrets Operator, and the generated configurations get every secret through it (external-secrets.md). The values live in namespace containerizer-secrets, which runs no pods, and each namespace can read only its own keys.

To deploy what the scans generate, set sandbox.env (output repository URL, branch, read-only token). Every 2 minutes cz-sandbox puts the read-only token in the secret store for Flux's root sync and for every app namespace, and creates the root GitRepository + Kustomization of the output repository's sandbox/flux/. Each app reconciles as its own ServiceAccount with its own copy of the token (the sandbox cluster). Allow the Git server on the Firewall page. kubectl (as root on the appliance) shows the result. Argo CD is not installed; Flux is the supported path on the appliance.

To reach the deployed apps over HTTPS, set up a wildcard domain and certificate on Admin → Sandbox HTTPS: Caddy answers for *.<domain> on the same port 443 and passes the requests to Traefik in k3s, and every web component gets https://<component>-<app>.<domain>/ (sandbox-https.md).

Components that sign users in get the sandbox identity provider, WSO2 Identity Server at https://containerizer-idp.<sandbox domain>/ (sandbox-idp.md). cz-sandbox creates its passwords and client secrets in the secret store once Flux has deployed it. containerizer idp users (as root) prints the test users and their passwords. Its images come from Docker Hub, which the default firewall rules allow.

docs.title: Upgrade and roll back
docs.text:
Admin → System (administrators only) shows the running version, the snapshots on the disk and the last upgrade or roll back with its outcome, and checks GHCR for newer releases.

  • Upgrade: pick a newer release and confirm. The system agent checks with cosign that the image was signed by this repository's release workflow (keyless signature, GitHub's OIDC identity of .github/workflows/release.yml on a vX.Y.Z tag), then installs exactly the verified digest as a new snapshot and restarts. Only release tags of the appliance's own image repository are accepted, whatever the web UI sends.
  • Automatic fallback: after an upgrade the boot assessment checks that the firewall is loaded and the DNS filter, Docker and k3s run and the application starts. If that fails 5 times, the appliance restarts into the previous snapshot, and the System page shows the upgrade as failed.
  • Roll back: pick an earlier snapshot. It is installed as a new active snapshot (no download) and the appliance restarts. Data on the persistent partition is not rolled back: the database keeps its schema (newer versions only add to it, and older code reads it).
  • The GRUB menu at start-up also lists the snapshots, and a recovery system.

On the console: python -m containerizer.sysagent upgrade vX.Y.Z or ... rollback <snapshot> (with /usr/lib/containerizer/venv/bin/python). The appliance checks GHCR anonymously, so the containerizer-appliance package must be public.

docs.title: Built-in LLM
docs.text:
For sites without an LLM server of their own (a GPU server, or the Claude API), the appliance can run one itself, on its CPU. It is off by default and is turned on under Admin → Source control & LLM (administrators only). Scans with Ask the LLM use it when no LLM is set on that page; an LLM set there always wins. See the LLM for what it is asked.

Model Qwen3-Coder 30B-A3B Instruct, ByteShape's IQ4_XS-4.20bpw GGUF build (16 GB, Apache 2.0), served as qwen3-coder-30b-a3b Server llama.cpp llama-server (image CZ_IMAGE_LLAMA_CPP in images.env, pinned by digest), containerizer-local-llm.service, container cz-llm Listens on 127.0.0.1:8082 only; metrics for Prometheus on the same port Memory at least 40 GB on the machine. The model (15.6 GB) is locked in RAM, so builds cannot push it out; each answer slot adds about 2 GB Disk about 20 GB free on the persistent partition for the download (16 GB plus 4 GB to spare) Speed about 7 to 12 tokens per second on a 22-core server; reading a 5,000 to 15,000 token evidence pack takes 1.5 to 5 minutes, so an answer takes about 5 minutes. Calls may take up to an hour (CONTAINERIZER_LLM_TIMEOUT=3600 is set for it)

Turning it on. The system agent checks the memory and the free space again (the page shows both), then downloads the model once from Hugging Face, from a fixed commit of the repository, resuming a partial download, and checks its size and SHA-256 before it is used. huggingface.co and hf.co (which covers the download servers it redirects to) are on the allow-list only while the download runs, as system rules on the Firewall page; then they are removed again. If the download is refused anyway, the refused names are listed on Admin → Firewall. The page shows the progress; after the download the server loads the model, which takes a minute or two, and the state turns to Running. A failed download (network, checksum) is not retried by itself: Try again resumes it. A file that fails the checksum is deleted.

Sizing. The answer slots (requests answered together, for about the cost of one, since speed follows memory bandwidth) and the container's memory limit follow the machine's memory:

Memory Slots Context per slot Memory limit of cz-llm 40 to 47 GB 1 22,016 tokens 24 GB 48 to 63 GB 2 22,016 tokens 27 GB 64 GB or more 3 22,016 tokens 30 GB

It gets a quarter of the CPU's weight (--cpu-shares 256), so the scans' builds go first when both want the CPU. Use the queued LLM mode for organization scans where it is offered, and leave LLM-heavy mode off: it makes many calls, and on a CPU that turns a scan into hours or days.

Turning it off stops the server (or the download) at once; the model file stays, so turning it on again starts the server without a new download. Remove next to Turn on deletes the model file to free its 16 GB.

Files:

What Where On or off, the download's state and the change history /var/lib/containerizer/system/local-llm.json The model file (re-downloadable) /var/lib/containerizer/llm/ What the page and the scan worker read /run/containerizer/system/local-llm-status.json The server's settings while it is on (slots, context, memory) /run/containerizer/local-llm.env

On the console: systemctl status containerizer-local-llm containerizer-local-llm-download, docker logs cz-llm, and curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8082/health. It is not part of the start-up check of an upgrade: a missing or slow model never makes the appliance go back to the previous snapshot. The Grafana dashboard has a Built-in LLM row: whether it is up, requests in progress and waiting, and the tokens per second it generates.

docs.title: Backup
docs.text:
The OS is rebuilt from the image; what has to be backed up is on the persistent partition. Scans rebuild the clones, images in the local registry and the sandbox apps, but not the rest:

What Where Why it matters Results database SQL Server, /var/lib/containerizer/mssql (back it up with BACKUP DATABASE, below) Results, history, mapping, scan settings, sealed tokens, rule review Configuration and secrets /etc/containerizer .env files, firewall allow-list, SQL Server and Grafana passwords, the root password, and secrets/credential-key: the tokens in the database open only with it Dev database uploads /var/lib/containerizer/devdb The uploaded backups. The database keeps only their name and SHA-256, so without the files the next scan of those apps has no backup to restore Appliance settings and their history /var/lib/containerizer/system Sandbox HTTPS certificate, key and settings, the lab service switches, and the change history of the firewall and Sandbox HTTPS (these two are files here, not in the database) Learned rules /var/lib/containerizer/learned Rules the learning loop added on this appliance. Rules approved in the rule review are in your rules repository HTTPS certificate authority /var/lib/caddy Without CZ_ACME_EMAIL, the appliance's own CA: a new one means every browser has to trust a new root Metrics (optional) /var/lib/containerizer/prometheus, /var/lib/containerizer/grafana 90 days of scan and LLM usage metrics, and changes made in Grafana

The built-in LLM's model file (/var/lib/containerizer/llm, 16 GB) can be downloaded again: leave it out of backups (the archive below does). Its on/off setting is in /var/lib/containerizer/system.

Lab service data and restored dev databases in the sandbox cluster (/var/lib/rancher) are test data: a new cluster starts them empty, or restores the uploaded backups again, and creates new credentials.

With an external database the results database is backed up with your SQL Server: skip its row and the BACKUP DATABASE step below. The files are still needed.

Back up the database (from the appliance):

docker exec cz-mssql /opt/mssql-tools18/bin/sqlcmd -C -S localhost -U sa -P "$(cat /etc/containerizer/secrets/mssql-sa)" \
  -Q "BACKUP DATABASE Containerizer TO DISK = N'/var/opt/mssql/backup/containerizer.bak' WITH COMPRESSION, INIT"
# the file is /var/lib/containerizer/mssql/backup/containerizer.bak

and the folders (the database backup above included):

tar -C / -czf /root/containerizer-backup.tgz etc/containerizer var/lib/containerizer/mssql/backup \
  var/lib/containerizer/devdb var/lib/containerizer/system var/lib/containerizer/learned var/lib/caddy

Copy the archive off the appliance (scp root@<appliance>:/root/containerizer-backup.tgz .): it holds every secret of the appliance, so keep it like one.

To restore on a new appliance, after its first start (with its own sa password, which you keep):

systemctl stop containerizer-web containerizer-worker
tar -C / -xzf /root/containerizer-backup.tgz \
  --exclude=etc/containerizer/secrets/mssql-sa --exclude=etc/containerizer/secrets/mssql.env
docker exec cz-mssql /opt/mssql-tools18/bin/sqlcmd -C -S localhost -U sa -P "$(cat /etc/containerizer/secrets/mssql-sa)" \
  -Q "RESTORE DATABASE Containerizer FROM DISK = N'/var/opt/mssql/backup/containerizer.bak' WITH REPLACE"
systemctl reboot

At the next start the schema is upgraded if the backup is older, and the logins of the web UI and the scan worker get the passwords of the backup and are linked to their users in the restored database again.

docs.title: Security notes
docs.text:
• OS: read-only, signed upgrades only, no package manager in use, kernel and network hardening sysctls, root's default password must be changed at the first sign-in (passwd -l root for SSH keys only), no service but SSH and HTTPS reachable, outbound allow-list for everything.
  • Web UI: no privileges (systemd sandbox: read-only system, no capabilities, system call filter); its database passwords come as systemd credentials. It cannot change the OS: upgrades, roll backs and the firewall go through the system agent, which checks every request again.
  • SQL Server: non-root, every capability dropped except binding its port, loopback only. An external database is reached encrypted, with the server certificate checked, and with the same three logins. Edition: Express by default (free, 10 GB per database); Developer is not licensed for production.
  • The scan worker is in the docker group, which is equivalent to root: it builds and runs the scanned repositories' images. That is why the appliance is a dedicated machine, and why the egress allow-list applies to every build. Give it no credentials beyond the scans' tokens.
  • k3s: secrets encrypted at rest, delivered by External Secrets Operator from a namespace without pods, audit log (/var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/logs/audit.log), kernel defaults protected, API reachable only from the appliance and its pods. Each app's namespace runs under Pod Security "restricted".
  • Containers of the appliance's own services are pinned by digest in the OS image (/usr/lib/containerizer/images.env); each release has an SPDX SBOM attested to the image with cosign.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Something does not start systemctl --failed, journalctl -b -u <unit>; units are containerizer-*, k3s, caddy, docker A scan cannot reach a host Admin → Firewall → Refused names; or journalctl -u containerizer-dns \| grep REFUSED The firewall did not load the SSH-only fallback ruleset is active; systemctl status containerizer-firewall shows why Status of the system agent /run/containerizer/system/status.json, journalctl -u containerizer-sysagent Locked out of SSH the console of the VM: GRUB menu → recovery, or a previous snapshot

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: Containerizer ships as one virtual machine, the appliance: an immutable OS image with the web UI and API, the scan worker, SQL Server, a sandbox cluster and monitoring. You install it, set up sign-in, and do everything else in the web UI. This page is the short path from download to the first scan; what the appliance runs and how to operate it is in Running the appliance.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• x86-64 VM (or server) with UEFI firmware (Secure Boot works: the shim and GRUB are Debian's signed ones). Hyper-V: generation 2. VMware: EFI firmware.
  • 4 vCPU and 16 GB memory or more (SQL Server takes 4 GB, CZ_MSSQL_MEMORY), more for parallel builds.
  • One disk of 64 GB or more: 16 GB for the OS snapshots, the rest is the persistent partition.
  • Optional, for the built-in LLM (off by default, for sites without an LLM server of their own): 40 GB memory or more (16 GB for the appliance, about 24 GB for the model) and about 20 GB more disk for the model file. 48 GB and 64 GB let it answer two and three requests at once.
  • Outbound HTTPS to the hosts on the Firewall page (the image registries the appliance uses are allowed by default) and DNS servers from DHCP or CZ_DNS_SERVERS.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Every release has:

File For containerizer-vX.Y.Z.iso Installer: boot it, answer the questions on the console. containerizer-vX.Y.Z.qcow2 KVM, Proxmox, OpenStack: resize the disk to 64 GB or more first (qemu-img resize). containerizer-vX.Y.Z.vhd.zst Hyper-V (generation 2): zstd -d, then expand the disk to 64 GB or more. SHA256SUMS, SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json Check the downloads (command in the release notes).

Check what you downloaded:

cosign verify-blob --bundle SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github\.com/olljanat-ai/containerizer/\.github/workflows/release\.yml@refs/tags/' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com SHA256SUMS
sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing

From the ISO: the console (screen or serial) shows the installer: the disk to install to (it is erased), an SSH public key for root (optional), and a host name. It installs and restarts; remove the ISO.

From a disk image: the first start installs the system to the whole disk (it takes a few minutes and restarts once), then shows the login prompt.

For unattended installs, see Running the appliance.

docs.title: First boot
docs.text:
Sign in as root with the password containerizer, over SSH (ssh root@<appliance>) or on the console. The first sign-in asks for the current password once more and then a new one; SSH closes the connection after the change if the login did not continue, so sign in again with the new password. Until the password is changed, an SSH key alone may be refused too. The new password is kept on the persistent partition, so it survives restarts, upgrades and roll backs.

The first boot created /etc/containerizer/ with the configuration files (configuration files). Then:

  1. Set CZ_HOSTNAME in appliance.env to the DNS name users will open, and register https://<CZ_HOSTNAME>/auth/callback as the redirect URI of an app registration at your identity provider (Entra ID, Okta, Keycloak, ...).
  2. Fill in web.env (issuer, client id and secret, CONTAINERIZER_ADMINS; sign-in and roles). Allow the identity provider's host on the Firewall page once you are in (or add it to egress.json now: e.g. login.microsoftonline.com), since the web UI fetches its keys.
  3. systemctl reboot (or systemctl restart containerizer-web caddy).
  4. Open https://<CZ_HOSTNAME>/admin. With the default certificate from the appliance's own CA, browsers warn until you trust its root: /var/lib/caddy/.local/share/caddy/pki/authorities/local/root.crt. With CZ_ACME_EMAIL, allow acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org on the Firewall page first; the name must resolve to the appliance from the internet (TLS-ALPN challenge on 443).
  5. Admin → Firewall: allow the hosts your scans need (Git servers, package feeds, registries).
  6. Admin → Source control & LLM: a read-only token for each organization to scan and a write token for each output repository (source-control.md), and the LLM if scans should ask one.
  7. Admin → Organization scans: define the scans (organization scans), and fill in sandbox.env so the sandbox cluster deploys what they generate.

Grafana is at https://<CZ_HOSTNAME>/grafana/, user admin, password in /etc/containerizer/secrets/grafana-admin (change it in Grafana, or set up sign-in in grafana.env).

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Organization scans: what a scan does and where its results go.
  • Rule review: approve what the learning loop proposes.
  • How it works: how applications are assessed and what is generated.

docs.title: Build pipelines
docs.text:
Containerizer generates the Dockerfiles that build an application's components, and builds them itself during a scan. For the application team to build the images themselves, from their own repository, it also generates a container image build pipeline for the CI system the code lives on: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI/CD or Azure Pipelines.

The pipeline is made without an LLM, from what the assessment generated: the same Dockerfiles, the same image names as the generated Kubernetes manifests, and the same tag scheme the sandbox's GitOps image automation follows. Containerizer never writes to the repository: you get the files, or a patch to apply with git am, and open the pull request yourself.

docs.title: Where to get it
docs.text:
• The results page: the application's Build pipeline box. Administrators, operators and the application's product owners see where the code lives, the files the pipeline adds, Download .patch, the same files as a .tar.gz, how to apply it and the files themselves as a diff. Choose another provider or signing there. Everyone else sees that the pipeline exists.
  • The output repository of an organization scan: <organization>/<project>/<repository>/pipeline/, next to the generated manifests. pipeline/<provider>/ mirrors the application's repository: copy its contents to the repository root. pipeline/README.md says what to do.
  • The command line, on a checkout:
containerizer pipeline <app-path> [--provider github|gitlab|azure-devops] [--registry R] \
    [--sign none|keyless|key] [--out DIR] [--patch]

Without --patch it writes DIR/pipeline/<provider>/...; with --patch a git am patch made on a scratch copy of the checkout's HEAD commit and checked by applying it to another clean copy.

Role The Build pipeline box Downloads (/admin/build-pipeline/<id>.patch, .tar.gz) Admin, Operator Everything Every application Product owner Everything, for the applications of their products Those applications Viewer, anyone without sign-in That it exists (and for which provider, from the repository URL) No access

docs.title: Which provider
docs.text: The provider comes from, in this order: the organization scan that has the repository (its Provider: GitHub, GitLab or Azure DevOps, also self-hosted ones through its API URL: GitHub Enterprise Server, GitLab self-managed, Azure DevOps Server / TFS); then the repository URL: github.com, *.ghe.com or a host named github/ghe; gitlab.com or a host named gitlab; dev.azure.com, *.visualstudio.com, or a URL with /_git/ or /tfs/. When neither tells, all three are offered (the output repository gets all three folders, the results page a download per provider). --provider or the box's provider list overrides it.

docs.title: What it adds to the repository
docs.text:
File containerizer/<component>/Dockerfile The generated Dockerfile, as the scan built it containerizer/<component>/Dockerfile.dockerignore The generated context filter, plus containerizer/ containerizer/README.md The components, images, what to set up first, the pins .github/workflows/containerizer-images.yml GitHub Actions .gitlab-ci.yml, or containerizer.gitlab-ci.yml GitLab CI/CD: when the repository has a .gitlab-ci.yml, a file to include: from it (add include: [{local: containerizer.gitlab-ci.yml}], and the stage build if your stages: list lacks it) azure-pipelines.containerizer.yml Azure Pipelines

For an application in a subfolder of its repository, the containerizer/ folder is in that subfolder; the CI file is at the repository root. If the application already has an entry called containerizer, the folder is containerizer-build/.

The build context is the application's folder, as in the scans (docker build -f <generated>/<component>/Dockerfile <application folder>): the generated Dockerfiles copy paths relative to it. Dockerfile.dockerignore next to the Dockerfile is the context filter: BuildKit (the default builder of current Docker, and of all three pipelines) reads <Dockerfile>.dockerignore instead of the context's .dockerignore. It leaves out bin/, obj/, node_modules/, secrets files and the pipeline's own containerizer/ folder. Build locally the same way:

DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 docker build -f containerizer/<component>/Dockerfile .

docs.title: What the pipeline does
docs.text:
Pull / merge requests The default branch Build Yes, each changed component Yes, each changed component SBOM (Syft, CycloneDX JSON) Kept as a pipeline artifact Kept as an artifact (and attested to the image when signing) Vulnerability scan (Trivy) Fails the job on the gate's severities Fails the job before anything is pushed Push No 1.<yyyymmdd>.<hhmm> and sha-<commit> (and latest when asked) Sign (cosign) No Optional: keyless or with a key
  • Monorepos: one job per component. A component is rebuilt when its project folder, the folders of the projects it references, the application folder's shared build files (Directory.Build.props, global.json, NuGet.config, root package.json, ...) or its own containerizer/<component>/ files change. GitHub: a first job compares the push or pull request with its base and starts the components that changed (a change to the workflow, a new branch or a manual run builds all). GitLab: rules: changes: per job. Azure Pipelines has no per-job path filters: the trigger's path filter is the union, and every component is built.
  • Scanning uses the security gate's settings (rules/60-security.yaml scan): it fails on fail_on and above (default CRITICAL), only for vulnerabilities with a fix (ignore_unfixed). Change it per repository without editing the file: GitHub repository variables CONTAINERIZER_TRIVY_SEVERITY and CONTAINERIZER_TRIVY_IGNORE_UNFIXED, GitLab CI/CD variables or Azure pipeline variables TRIVY_SEVERITY and TRIVY_IGNORE_UNFIXED. Trivy and Syft run as containers that read the image from the job's Docker daemon (on GitLab: from the Docker-in-Docker service), so nothing is installed on the runner.
  • The image is <registry>/<app>/<component>, the name in the generated manifests. The registry is the organization scan's Registry setting when it has one; otherwise GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io/<owner>), the GitLab project's registry ($CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE), or on Azure a placeholder (REPLACE-ME.azurecr.io) that fails the push job with a message until you set it. The variable CONTAINERIZER_REGISTRY overrides it in each provider.
  • Tags: 1.<yyyymmdd>.<hhmm> (UTC, when the pipeline started) is the same semver scheme as the scans' own images, and sha-<first 12 characters of the commit>. latest is off by default (CONTAINERIZER_PUSH_LATEST=true).

docs.title: GitHub Actions
docs.text:
• permissions: {} for the workflow, and per job only what it needs: contents: read for the change detection and the pull request builds; the push job adds packages: write (only when the registry is GitHub Container Registry) and id-token: write (only with keyless signing). Pull requests from forks get no secrets, and the pull request job uses none.
  • GitHub Container Registry: nothing to set up, the job's GITHUB_TOKEN pushes. After the first push, link each package to the repository (package settings) and make it public, or give the cluster a pull secret.
  • Another registry: repository secrets CONTAINERIZER_REGISTRY_USERNAME and CONTAINERIZER_REGISTRY_PASSWORD; the repository variable CONTAINERIZER_REGISTRY for another registry or path.
  • Key-based signing: secrets COSIGN_PRIVATE_KEY (the contents of cosign.key) and COSIGN_PASSWORD.
  • Actions are pinned by full commit SHA with the version in a comment (actions/checkout, actions/upload-artifact; the rest is plain docker). Checkouts do not keep the token (persist-credentials: false). Protect the default branch so that only reviewed changes publish images.

docs.title: GitLab CI/CD
docs.text:
• The jobs run docker:<version>-cli with a docker:<version>-dind service (both pinned by digest): the runner needs a privileged Docker executor (GitLab.com's hosted runners have one).
  • The project's registry: nothing to set up, the job token (CI_REGISTRY_USER, CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD) pushes. Another registry: CI/CD variables CONTAINERIZER_REGISTRY_USER and CONTAINERIZER_REGISTRY_PASSWORD, protected and masked, and CONTAINERIZER_REGISTRY.
  • Push jobs run only for the default branch when it is protected ($CI_COMMIT_REF_PROTECTED); merge request jobs never push, and protected variables do not reach them.
  • Keyless signing: the push jobs get an id_tokens: SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN (audience sigstore); the merge request jobs do not. Key-based: a protected File variable COSIGN_PRIVATE_KEY and a masked COSIGN_PASSWORD.
  • The template jobs set their variables on the jobs only, so an including .gitlab-ci.yml is not changed.

docs.title: Azure Pipelines
docs.text:
• Push with a Docker Registry service connection named containerizer-registry (Project settings → Service connections; change the name in the registryConnection variable): Docker@2 logs in with it, so no password or PAT is in the YAML or the variables. Allow the pipeline to use it.
  • Create the pipeline from azure-pipelines.containerizer.yml (Pipelines → New pipeline → Existing Azure Pipelines YAML file). Azure Repos pull requests: add it as a build validation policy of the default branch (the pr: trigger applies to GitHub and Bitbucket repositories only).
  • Signing is key-based only (Azure Pipelines has no OIDC token Sigstore accepts): upload cosign.key as the secure file cosign.key (Pipelines → Library) and set the secret variable COSIGN_PASSWORD.
  • pool: vmImage: ubuntu-latest. Self-hosted agents: replace it with pool: name: <your pool>; the agent needs Linux, bash and Docker. Tasks are pinned to their major version (Docker@2, DownloadSecureFile@1): Azure Pipelines cannot pin a task by digest.

docs.title: Signing
docs.text:
--sign on the command line, Signing in the box:

  • none (default): no signature.
  • keyless: cosign signs with the pipeline's OIDC identity (GitHub id-token: write, GitLab id_tokens); Fulcio issues a short-lived certificate and the signature is recorded in the public Rekor transparency log. Verify with, for example, cosign verify --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/' --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com <image>. Not for images whose names must not appear in a public log.
  • key: cosign signs with your key (cosign generate-key-pair). The signature is recorded in Rekor unless sbom.cosign_tlog_upload in rules/60-security.yaml is false (then --tlog-upload=false). This is the same key the generated cluster/verify-images.yaml (Kyverno) can enforce.

When signing, the SBOM is also attached to the image as a signed CycloneDX attestation (cosign attest --type cyclonedx). cosign is the release binary, checked against the release's SHA-256.

docs.title: The sandbox and GitOps
docs.text:
The generated GitOps files follow new images by tag: Flux's gitops/flux/git/image-automation.yaml (an ImageRepository and an ImagePolicy per component, semver range >=1.0.0, and an ImageUpdateAutomation that writes the new tag to the kustomization.yaml setters of the output repository), and the Argo CD Image Updater annotations (semver tags ^v?\d+\.\d+\.\d+$). The pipeline's version tag 1.<yyyymmdd>.<hhmm> is that scheme, the same as the scans' own pushes (org.default_tag), so:

  1. a merge to the default branch pushes <registry>/<app>/<component>:1.20261101.1530;
  2. Flux sees it within the ImageRepository interval (10 minutes) and commits the tag to the output repository within the automation interval (30 minutes); the sandbox then rolls it out.

This needs the pipeline and the generated manifests to use the same registry: the organization scan's Registry setting, which is the pipeline's default. The sha-<commit> tag does not match the policy and is never rolled out by itself: it is for finding the image of a commit. No pipeline step writes to the output repository.

docs.title: Pins and updates
docs.text:
What Pinned to Trivy aquasec/trivy:0.67.2@sha256:e2b22eac59c02003d8749f5b8d9bd073b62e30fefaef5b7c8371204e0a4b0c08 (the security gate's version) Syft anchore/syft:v1.33.0@sha256:f94e5d9fce1f2278491a8e3a63bd5f6ddb81fdfdbb8bf7a1637565c1d5344357 (the SBOM generator's version) Docker CLI and Docker-in-Docker (GitLab) docker:29.9.2-cli@sha256:5e6baf67…, docker:29.9.2-dind@sha256:9e79b879… actions/checkout 3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 (v7.0.1) actions/upload-artifact cf430e030ddbb5b0abf93d22962f4752f3646cd9 (v7.0.2) cosign v2.6.1, cosign-linux-amd64 SHA-256 064954c5d8c7e3b2…

Digests are of the multi-architecture index. To update: generate the pipeline again with a newer Containerizer, or by hand: docker buildx imagetools inspect <image>:<tag> for an image's digest, git ls-remote https://github.com/<action> refs/tags/<tag> for an action's commit (a Dependabot or Renovate configuration keeps both current). In Containerizer itself the pins are in containerizer/pipelines.py; the Trivy and Syft versions come from rules/60-security.yaml, and a test fails when a version there has no digest in the code.

docs.title: How the patch is made
docs.text:
The results page makes the patch from what the scan recorded with the assessment (the generated Dockerfiles, the components' folders, which of the files the repository already has, the default branch): nothing is cloned and no LLM is asked. The patch only adds files, so it is made on an empty commit and git am applies it on the assessed commit and on later commits that do not have these files (the box warns when the scan found one of them already). If one exists, use the .tar.gz and merge by hand. containerizer pipeline --patch makes it on the checkout's HEAD commit and checks it with git am on a clean copy.

An assessment made before this feature, or by containerizer assess (which generates nothing), has no build pipeline: scan the repository again, or run containerizer pipeline on a checkout.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text:
• It does not run on Windows runners: Windows containers (Dockerfile.windows) are not included.
  • It does not include the scan's last-minute changes that are not in the generated Dockerfile at assessment time (the security gate's OS package upgrades); the output repository's pipeline/ copy does have them. The pipeline's own scan catches what they fixed.
  • It is not tested on GitHub, GitLab or Azure DevOps by Containerizer's CI: the files are checked against the providers' schemas and linters, and the build, SBOM, scan, push and key-based signing steps are run locally with Docker (docs: the tests in tests/test_pipelines.py).

docs.title: Dev database backups for the sandbox
docs.text:
Many applications don't start without their database. Operators can upload a backup of an application's development database (SQL Server, PostgreSQL or MySQL) on the admin pages, together with instructions for the AI on how to point the application at it. The next scan of the application restores the backup into a database that runs next to the application in the sandbox namespace, and sets the application's connection settings. The application's code is not changed: only the generated Kubernetes manifests are.

On the appliance, the backup's engine must be on under Admin → Lab services. SQL Server is on by default. An app without a backup gets an empty database of its own on the lab's server instead.

Engine Files Restored with SQL Server .bak made with BACKUP DATABASE ... TO DISK, compressed or not RESTORE DATABASE ... WITH MOVE PostgreSQL pg_dump custom format (-Fc), or a plain SQL dump (.sql, .sql.gz) pg_restore, or psql MySQL mysqldump or mariadb-dump output (.sql, .sql.gz) mysql

The file's first bytes decide what it is: TAPE or MSSQLBAK (SQL Server), PGDMP (pg_dump custom format), or the dump header -- PostgreSQL database dump, -- MySQL dump or -- MariaDB dump (also inside a gzip file). A plain dump made from another database name is restored into the name you give. For PostgreSQL and MySQL, its CREATE DATABASE, USE and \connect lines are left out.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
operator ──upload backup + instructions──> web UI ──> /var/lib/containerizer/devdb/<sha256>.<bak|dump|sql|sql.gz>
                                           └──> DevDatabase row (name, size, SHA-256, instructions, who)
scan worker ──reads DevDatabase──> builds <registry>/<app>/devdb:<tag> (backup inside) ──push──> registry
            └──> generated manifests: devdb Deployment + Service + NetworkPolicy, app env → devdb
  1. Upload (Admin → Dev databases, admins and operators). The file is streamed to disk, so it is never held in memory. The page checks the session, the role and the Origin header before it reads the request body. It checks the form's CSRF token, which is the first field, before it writes any of the file. The file must start with the signature of the selected engine (see above). It is stored under its SHA-256, readable only by the web UI and the scan worker, and the web UI never serves it back. The size limit is 2048 MB.
  2. Instructions. The form starts from a template. Name the setting that holds the connection string (for example ConnectionStrings:Shop), test users, and anything else the AI needs. Never put a password here. You can edit the instructions later without uploading the file again.
  3. The scan. When an application has a backup, the scan:
  4. checks the file against its SHA-256;
  5. builds an image that contains the backup, FROM mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server:2025-latest, postgres:18-alpine or mysql:8.4 (override them with devdb: <engine>: in rules/images.yaml). SQL Server 2025 restores backups from older versions too (SQL Server 2008 and later), and upgrades the database as it restores it;
  6. pushes the image as <registry>/<app>/devdb:<tag>, also tagged sha-<first 12 of the SHA-256>.

Each time the database pod starts, it: - restores the backup. SQL Server moves every data and log file into its data volume. PostgreSQL and MySQL restore it through the image's own /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d, while the server listens only on its local socket; - creates the user app, which owns the restored database and nothing else. On SQL Server it is a member of db_owner, not sysadmin. On PostgreSQL it owns the database, and the dump is restored as app without the dump's owners and grants. On MySQL it has all rights on that database only, and root can log in only from inside the container; - only then reports ready, because it listens on TCP only after the restore.

Nothing is kept on a persistent volume. The database is a disposable copy, and it is restored again whenever its pod starts. 4. The application's settings. - With the LLM (Ask the LLM on the scan): the AI reads the instructions and the configuration the scan found. It answers with environment variables written as templates (only {host} {port} {database} {user} {password}). Every answer is validated, and anything that contains a literal password, a $(...) reference or an unknown placeholder is dropped. - Without the LLM (or when its answer has nothing usable): every connection string the scan found in appsettings*.json points at the database. If it found none, the scan sets ConnectionStrings__DefaultConnection.

The password is never written into a manifest. The container gets CZ_DEVDB_PASSWORD from the Secret devdb, and the connection string refers to it with Kubernetes' $(CZ_DEVDB_PASSWORD) expansion.

These settings replace any secret reference with the same name that the generator made for the connection string. devdb/README.md in the generated folder lists what was set, and why.

docs.title: What runs in the sandbox
docs.text:
Object What it does Deployment devdb One replica, Recreate strategy. Pod Security "restricted": runs as a non-root user (SQL Server 10001, PostgreSQL 70, MySQL 999), read-only root filesystem, all capabilities dropped, no privilege escalation, RuntimeDefault seccomp, no service account token. A 4 GiB emptyDir for the data folder and small ones where the server writes its socket and temporary files. Memory: SQL Server 2 to 3 GiB, PostgreSQL 256 MiB to 1 GiB, MySQL 512 MiB to 1 GiB (fits the namespace LimitRange; the ResourceQuota counts it). Service devdb The engine's port (1433, 5432 or 3306), so the application connects to devdb. NetworkPolicy devdb Ingress on that port only from the application's own pods (app.kubernetes.io/part-of); egress to DNS only. Password + ExternalSecret devdb, devdb-admin External Secrets Operator's Password generator creates the app and admin (sa, postgres or root) passwords in the cluster, once (refreshInterval: "0"). They never leave the cluster and need nothing in the secret store (external-secrets.md).

The Argo CD AppProject allows exactly these kinds, because they are part of the generated set.

Two details of the SQL Server image:

  • setcap -r /opt/mssql/bin/sqlservr. The SQL Server binary carries the file capability cap_net_bind_service. Linux refuses to start a binary like that in a container that drops all capabilities ("Operation not permitted"). The server listens on 1433, so it doesn't need the capability, and the image removes it instead of adding the capability back to the pod.
  • MSSQL_PID=Developer. SQL Server Developer edition is free for development and test use, and not licensed for production. These databases only run in the sandbox.

docs.title: Setting it up
docs.text: Nothing to set up: the appliance keeps the backups on its data partition in /var/lib/containerizer/devdb, where the web UI writes them and the scan worker reads them. To allow larger uploads than 2048 MB, set CONTAINERIZER_DEV_DB_MAX_MB in /etc/containerizer/web.env and restart the web UI.

docs.title: Security notes
docs.text:
• The backup is data. It is stored on the web UI's volume and in the registry, inside the devdb image. Use backups with test data only. Treat the registry repository <registry>/<app>/devdb like the database itself, and restrict who can pull it.
  • What the audit log records. Uploads, instruction edits and removals go to the change history (AuditLog, table DevDatabase): engine, database name, file name, size, SHA-256 and a SHA-256 of the instructions, with who made the change and in which role. The instructions themselves stay only in DevDatabase.Prompt.
  • No security gate on this image. The security gate does not scan the database image. Its base is the engine's official image, which you can pin and update through rules/images.yaml.
  • Removing a backup deletes the stored file once no application refers to it. The next scan deploys the application without the database.

docs.title: Secrets: External Secrets Operator
docs.text:
Nothing containerizer generates is a Kubernetes Secret, and no generated file holds a secret value. Every Secret a workload, a Flux source or an image pull needs is an External Secrets Operator (ESO) ExternalSecret. ESO reads the value from a secret store and creates the Secret in the cluster. The store can be a vault, a cloud secret manager, or on the appliance a locked-down namespace of the same cluster. Git only holds the references.

What ExternalSecret Remote key Properties Connection strings and secret settings of a component <component>-secrets <namespace>--<component> one per environment variable, e.g. ConnectionStrings__Main Key and certificate files (mounted under /secrets), Kerberos keytab <component>-files, <component>-keytab <namespace>--<component> the file names Flux GitRepository credential <namespace>-git <namespace>--cz-git username + password, or identity + known_hosts Flux commit verification keys <namespace>-git-gpg <namespace>--cz-git-gpg the public keys Registry read credential (Flux OCIRepository/ImageRepository; the image pull secret of an organization scan) <namespace>-registry, the pull secret's name <namespace>--cz-registry .dockerconfigjson cosign public key for signed OCI artifacts <namespace>-cosign-pub <namespace>--cz-cosign-pub cosign.pub Sandbox root sync (sandbox/flux/bootstrap.yaml, sandbox/argocd/bootstrap.yaml) containerizer-sandbox-git, containerizer-sandbox-repo flux-system--cz-git, argocd--cz-git username + password Dev database passwords (dev-databases.md) devdb, devdb-admin none: ESO's Password generator creates them in the cluster

<namespace> is the app's namespace. Each app's HARDENING.md lists the exact remote keys and properties under Secret store keys. The <namespace>--<name> form is valid as a Kubernetes Secret name, an Azure Key Vault secret name, an AWS Secrets Manager name and a Vault path, so the same generated files work with every store below.

docs.title: Isolation: each namespace reads only its own keys
docs.text:
All ExternalSecrets use one ClusterSecretStore, app-secrets. The store names its identity, the ServiceAccount app-secrets-reader, without a namespace. ESO then authenticates as app-secrets-reader in the namespace of the ExternalSecret ("referent" authentication). So namespace shop reads the store as shop:app-secrets-reader and can get only what that identity is granted:

  • kubernetes provider (appliance, default): a Role in containerizer-secrets with get on exactly the remote Secrets of shop (resourceNames, no list, no watch). It is generated in cluster/secret-store.yaml and, for Flux, in gitops/flux/tenant.yaml.
  • Vault / OpenBao: a policy that allows <mount>/data/<namespace>--* for the namespace of the caller.
  • AWS Secrets Manager: an IAM role per namespace (IRSA) limited to secret:<namespace>--*.
  • Azure Key Vault: a workload identity per namespace with Key Vault Secrets User on its own secrets.

The reader ServiceAccount runs no pod and mounts no token. ESO asks the API server for a short-lived token of it (TokenRequest, one hour) each time it reads. Every app namespace gets the ServiceAccount from the generated security.yaml; on Flux it is in the platform-owned tenant.yaml instead, because the Git source's own ExternalSecret needs it before the first sync.

The rules behind this are in rules/60-security.yaml (secrets): store name and kind, refresh interval, key format, reader name and annotations, and the provider definitions. CONTAINERIZER_SECRET_STORE=kubernetes|vault|azurekv|aws in /etc/containerizer/worker.env chooses which store the scans write into cluster/secret-store.yaml (default kubernetes, the appliance's own store).

docs.title: Hardening checks
docs.text:
The security gate and HARDENING.md (NSA/CISA "Secrets", CIS 5.4.2 and 5.1.2) check:

Check Severity Fails when plain-secret error a Secret object is in the manifests secret-literals error a Secret, an env variable with a secret-looking name, or an ExternalSecret template carries a literal value secret-source error a workload references a Secret (env, envFrom, volume, projected volume, imagePullSecrets) that no ExternalSecret of the app produces external-secret-store error an ExternalSecret names no SecretStore/ClusterSecretStore (generators excepted), or the app ships its own store

The Argo CD AppProject does not allow the Secret kind, so a Secret added to the app repository later fails to sync. A component that needs a different Secret source declares a waiver in its exception (containerizer.io/waives), and the waiver appears in the report.

docs.title: The appliance sandbox
docs.text:
The appliance installs ESO 2.14.0 in its k3s cluster at boot. The chart is part of the OS image, checked against its digest, and the images are pinned by digest. PushSecret, ClusterExternalSecret and ClusterGenerator are switched off. Every 2 minutes cz-sandbox:

  1. creates namespace containerizer-secrets (Pod Security "restricted", a ResourceQuota of zero pods, so nothing can run next to the values) and ClusterSecretStore app-secrets (kubernetes provider over that namespace, referent ServiceAccount app-secrets-reader);
  2. puts the read-only Git token of sandbox.env there as flux-system--cz-git and as <namespace>--cz-git for every app that the output repository deploys. Flux reads them through the generated ExternalSecrets.

Other appliance scripts write values with the helpers in /usr/lib/containerizer/lib/secret-store.sh:

k() { k3s kubectl "$@"; }; . /usr/lib/containerizer/lib/secret-store.sh
cz_store_put shop--web ConnectionStrings__Main='Server=db;...'   # or key=@file
cz_store_grant some-platform-namespace some-key                  # app namespaces get theirs from tenant.yaml

cz_store_put uses server-side apply with its own field manager (--manager NAME), so two writers can own different keys of the same remote Secret without removing each other's. The values reach kubectl on standard input, never on a command line. To set a component's secret settings by hand on the appliance, as root:

kubectl -n containerizer-secrets create secret generic shop--web \
  --from-literal=ConnectionStrings__Main='Server=...' --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

k3s encrypts Secrets at rest (secrets-encryption: true), and the audit policy logs Secret access at metadata level only.

docs.title: Real clusters
docs.text: Install ESO (the Helm chart), apply one app's cluster/secret-store.yaml (the store is the same for every app; the Role in it is per app), and put the remote keys from HARDENING.md in the store. Then deploy as usual. To use another backend, set CONTAINERIZER_SECRET_STORE for the scans, or edit the store. The app manifests stay the same.

docs.title: HashiCorp Vault or OpenBao
docs.text:
secrets.providers.vault in the rules (KV version 2 at secret/, Kubernetes auth at kubernetes/):

apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ClusterSecretStore
metadata: {name: app-secrets}
spec:
  provider:
    vault:
      server: https://vault.example.com:8200
      path: secret
      version: v2
      auth:
        kubernetes:
          mountPath: kubernetes
          role: app-secrets
          serviceAccountRef: {name: app-secrets-reader, audiences: [vault]}   # no namespace: the caller's

On the Vault side, one role for every namespace, and a policy templated on the caller's namespace so shop reads only secret/data/shop--*:

ACCESSOR=$(vault auth list -format=json | jq -r '."kubernetes/".accessor')
vault policy write app-secrets - <<EOF
path "secret/data/{{identity.entity.aliases.$ACCESSOR.metadata.service_account_namespace}}--*" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}
EOF
vault write auth/kubernetes/role/app-secrets bound_service_account_names=app-secrets-reader \
  bound_service_account_namespaces='*' audience=vault policies=app-secrets token_ttl=10m
vault kv put secret/shop--web ConnectionStrings__Main='Server=...'

Vault must be able to call the cluster's TokenReview API (Vault's Kubernetes auth documentation covers kubernetes_host and the system:auth-delegator binding). OpenBao uses the same vault provider.

docs.title: Azure Key Vault
docs.text:
secrets.providers.azurekv (workload identity of each namespace's reader):

apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ClusterSecretStore
metadata: {name: app-secrets}
spec:
  provider:
    azurekv:
      authType: WorkloadIdentity
      vaultUrl: https://contoso-apps.vault.azure.net
      serviceAccountRef: {name: app-secrets-reader}     # no namespace: the caller's
  • Store each remote key as one secret whose value is a JSON object, e.g. secret shop--web with value {"ConnectionStrings__Main": "Server=..."}. ESO reads the properties from the JSON.
  • Give each app namespace its own user-assigned managed identity. Add a federated credential for subject system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:app-secrets-reader, and set the identity's client id on that namespace's reader. secrets.reader.annotations / readerAnnotations in the rules set one client id for all namespaces; use a kustomize patch per app for one identity each.
  • Grant Key Vault Secrets User to each identity on its own secrets only (role assignments scoped to .../vaults/<vault>/secrets/<namespace>--<name>), or give each app its own vault. A vault-wide assignment lets every namespace read every key.

docs.title: AWS Secrets Manager
docs.text:
secrets.providers.aws (IRSA role of each namespace's reader):

apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ClusterSecretStore
metadata: {name: app-secrets}
spec:
  provider:
    aws:
      service: SecretsManager
      region: eu-north-1
      auth:
        jwt:
          serviceAccountRef: {name: app-secrets-reader}  # no namespace: the caller's
  • The reader of each namespace carries eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn. The rules template it as arn:aws:iam::<account>:role/app-secrets-{namespace}, so create one IAM role per app namespace, trusted by the cluster's OIDC provider for system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:app-secrets-reader.
  • Allow that role secretsmanager:GetSecretValue (and DescribeSecret) on arn:aws:secretsmanager:<region>:<account>:secret:<namespace>--* only.
  • Store each remote key as a JSON secret (shop--web → {"ConnectionStrings__Main": "..."}).

docs.title: Other stores
docs.text: Any ESO provider works: add it under secrets.providers, keep the store named app-secrets, and, where the provider supports it, name app-secrets-reader without a namespace so each namespace keeps its own identity. A namespaced SecretStore per app (secrets.store.kind: SecretStore) is the alternative when a provider has no referent authentication. Apply it in each app namespace, and drop the namespaces from its references (a namespaced store may only refer to its own namespace).

docs.title: Java and Node.js
docs.text: The rule engine assesses Java (Maven and Gradle, Spring Boot, Quarkus, Micronaut, plain JVM programs and WAR files) and Node.js (npm, yarn and pnpm; Express, Fastify, Koa, NestJS, Next.js, Nuxt and others) the same way as .NET: rules first, every finding explained with references, the same ratings, and the same stateless requirement for an A. Nothing from the repository is built or run during the assessment.

docs.title: What is read
docs.text:
Java (containerizer/scan_java.py)

  • pom.xml: coordinates, packaging (jar, war, ear, pom), properties and ${...} references, in-repository parents (<relativePath>), inherited dependencies and plugins, profiles, dependencyManagement versions, the Spring Boot line, the Java version and the main class.
  • build.gradle / build.gradle.kts: plugins (id, apply plugin, alias(libs.plugins.x)), dependencies by configuration (string, map and version catalog notations), project(':x') references, subprojects {} and allprojects {} blocks, toolchains and settings.gradle includes; gradle/libs.versions.toml is resolved, bundles included.
  • A folder with both pom.xml and build.gradle is one project (Maven's).
  • Dependencies are named groupId:artifactId. Test-scoped dependencies (Maven test, Gradle test* configurations) are kept apart, and src/test/ is not searched by code rules.

Node.js (containerizer/scan_node.py)

  • package.json: dependencies (devDependencies kept apart), scripts and the start command, main, bin, engines.node, packageManager, library markers (exports, files, peerDependencies) and npm/yarn workspaces or pnpm-workspace.yaml.
  • Workspace packages that depend on each other become project references, so a finding in a shared package reaches the applications that use it.
  • The lockfile (package-lock.json v2/v3 or pnpm-lock.yaml) is walked from the package's own runtime dependencies: packages that install only on Windows ("os": ["win32"], not optional) and packages that compile a native addon are recorded.
  • Test files and folders (__tests__/, test/, *.spec.ts, ...) are not searched by code rules.

A front end inside a Java module (src/main/webui, frontend-maven-plugin, the Gradle node plugin, a build that writes into the module) is served by that module, like a ClientApp in an ASP.NET Core project.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text: Role Java Node.js web @SpringBootApplication with a web stack (also through a shared module), Quarkus/Micronaut/Helidon HTTP, Javalin/Dropwizard/Vert.x with a main, a WAR or EAR a server framework among the runtime dependencies and a start script, .listen() or a self-starting framework (Next.js, Nuxt, NestJS) worker a Spring Boot/Quarkus application with listeners or schedulers and no HTTP a start script and a queue, scheduler or bot package console Spring Batch, other Spring Boot applications, a declared main class a start script that runs node spa React/Angular/Vue/Svelte apps with an index.html or app tooling desktop Swing, JavaFX, SWT, Android Electron, React Native, Ionic, Tauri library Maven aggregators and BOMs, modules without an application workspace roots, component libraries, middleware packages tool command line packages (bin)

docs.title: Findings
docs.text:
Rules are in rules/12-java.yaml, rules/13-node.yaml and rules/14-java-node-common.yaml.

  • Blockers and rewrites: COM automation (JACOB, com4j, winax), Windows API calls through JNA, FFI or NodeRT with no OS check, native libraries shipped only as DLLs, the JDBC-ODBC bridge. Each has an entry in the migration assistant (rules/migrations.yaml).
  • Refactoring: Windows integrated authentication (WAFFLE, node-sspi), the Windows registry, Windows-only helper packages and dependencies, Edge.js, starting Windows programs, Java 7 or older, Node.js 17 or older, node-sass, full Jakarta EE servers (EJB, EAR) and vendor server APIs.
  • Configuration: SQL Server integrated security from JDBC, msnodesqlv8, iisnode, Windows service wrappers (procrun, WinSW, node-windows), file-only logging, schedulers that run in every replica, Quartz's in-memory store, Socket.IO without an adapter, headless browsers, Oracle Thick mode, process managers, Windows environment variables and drive paths in code.

docs.title: Stateless
docs.text:
As for .NET, an application is A only when every server component keeps its data in external services. These keep a component stateful (rated B when otherwise ready):

  • an embedded database in file mode (H2/HSQLDB file URLs, Derby, SQLite, LowDB, NeDB, LevelDB) with no server database driver in the repository;
  • an embedded in-memory database (H2, HSQLDB, Derby) as the only database;
  • HTTP sessions in process memory (HttpSession, form login, Vaadin/JSF without Spring Session; express-session's default store) or in local files;
  • uploads and data files written to the local disk without an object storage client;
  • a local Lucene index (FSDirectory, the Hibernate Search Lucene backend).

Not counted: an embedded database next to a server database driver (the deployment can choose the server one), and in-memory test databases.

docs.title: Confidence
docs.text: Java runtime dependencies that are not in rules/packages-java.yaml lower the confidence, as do Node.js native addons and Windows-only packages not in rules/packages-node.yaml (pure JavaScript packages are portable and do not count). Low confidence triggers verification and the optional LLM review, as for .NET.

docs.title: Containers
docs.text:
The scan generates Java and Node.js components the same way as .NET ones: a multi-stage Dockerfile that uses the application folder as build context, a hardened Kubernetes manifest (non-root, read-only root file system, no capabilities, seccomp, resource limits, NetworkPolicy) and a plan.json that explains every non-default decision. Base images are in rules/images.yaml, with patched tags pinned in rules/images.lock.yaml.

Java (containerizer/gen_jvm_node.py)

Java line the version the build declares (maven.compiler.release, java.version, toolchains), rounded up to an LTS line: 8, 11, 17, 21 or 25. The build and the runtime use the same line. Build Maven from the image (-pl <module> -am from the in-repository aggregator), or the repository's Gradle wrapper (bootJar, quarkusBuild, installDist, shadowJar, war). Tests are skipped in the image build. A CA bundle passed as the ca build secret is added to the build JDK; HTTPS_PROXY is passed to Maven and Gradle. Runtime distroless Java 17/21/25, or the Temurin JRE for Java 8 and 11, as uid 65532. Spring Boot and executable jars or WARs run with java -jar; Quarkus runs its fast-jar; a plain program runs its main class with its dependencies on the class path; a WAR without an embedded server is unpacked into Tomcat 9 (javax.servlet) or 10.1 (jakarta.servlet). Port SERVER_PORT, QUARKUS_HTTP_PORT, MICRONAUT_SERVER_PORT or PORT set to 8080; a port fixed in code is kept. Probes Spring Boot Actuator liveness and readiness groups (not when Spring Security protects them and the code does not open them), SmallRye Health, Micronaut management; a TCP probe otherwise. The context path is taken into account. Configuration Windows paths in application.properties/.yml (and the prod profile) are overridden through environment variables (Spring relaxed binding, MicroProfile names) to folders under /data. Credentials (passwords, secrets, JDBC URLs) become optional Secret references; a ${DB_PASSWORD} placeholder references that variable. Memory -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75, request 512Mi, limit 1Gi.

Node.js

Node.js line the newest supported LTS line (22 or 24) that engines.node allows. Install npm ci, pnpm install --frozen-lockfile or yarn install (classic or Berry, with the node-modules linker) through corepack, at the workspace root. Packages with native addons build on the full Debian image (Python, make, g++). Build the build script of the package and of the in-repository packages it uses, dependencies first (pnpm orders a filtered run itself). devDependencies are pruned afterwards with npm and pnpm (not in pnpm or yarn workspaces, where that means a reinstall). Start the production start script (start:prod, start, ...), parsed without a shell: node <file>, a package's command (next start, resolved at build time to the file it runs), nest start and nx serve mapped to their compiled output.
