Without a start script: server.js, main or index.js. A start command that needs a shell runs with npm run on the slim image. Runtime distroless Node.js as uid 65532, NODE_ENV=production, PORT=8080, HOST=0.0.0.0. Probes a /health-style route on the application object, a NestJS Terminus controller; a TCP probe otherwise. Configuration variables listed in .env.example that hold credentials or connection URLs become Secret references; Windows paths in node-config files (config/default.json) are overridden with NODE_CONFIG.

Single-page apps build with the repository's package manager and are served by unprivileged nginx.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: The scan builds and runs Java and Node.js images hardened, as for .NET. Failure rules in rules/50-failures.yaml recognise Java and Node.js build and start failures: a dependency that needs a newer Java line, Maven version enforcement (the build switches to the Maven wrapper), a lockfile out of sync, missing native toolchains, the V8 heap during builds, a devDependency needed at run time, writes to read-only folders, and databases, brokers, config servers or variables that only the real environment provides. Unknown failures go to the optional LLM, which gets a language-specific evidence pack and plan vocabulary; what works is learned for review, as for .NET.

docs.title: Organization scans
docs.text: Organization scans treat Java and Node.js repositories like .NET ones: each buildable component (a Maven or Gradle jar/war, a Node.js server or single-page app) gets its Dockerfile, hardened manifests and GitOps entries. Repositories without .NET, Java or Node.js code are still skipped and say so.

docs.title: Validation corpus
docs.text:
bench/realworld.yaml holds 17 public Java (jv-*) and Node.js (nd-*) repositories, pinned to a commit, with ratings and roles judged by reading each repository. Run them with python -m containerizer.realworld --root <dir> --clone jv-petclinic nd-ghost ....

All 17 match. Jenkins and Ghost are the two that need a volume for state that is easy to miss: Jenkins keeps jobs, configuration and history in its home directory (JENKINS_HOME, by default ~/.jenkins), found by java-app-home-directory; Ghost unpacks uploaded themes into content/themes, which its S3 adapter does not cover, found by node-local-extensions.

Images were built and run hardened (verify) for Spring PetClinic, Quarkus rest-heroes (Java 25), PiggyMetrics account-service (Java 8), Halo, RealWorld Express (Nx), Node-RED, Uptime Kuma and the React RealWorld single-page app; each either served or stopped only at a database or config server it needs from the real environment. Taxonomy's build needs its runtime variables (reported as a finding) and the NestJS RealWorld app fails on its own outdated dependencies.

docs.title: Lab services
docs.text:
Many applications need a database, a cache, a message broker, object storage or a file server before they start. On the appliance, administrators can turn on lab services: backing services that run in the sandbox cluster next to the apps that the organization scans deploy. When an app depends on a service that is on, the generated manifests point the app at it. The app's code does not change: only its configuration, through environment variables.

Service What runs What each app gets On by default SQL Server SQL Server 2025, Developer edition (the appliance's own pinned image) Its own database and login, owner of that database only yes PostgreSQL PostgreSQL 18 Its own database and role, owner of that database only no Redis Redis 8.8 Its own instance and password no S3 object storage Versity S3 Gateway (Apache 2.0) Its own S3 endpoint and access key no Azure Blob storage Azurite, blob service Its own Azurite endpoint and account key no MySQL MySQL 8.4 LTS Its own database and user, with all rights on that database only no MongoDB MongoDB 8.0 Community Its own database and user, dbOwner of that database only no RabbitMQ RabbitMQ 4.4 Its own virtual host and user, with rights on that virtual host only no Kafka Apache Kafka 4.4, one node (KRaft) Its own broker no SFTP SFTPGo, SFTP only Its own SFTP server, user and password, on port 22 no

MongoDB 8.0 does not start on Linux 6.19 and newer (a tcmalloc bug, SERVER-121912). The appliance runs Debian 13's kernel, so this only matters on a self-built cluster with a newer kernel.

SQL Server is on by default because the appliance already ran SQL Server for dev database restores. An app with an uploaded backup (SQL Server, PostgreSQL or MySQL) still gets that backup restored next to it, and the lab's server for that engine is not used for it. Turning the engine off stops those restores too.

docs.title: Turn a service on or off
docs.text: Administrators turn each service on or off under Admin → Lab services, with a note for the change history. A service that is on starts only when the first app asks for it, so a service nobody uses costs nothing. Turning off a service that apps use takes it from them at once (the page asks first), and the next scan generates them without it. Needed but off lists the apps whose latest scan found that they need a service that is off, and the repository's page shows the same warning: turn the service on, then scan again.

docs.title: What the scan changes in an app
docs.text:
The scan decides, for each component, which services the component needs:

  • Packages, the component's own or those of the projects it references (rules/lab-services.yaml):
    • SQL Server: Microsoft.Data.SqlClient, System.Data.SqlClient, Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.SqlServer, Hangfire.SqlServer, dbup-sqlserver
    • PostgreSQL: Npgsql*, Hangfire.PostgreSql, dbup-postgresql
    • Redis: StackExchange.Redis, Microsoft.Extensions.Caching.StackExchangeRedis, the SignalR and Data Protection Redis packages
    • S3: AWSSDK.S3, Minio
    • Azure Blob storage: Azure.Storage.Blobs, Microsoft.Azure.Storage.Blob, WindowsAzure.Storage
    • MySQL: MySqlConnector, MySql.Data, Pomelo.EntityFrameworkCore.MySql, MySql.EntityFrameworkCore, Hangfire.MySqlStorage, dbup-mysql
    • MongoDB: MongoDB.Driver*, MongoDB.Entities, MongoDB.EntityFrameworkCore, Hangfire.Mongo
    • RabbitMQ: RabbitMQ.Client, MassTransit.RabbitMQ, EasyNetQ*, NServiceBus.RabbitMQ, RawRabbit*, Rebus.RabbitMq
    • Kafka: Confluent.Kafka, MassTransit.Kafka, KafkaFlow*, Silverback.Integration.Kafka, Rebus.Kafka
    • SFTP: SSH.NET, Renci.SshNet*, WinSCP

The Aspire client packages for these services count too. - Settings in appsettings.json (with appsettings.Production.json on top). Each connection string and setting is classified by its value: - Initial Catalog= or Server=host,1433 means SQL Server; - Host=...;Username= means PostgreSQL; - host:6379,abortConnect=false means Redis; - UseDevelopmentStorage=true or AccountName=...;AccountKey= means Azure Storage; - ServiceURL, AccessKey and similar keys under an AWS, S3 or Minio section mean S3; - Server=...;Uid= or Port=3306 means MySQL; - mongodb:// means MongoDB, and DatabaseName under a Mongo... section is its database; - amqp://, or host= under a key that names RabbitMQ or EasyNetQ, means RabbitMQ. So do HostName, UserName, Password, Port and VirtualHost under a RabbitMQ section; - BootstrapServers (or bootstrap.servers) means Kafka; - Host, Port, Username and Password under an Sftp or Ssh section mean SFTP.

For each service that the component needs and that is on, the scan writes the following.

  • Environment variables that override the component's configuration:
Service Settings that are overridden SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL Each connection string of that engine, from the Secret lab-<service> (key connection-string). If no connection string says which engine it is and the component needs only this database, the unclassified ones are used. If there are no connection strings at all, ConnectionStrings__DefaultConnection is set. Redis Each Redis connection string or setting (Redis:Configuration, ConnectionStrings:Cache, ...). If none is found, ConnectionStrings__Redis is set. S3 AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, AWS_REGION, and AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3, which AWSSDK.S3 3.7.300 and later read. The ServiceURL, access key, secret key and region settings that were found are overridden too. Azure Blob storage Each Azure Storage connection string, from the Secret (key connection-string). MongoDB Each MongoDB connection string (key connection-string) and each database name setting (key database). The database name has to change too: the app's user may use only its own database. RabbitMQ Each AMQP URI or EasyNetQ connection string (key connection-string), and each host, port, user name, password and virtual host setting (keys host, port, username, password, vhost). Kafka Each bootstrap servers setting (key bootstrap-servers). A SecurityProtocol setting becomes Plaintext. SFTP Each host, port, user name and password setting (keys host, port, username, password).

The whole connection string, or each part of it, comes from the Secret, so no password appears in a manifest. When no setting is found for a service the component needs, lab/README.md names the Secret and its keys. Entries with the same name that the generator made before (references to the component's own secrets) are replaced. - lab/k8s.yaml: an ExternalSecret lab-<service> for each service. It reads remote key <namespace>--cz-lab-<service> from the store app-secrets (External Secrets). The namespace's reader Role grants exactly these keys, like every other key of the app. - NetworkPolicy egress from the component to the service's port. Only the service's pods are allowed (for a per-app service, only the app's own instance), in namespace containerizer-lab. - lab/README.md lists the host names, the Secrets, which settings were overridden, and the services that were needed but off. The scan result has the same, as lab_services in containerizer.json.

docs.title: Things the scan cannot see
docs.text:
• Settings made in code. A RabbitMQ ConnectionFactory without a user name in the configuration uses guest, which the lab does not allow, and a Kafka client that sets SASL in code cannot log in to the lab broker, which has no logins. An S3 client built with new AmazonS3Client(new AmazonS3Config { ServiceURL = "..." }) uses the URL in the code. The AWS SDK reads AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3 only when the code does not set an endpoint. The same is true for Azure clients created from a serviceUri with managed identity: the lab gives each app a connection string, not an identity. lab/README.md says when no setting was found.
  • Database schema. The databases start empty. Run the app's migrations at start-up, as most EF Core apps do, or upload a dev database backup for SQL Server, PostgreSQL or MySQL.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Admin -> Lab services --(cz.LabService, audited)--> system agent --> lab-services.json
                                                                      │            │
           scan worker: needs + overrides + ExternalSecret <──────────┘            │
                                                                                   ▼
app namespace: ExternalSecret lab-<service> ──ESO──> containerizer-secrets/<ns>--cz-lab-<service>
                                                                                   ▲
lab agent (root, every 2 min) ──finds the ExternalSecrets──> creates database/login or instance,
                                                             writes the credentials ─┘
containerizer-lab: sqlserver, postgres, mysql, mongodb, rabbitmq (shared)
                   redis-<ns>, s3-<ns>, azure-blob-<ns>, kafka-<ns>, sftp-<ns> (per app)

The lab agent (python -m containerizer.labagent reconcile, containerizer-lab.timer) runs as root with the k3s admin kubeconfig. Each time it runs, it does the following.

  1. It applies namespace containerizer-lab with Pod Security restricted, a default-deny NetworkPolicy, a LimitRange and a ServiceAccount without a token.
  2. It finds the apps that asked for a service: every ExternalSecret labelled containerizer.io/lab-service. It accepts one only if it reads its own namespace's key, <namespace>--cz-lab-<service>. A namespace therefore can never ask for another app's credentials, and system namespaces cannot ask at all.

  3. For each service that is on and asked for:

    • Shared server (SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, RabbitMQ). It runs one Deployment with a data volume. The admin password (not for RabbitMQ, which rabbitmqctl manages through its Erlang cookie) is created once, in the Secret <service>-admin in containerizer-lab. For each app, it creates the app's credentials once and stores them in the secret store. Then it runs the provisioning script in the server's container (kubectl exec, script on stdin). The script is idempotent:
      • SQL Server: login <ns> (hyphens become underscores) with CHECK_POLICY = ON, database <ns> owned by that login, DENY VIEW ANY DATABASE and DENY VIEW SERVER STATE.
      • PostgreSQL: role <ns> with NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE, database <ns> owned by it, CONNECT revoked from PUBLIC on every database (including postgres and template1), and schema public owned by the app.
      • MySQL: user '<ns>'@'%' with all privileges on database <ns> only. root can log in only from inside the server's container.
      • MongoDB: user <ns> in database <ns> with role dbOwner on that database only. mongod runs with authentication on.
      • RabbitMQ: virtual host <ns> and user <ns> with configure, write and read rights on it only. The guest user is deleted, and the lab's configuration replaces the image's, which lets guest log in from anywhere. The node name is fixed (rabbit@localhost), so the data survives a new pod.

    The script runs again only when the server's pod or the password changes. - Per-app instance (Redis, S3, Azure Blob, Kafka, SFTP). It runs a Deployment, a Service and a data volume named <service>-<ns>. Their config Secret is built from the app's credentials: - Redis keeps only the SHA-256 of the password in its ACL. Commands in @admin are denied, and the append-only file is on. - Azurite's AZURITE_ACCOUNTS holds only the app's account, so the emulator's well-known devstoreaccount1 key does not work. Telemetry is off. - Versity S3 Gateway runs with the app's root key. Objects are under /data/buckets, and their metadata is in a sidecar folder. - Kafka is one node that is both broker and controller. The controller listens on localhost only, and the broker advertises the instance's Service name. Clients connect without a login: an app reaches only its own broker, so the NetworkPolicy is the access control. - SFTPGo serves SFTP only. The web admin, REST API, FTP, WebDAV and telemetry listeners are off, and the brute-force defender is on. Its user store is the app's one user, read from the config Secret. The Service listens on port 22, so a client that uses the default port works. The host keys are on the data volume, so they stay the same. - A NetworkPolicy per app lets in only that app's pods (app.kubernetes.io/part-of: <ns> in namespace <ns>), on the service's port. - When the store gets new credentials, the agent annotates the app's ExternalSecret, so ESO syncs it straight away. 4. For each service that is off, it deletes the Deployments, Services, NetworkPolicies and config Secrets. It keeps the volumes, the admin passwords and the apps' credentials in the store. Turning the service on again brings back the same data with the same passwords. Instances of apps that no longer ask are stopped the same way. 5. It writes /run/containerizer/system/lab-status.json for the page. The file holds no secrets.

Secret values never appear on a command line. They reach kubectl on stdin, the provisioning scripts reach the server's own client on stdin, and the admin passwords stay in the servers' environment (SQLCMDPASSWORD for sqlcmd, MYSQL_PWD for mysql, and mongosh reads it from the environment). psql connects over the local socket with peer authentication. For RabbitMQ, the shell's printf builtin pipes the app's password to rabbitmqctl.

docs.title: Hardening
docs.text:
The lab follows the same baseline as the generated apps (NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guide, rules/60-security.yaml):

  • Pods. They run as non-root users: SQL Server as 10001, PostgreSQL as 70, MySQL, MongoDB and Redis as 999, RabbitMQ as 100, Azurite, Kafka and SFTPGo as 1000, the S3 gateway as 10001. The root file system is read-only, with emptyDir folders (size limited) where the server needs to write. All capabilities are dropped, privilege escalation is off, seccomp and AppArmor use RuntimeDefault, no service account token is mounted, and service links are off. There are memory requests and limits and ephemeral-storage limits. SQL Server keeps NET_BIND_SERVICE in its bounding set, the only capability Pod Security restricted allows, because its binary carries that file capability. With no_new_privs the capability is never raised.
  • Network. Default deny, in and out. Each app gets an ingress rule to its own service, and lab pods make no outgoing connections. The apps' own NetworkPolicies allow only the service's pods and port.
  • Secrets. Credentials are in the secret store only, read by each namespace's own reader. The store namespace runs no pods. The admin passwords are in containerizer-lab Secrets. k3s encrypts Secrets at rest (secrets-encryption: true).
  • Images. They are pinned by digest in /usr/lib/containerizer/images.env, and an OS upgrade brings new pins. SQL Server uses the same pinned image as the results database.
  • Least privilege in the data. Each app is the owner of its own database only, and on SQL Server cannot even list the others. An app cannot reach another app's Redis, S3 or Azurite instance on the network, and the same goes for Kafka and SFTP.

Encryption in transit. SQL Server connections are encrypted (Encrypt=True) with the server's own certificate (TrustServerCertificate=True, as for the dev databases). MySQL connections are encrypted too (SslMode=Required, with the certificate MySQL makes at first start). SFTP is SSH. PostgreSQL, MongoDB, RabbitMQ, Kafka, Redis, S3 and Azurite use plain connections. The sandbox is a single-node cluster, so lab traffic never leaves the appliance: it stays on the node's pod network, and the NetworkPolicies limit who can open a connection.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
Each service keeps its data on a PersistentVolumeClaim of the default StorageClass. On the appliance, this is k3s local-path, under /var/lib/rancher/k3s/storage on the persistent partition, so the data survives restarts and OS upgrades. The requested sizes are 20 GiB for SQL Server, 10 GiB each for PostgreSQL, MySQL and MongoDB, 5 GiB for RabbitMQ, 1 GiB for each Redis and 5 GiB for each S3, Azurite, Kafka or SFTP instance. local-path does not enforce these sizes: the appliance's disk is the limit.

To delete an app's data for good, delete its volume and its credentials:

k3s kubectl -n containerizer-lab delete pvc -l containerizer.io/lab-app=<namespace>
k3s kubectl -n containerizer-secrets delete secret -l containerizer.io/lab-app=<namespace>

On a shared server, drop the app's database and login with the server's tools.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text: When it is in use, SQL Server takes 2 to 3 GiB of memory, on top of the appliance's own SQL Server. PostgreSQL, MySQL and MongoDB take up to 1 GiB each, and RabbitMQ up to 768 MiB. Each Kafka instance takes 512 MiB to 1 GiB. Each Redis, S3, Azurite or SFTP instance takes 32 to 512 MiB. Size the VM for the services you turn on.

docs.title: Local development server
docs.text:
How to set up a Debian 13 (trixie) server where Claude Code (or you) can develop Containerizer and run the whole end-to-end test suite locally, instead of pushing and waiting for GitHub workflows. Everything the workflows in .github/workflows do, except publishing (GHCR push, cosign signing, release assets, gh-pages), runs here with one command:

ci/local.sh            # the fast set, about 10-15 minutes
ci/local.sh all        # everything, including the one-shot assessment and the appliance boot test

docs.title: What the workflows need
docs.text:
Derived from the workflows themselves, so the local run matches CI:

Workflow job Needs on the server ci/local.sh job ci.yml test Python 3.12, requirements.txt, pytest test docs.yml build mkdocs==1.6.1, mkdocs-material==9.8.0 docs ci.yml containerizer, containerizer-head Python, git (the composite action is python -m containerizer check) gate ci.yml action-selftest git, network access to github.com/onek8s/containerization-challenge selftest security.yml gate Docker; Trivy and Grype run as containers (aquasec/trivy, anchore/grype, pinned in rules/60-security.yaml) security ci.yml sql Docker, mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server:2025-latest, requirements-sql.txt (pymssql) sql ci.yml sandbox Docker, kind, kubectl sandbox ci.yml assess-oneshot Docker with BuildKit (builds and runs every generated container), a lot of disk assess release.yml appliance Docker + buildx, KVM, qemu-system-x86, qemu-utils, ovmf, zstd, expect (the boot test changes the expired root password over SSH); the Elemental toolkit is built inside appliance/Dockerfile, so it needs no install appliance

Not needed: Node.js (the repository has no JavaScript build), Syft as a binary (it runs as the anchore/syft container), and cosign / oras unless you test sbom attach or release signing by hand.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
x86_64 only: the SQL Server image, OVMF and the appliance are amd64.

Fast set Everything (all) With Ollama CPU 4 cores 8+ cores 8+ cores, or a GPU RAM 16 GB 32 GB 64 GB on CPU, or a 24 GB GPU for a 30B model (Qwen3-Coder 30B-A3B on CPU: + 20 GB) Disk (SSD/NVMe) 100 GB 250 GB + 20-40 GB per model

The appliance boot test gives its VM all CPUs and the free memory less 1 GiB (at most 11 GiB, at least 4 GiB; SQL Server inside it needs 2 GiB), and grows the disk image to 96 GB (sparse). The one-shot assessment builds .NET images for three apps; Docker's build cache grows quickly, so prune it now and then (docker system prune -af --volumes when nothing else runs).

If the server is itself a VM, turn on nested virtualization so /dev/kvm exists: CPU type host on Proxmox / libvirt, Set-VMProcessor -VMName <vm> -ExposeVirtualizationExtensions $true on Hyper-V. Check with ls -l /dev/kvm.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Start from a minimal Debian 13 install with SSH. As root (or with sudo), once:

# a dedicated, unprivileged user for development; Claude Code runs as this user
adduser --disabled-password --gecos "" dev
install -d -m 700 -o dev -g dev /home/dev/.ssh
cp ~/.ssh/authorized_keys /home/dev/.ssh/ && chown dev:dev /home/dev/.ssh/authorized_keys

apt-get update
apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ca-certificates curl git jq make openssh-client \
  qemu-system-x86 qemu-utils ovmf zstd expect nftables unattended-upgrades

# Docker Engine with BuildKit / buildx, from Docker's repository (Debian's docker.io has no buildx plugin)
install -m 0755 -d /etc/apt/keyrings
curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/debian/gpg -o /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc
echo "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc] https://download.docker.com/linux/debian trixie stable" \
  > /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list
apt-get update
apt-get install -y docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin

# kind and kubectl for the sandbox test (ci.yml uses helm/kind-action; any recent kind works)
curl -fsSLo /usr/local/bin/kind https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kind/releases/download/v0.26.0/kind-linux-amd64
curl -fsSLo /usr/local/bin/kubectl https://dl.k8s.io/release/v1.32.0/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl
chmod 0755 /usr/local/bin/kind /usr/local/bin/kubectl

# docker: run containers without sudo (see Security); kvm: the appliance boot test
usermod -aG docker,kvm dev

Debian 13 ships Python 3.13; the workflows use 3.12. ci/local.sh creates its environment with uv, which fetches 3.12 for the user, so the system Python is left alone. As dev (log in again first, so the new groups apply):

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh      # installs to ~/.local/bin
uv python install 3.12
docker run --rm hello-world && ls -l /dev/kvm        # both must work without sudo

Without uv the script falls back to python3 -m venv with Debian's 3.13 (install python3-venv for it), which works for development but is not exactly what CI runs. If .venv-ci/ was created that way and uv is installed later, the next ci/local.sh run notices the version and recreates it with 3.12.

docs.title: Optional: cosign
docs.text:
Only for testing release signing or containerizer sbom attach by hand. The same pinned version and checksum as release.yml:

curl -fsSLo /tmp/cosign https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/releases/download/v3.1.4/cosign-linux-amd64
echo "424e2c97d0b45fd7a6b608a87f090f35633f4c23ece5f092d48bba11aaf4bbfa  /tmp/cosign" | sha256sum -c -
sudo install -m 0755 /tmp/cosign /usr/local/bin/cosign

docs.title: Optional: Ollama for the self-hosted LLM backend
docs.text:
To test --ai against a local model (the LLM):

curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh       # a systemd service on 127.0.0.1:11434
ollama pull qwen3:32b                                # or a smaller model for quick checks, e.g. qwen3:8b

export CONTAINERIZER_LLM_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434/v1
export CONTAINERIZER_MODEL=qwen3:32b
.venv-ci/bin/python -m containerizer assess examples/ci-demo --ai

docs.title: Optional: Qwen3-Coder 30B-A3B on CPU only (no GPU)
docs.text:
For a lab server without a GPU. This is for development and testing only: real environments use an external LLM, or the appliance's built-in LLM, which runs the same model and server with the settings below (on port 8082, sized from the machine's memory). ByteShape publishes quantized builds of Qwen3-Coder 30B-A3B tuned for CPUs (Apache 2.0). The model is a mixture of experts with only 3B of its 30B parameters active per token, so it is several times faster on a CPU than a dense model of similar quality. Their dense Devstral Small 2 24B builds stay under 10 tokens/s on CPUs.

Build (file) Size Quality (vs. baseline) Intel Core i7 Memory with a 32K context Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-IQ4_XS-4.20bpw.gguf 16 GB 99.0% 15.9 tokens/s about 20 GB Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-Q3_K_M-3.31bpw.gguf 12.7 GB 97.5% 18.3 tokens/s about 16 GB

The quality and speed figures are ByteShape's. Generation speed follows memory bandwidth, so a dual-channel desktop is slower than a many-channel server. Reading the prompt is slower too: the evidence packs are 5,000 to 15,000 tokens, so expect up to a few minutes per answer. LLM-heavy mode makes many calls and turns a scan into hours. Use the 4.20 bpw build when the memory is there, and stay above about 3 bpw.

Run llama.cpp's server on loopback, as an unprivileged container. The model file is read-only:

sudo install -d -m 0755 /srv/llm
cd /srv/llm
f=Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-IQ4_XS-4.20bpw.gguf
sudo curl -fL -C - -o $f \
  https://huggingface.co/byteshape/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-GGUF/resolve/0436a5b1e12e051e8a8568d56a1526734d3ed572/$f
echo "618f0a45a5a85f099106c80e44e0eb8ce9ee094b6268395b84e8b5b729f865dd  $f" | sha256sum -c -
sudo chmod 0644 $f

docker run -d --name llm --restart unless-stopped --network host \
  --volume /srv/llm:/models:ro --memory 24g --cpu-shares 256 \
  --user 65534:65534 --read-only --tmpfs /tmp:size=64m --cap-drop ALL --cap-add IPC_LOCK --ulimit memlock=-1:-1 \
  --security-opt no-new-privileges \
  -e LLAMA_ARG_HOST=127.0.0.1 -e LLAMA_ARG_PORT=8081 \
  --health-cmd 'curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8081/health' --health-start-period 5m \
  ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server-b12030@sha256:e67d88af487390098c76d7982b1761484339fa147b7e41d3c64ae1318759f78b \
  --model /models/$f --alias qwen3-coder-30b-a3b \
  --ctx-size 32768 --parallel 1 --jinja --load-mode mmap+mlock --lazy-mode off \
  --cors-origins localhost --no-cors-credentials --cache-ram 1024
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8081/health                 # {"status":"ok"} once the model is loaded
sudo grep VmLck /proc/$(docker inspect llm --format '{{.State.Pid}}')/status   # about 15 GB: the model is pinned

Why the options:

  • --load-mode mmap+mlock with IPC_LOCK and an unlimited memlock keeps the model in RAM. The file is memory-mapped, so its 16 GB is page cache, not container memory (docker stats shows only the 3 GB or so of context buffers), and without the lock the kernel drops it when the test suite's builds fill the cache, so the next answer first reads the model from disk again. --lazy-mode off keeps large tensors resident too. This build has no --mlock: it fails with invalid argument.
  • The image sets LLAMA_ARG_HOST=0.0.0.0 and LLAMA_ARG_PORT=8080. Setting the variables, instead of --host and --port, avoids a warning that they are overridden, and --health-cmd replaces the image's health check, which probes port 8080 and would mark the container unhealthy.
  • --cache-ram 1024: llama.cpp keeps up to 8 GiB of earlier prompts in RAM by default (its RSS grows from about 6 to 11 GiB and more over a scan). Review prompts rarely repeat, so a small cache is enough.
  • --cors-origins localhost --no-cors-credentials: by default any web page can call the server (the no API key is set and CORS allows all origins warning). Containerizer is not a browser, so it is not affected. The remaining warning, control-looking token: 128247 '</s>' was not control-type, comes from the model file's metadata and is harmless.

--threads N limits the CPU it takes (the default is about one thread per core). --cpu-shares 256 gives the test suite's builds the CPU first when both want it. For several scans at once (one shard of apps per process, or an organization scan with several workers), --parallel N with --ctx-size N times as large decodes N answers together for about the cost of one, since speed follows memory bandwidth; keep the context per slot (n_ctx_slot in the log) above about 20,000 tokens, use a multiple of 256 per slot to avoid a rounding warning (--parallel 3 --ctx-size 66048), and raise --memory by about 3 GB per extra slot. Restarting the container while a scan runs is safe: requests are retried while the model loads. Then point Containerizer at it. Raise the timeout, because the default of 15 minutes per call is tight on a CPU:

export CONTAINERIZER_LLM_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8081/v1
export CONTAINERIZER_MODEL=qwen3-coder-30b-a3b
export CONTAINERIZER_LLM_TIMEOUT=3600
.venv-ci/bin/python -m containerizer assess examples/ci-demo --ai

--ai asks the LLM only about server and platform components with a confidence below 0.85, and examples/ci-demo has none, so the command above checks the configuration but never calls the model. To see a real answer, scan a challenge scenario with a low-confidence component, for example freight-rates (after ci/local.sh selftest or assess has cloned the challenge repository):

cp -r .work/ci-local/challenge/scenarios/freight-rates /tmp/freight-rates
.venv-ci/bin/python -m containerizer assess /tmp/freight-rates --ai -v

Answers are cached in .work/ai-cache/ (CONTAINERIZER_AI_CACHE), so delete the entry, or point the variable at an empty folder, to make the model answer again.

To test it from an appliance VM on the same server, enter the same server URL (the server's address instead of localhost, with LLAMA_ARG_HOST set to match) and model on Admin → Source control, and allow the address on Admin → Firewall. Plain http is accepted only when there is no API key: put TLS and a key (llama.cpp --api-key, behind a reverse proxy) in front of it otherwise.

With Ollama instead of llama.cpp, run ollama pull hf.co/byteshape/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-GGUF:Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-IQ4_XS-4.20bpw.gguf and use that name as the model, with the base URL http://localhost:11434/v1.

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
As dev:

curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash        # native installer, to ~/.local/bin/claude
claude                                               # first start: choose a login method

Ways to sign in on a headless server:

  • Claude subscription: start claude, pick the Claude account login, open the URL it prints in a browser on your own machine, and paste the code back into the SSH session.
  • Long-lived token: on a machine with a browser run claude setup-token, then put export CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN=... in ~dev/.bashrc (mode 600) on the server.
  • API key: export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... from the Anthropic Console.

claude doctor checks the install. With claude on PATH, Containerizer's --ai option can also use it as its backend (CONTAINERIZER_AI_BACKEND=cli).

docs.title: Clone and run
docs.text:
# GitHub access for git push and pull requests: a fine-grained token for this one repository
# (Contents and Pull requests: read and write), or an SSH deploy key with write access
git clone https://github.com/olljanat-ai/containerizer.git ~/containerizer
cd ~/containerizer
ci/local.sh --list
ci/local.sh

The first run creates .venv-ci/ with Python 3.12, the requirements, pytest and the pinned MkDocs. Use that environment for ad hoc runs too: .venv-ci/bin/python -m pytest -q tests/test_engine.py.

Command Runs ci/local.sh test docs gate selftest security sql sandbox ci/local.sh all the above, then assess (up to about an hour) and appliance (one to two hours) ci/local.sh sql sandbox only the jobs named, in that order KEEP=1 ci/local.sh sql leaves SQL Server (cz-ci-mssql) and the web UI (cz-ci-web) running for debugging

Each job keeps going after another fails; the summary at the end lists pass / FAIL and the time per job, and the exit code is non-zero if any failed. Logs are in .work/ci-local/logs/<job>.log, and reports, SARIF files, the kind kubeconfig and the appliance images in .work/ci-local/ (git ignores .work/).

Differences from the GitHub runners, on purpose:

  • SQL Server is published on 127.0.0.1:11433 only (CI_LOCAL_SQL_PORT), and the web UI smoke test uses port 18080 instead of 8080, so nothing on the server's network can reach them, and the sql job runs while the web UI without an appliance holds 1433 and 8080.
  • The kind cluster is called cz-sandbox, as in CI; it is deleted after the test unless it already existed or KEEP=1 is set. Keep one running between runs to save a minute or two.
  • The appliance job builds, boots and tests the image but never pushes, signs or publishes it. It hands the root-owned Elemental output back to dev through a container, so it needs no sudo.
  • The gate job compares HEAD with its merge base on origin/main, as containerizer-head does on a pull request.

docs.title: Telling Claude Code about it
docs.text:
Put this in ~dev/.claude/CLAUDE.md on the server (your own instructions, not committed), so every session tests locally before pushing:

This server can run the whole CI suite locally: see docs/local-dev-server.md.
Before pushing, run `ci/local.sh` (and `ci/local.sh assess` or `ci/local.sh appliance` when the change
touches the assessment or the appliance). Use .venv-ci/bin/python for ad hoc test runs.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Use a dedicated machine or VM, not your workstation, and keep no other credentials on it. The tests build and run third-party code (the challenge apps, base images, scanner images), and Claude Code runs commands as dev.
  • The docker group is root. Anyone in it can start a privileged container and mount /, and the appliance and kind jobs need exactly that (--privileged). So dev is effectively root on this machine: that is acceptable only because the machine is dedicated to this. Do not add other users to docker, and do not give dev sudo as well; nothing here needs it after the install. Rootless Docker does not work for the appliance build or kind.
  • Docker bypasses the host firewall for published ports. -p 1433:1433 would open SQL Server to the network even with ufw or an nftables input policy of drop, because Docker inserts its own rules. ci/local.sh binds everything to 127.0.0.1; do the same in anything you run by hand.
  • Firewall: allow only SSH in, for example with nftables:
cat > /etc/nftables.conf <<'EOF'
#!/usr/sbin/nft -f
flush ruleset
table inet filter {
  chain input {
    type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop;
    iif lo accept
    ct state established,related accept
    ip protocol icmp accept
    ip6 nexthdr icmpv6 accept
    udp dport 68 accept     # DHCP client (offers and acknowledgements can be broadcasts)
    udp dport 546 accept    # DHCPv6 client
    tcp dport 22 accept
  }
}
EOF
systemctl enable --now nftables && systemctl restart docker   # Docker re-adds its own tables

The DHCP lines matter on a server that gets its address by DHCP: renewals are answered as established traffic, but a new lease (after a reboot or a lost lease) can arrive as a broadcast that conntrack does not match, and the server would lose its address. Restarting Docker restarts the containers that have a restart policy; give long-running ones you started by hand one (docker update --restart unless-stopped <name>), or they stay stopped. A kind cluster does not survive it: the sandbox job creates it again.

  • SSH: key login only. In /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/hardening.conf set PasswordAuthentication no and PermitRootLogin no, then systemctl reload ssh.
  • Ollama listens on 127.0.0.1:11434 only, and the llama.cpp container on 127.0.0.1:8081; leave OLLAMA_HOST unset unless you put TLS and a key in front of it.
  • GitHub: give the server a fine-grained token (or deploy key) scoped to this repository only, with no admin or workflow permissions, so a mistake on the server cannot change other repositories or the release workflow's secrets.
  • Claude Code permissions: on this dedicated VM it is reasonable to allow the commands the suite needs (ci/local.sh, docker, kind, kubectl, git, .venv-ci/bin/python) in ~/.claude/settings.json instead of approving each one. Keep git push behind a prompt if you want to review before anything leaves the machine.
  • The SQL Server and web passwords in ci/local.sh are the throwaway values from ci.yml; the database is recreated on every run and is reachable from localhost only.
  • Keep the OS patched: dpkg-reconfigure -plow unattended-upgrades.

docs.title: The web UI without an appliance
docs.text:
results/compose.yaml runs SQL Server 2025 Developer edition, creates the database, the schema and the three logins (cz_scanner, cz_web, cz_admin), and starts the web UI hardened, all on 127.0.0.1:

cp results/.env.example results/.env          # four strong passwords, and sign-in (docs/sign-in.md)
docker compose -f results/compose.yaml up -d --build
# http://127.0.0.1:8080/ shows the (empty) portfolio

# scan an app into it, static analysis only (mount it under its real folder name)
docker compose -f results/compose.yaml run --rm -v "$PWD/../my-app:/apps/my-app:ro" scan assess /apps/my-app

docs.title: Admin pages without sign-in
docs.text:
The admin pages need sign-in through an OpenID Connect provider. For development, a lab or your own machine, development mode skips it: set in results/.env

CONTAINERIZER_DEV_NO_AUTH=1
CONTAINERIZER_PUBLIC_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8080   # the address you open in the browser (forms check it)
# optional: who you are and your roles (admin, operator, viewer); default John Doe, admin
CONTAINERIZER_DEV_USER=john.doe@example.com
CONTAINERIZER_DEV_NAME=John Doe
CONTAINERIZER_DEV_ROLES=admin

and restart the web UI (docker compose -f results/compose.yaml up -d). Opening /admin then signs you in as that person at once. Everything else works as with sign-in: the roles decide what you see, every form needs its CSRF token, and the change history records the changes as made by that person in development mode. A red banner on every page says so. The JSON API works with API keys made on Admin → API (access tokens need sign-in).

Never on a shared network

Everyone who reaches the web UI is an administrator. The web UI refuses to start in development mode on the appliance, and when sign-in (CONTAINERIZER_OIDC_ISSUER) is set as well. Keep it on 127.0.0.1, or limit who reaches it with the firewall, as for the rest of this server.

docs.title: Building the appliance image
docs.text:
docker build -f appliance/Dockerfile --build-arg VERSION=v0.0.0-dev -t containerizer-appliance:dev .
# disk image (expandable), ISO
docker run --rm --privileged -v /dev:/dev -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock -v "$PWD/build:/build" \
  --entrypoint /usr/bin/elemental containerizer-appliance:dev build-disk --expandable --local \
  --system containerizer-appliance:dev -n containerizer -o /build
docker run --rm --privileged -v /dev:/dev -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock -v "$PWD/build:/build" \
  --entrypoint /usr/bin/elemental containerizer-appliance:dev build-iso --local --bootloader-in-rootfs \
  --extra-cmdline "console=tty1 console=ttyS0" -n containerizer -o /build containerizer-appliance:dev

A fork that publishes its own images sets --build-arg IMAGE=ghcr.io/<owner>/containerizer-appliance --build-arg SIGNER_REPO=<owner>/<repo>, so its appliances accept only its own signed releases. .github/workflows/release.yml builds, boot-tests (QEMU: firewall, DNS filter, services, sandbox cluster, registry, roll back) and, on a vX.Y.Z tag, pushes, signs and publishes.

docs.title: Lab sandbox (k3s, Flux, Git server)
docs.text:
A persistent copy of the appliance's sandbox deployment path on this server, for testing features that deploy applications to the sandbox through GitOps end to end: the same k3s, Flux and External Secrets versions and settings as the appliance, a Git server for the output repository, and what the appliance's cz-sandbox timer does. It is not the sandbox job of ci/local.sh (a throwaway kind cluster cz-sandbox): the two run side by side. The scripts are in ci/lab-sandbox/; its state lives in LAB_DIR (default /home/dev/lab-sandbox):

mkdir -p ~/lab-sandbox && cp -r ci/lab-sandbox/. ~/lab-sandbox/   # the timer runs sync.sh from where up.sh ran
~/lab-sandbox/up.sh        # install or start everything; idempotent, needs sudo; about 3 minutes the first time
~/lab-sandbox/status.sh
~/lab-sandbox/smoke.sh     # the end-to-end test below
~/lab-sandbox/down.sh      # stop, data kept (--purge: remove the cluster, Gitea and all state)

docs.title: What runs where
docs.text:
What How Reached at k3s v1.37.1+k3s1, the appliance's binary and checksum, single node lab systemd k3s-lab, config /etc/rancher/k3s-lab/config.yaml API https://127.0.0.1:6443; admin kubeconfig $LAB_DIR/kubeconfig (mode 600) Flux v2.10.0 (the appliance's install.yaml and checksum, images pinned by digest in lib.sh) k3s, flux-system External Secrets Operator 2.14.0 (the appliance's chart digest and values), ClusterSecretStore app-secrets over namespace containerizer-secrets k3s; the store is made by the appliance's own lib/secret-store.sh secret.sh <remote-key> <json-or-literal> Gitea 28.3 (rootless, pinned by digest), HTTPS with a certificate from the lab CA container lab-git, runs as dev, data in $LAB_DIR/state/gitea https://lab-git:3001/: published on 127.0.0.1:3001 and on the Docker bridge address 172.17.0.1:3001 Output repository Gitea organization lab, private https://lab-git:3001/lab/sandbox-deployments.git Traefik (k3s's, as on the appliance) NodePorts 30080 / 30443 on loopback only, default certificate *.sandbox.lab.test from the lab CA https://<component>-<app>.sandbox.lab.test through 127.0.0.1:30443 The cz-sandbox equivalent (sync.sh) systemd lab-sandbox-sync.timer, every 2 minutes, as dev systemctl status lab-sandbox-sync.timer; sudo systemctl stop lab-sandbox-sync.timer to pause it Read-only verifier for containerizer sandbox verify ServiceAccount from the output repository's sandbox/verify-rbac.yaml $LAB_DIR/verifier.kubeconfig (24-hour token, renewed every 12 hours)

$LAB_DIR/secrets.env (mode 600) holds the Gitea administrator lab-admin's generated password, a write token for the output repository (write:repository) and a read-only token (read:repository, read:organization) that Flux uses.

The Git URL is the same everywhere because the GitOps files name it: /etc/hosts maps lab-git to the Docker bridge address, CoreDNS in k3s does the same (ConfigMap coredns-custom), and Gitea is published on that address. git on the host trusts the lab CA for this one URL (http.https://lab-git:3001/.sslCAInfo in ~/.gitconfig); Flux gets it as ca.crt next to the token in <namespace>--cz-git (on the appliance the Git servers have public certificates). The appliance's cz-sandbox accepts only https URLs, so the lab uses HTTPS too.

docs.title: Differences from the appliance
docs.text:
• Images come from Docker's image store, not a registry. k3s runs with docker: true (its embedded cri-dockerd), so a pod can run any image docker build made on this host, and the manifests containerizer generates use imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent: nothing is pushed or pulled. The kubelet's image garbage collection is off, because the store is shared with the builds and ci/local.sh. Pods show up in docker ps as k8s_* containers. The appliance still pushes to its registry at localhost:5000/<path>.
  • The appliance's k3s settings are kept (servicelb off, secrets encryption, no anonymous API access), except resolv-conf, the audit log and protect-kernel-defaults, which depend on the appliance's OS.
  • Traefik is on loopback NodePorts instead of behind Caddy on 443, without the HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect.
  • Flux runs only; there is no Argo CD, so sync.sh leaves the Argo CD part out of verify-rbac.yaml.
  • The k3s system images (pause, CoreDNS, Traefik, metrics-server, local-path, klipper-helm) are pinned by the k3s release's tags, as on the appliance, not by digest.

docs.title: Firewall
docs.text:
k3s runs on the host network. Its pods reach the host (the API server, Gitea through the Docker bridge) through cni0, so the input chain of /etc/nftables.conf gets two accept rules, which up.sh adds to the file and to the running rule set (with nft add rule, not by loading the file again: its flush ruleset would also remove Docker's and k3s's tables):

    iifname { "cni0", "flannel.1" } accept
    ip saddr { 10.42.0.0/16, 10.43.0.0/16 } accept

The API server (6443) and the kubelet (10250) listen on every address and are kept off the network by the input chain's drop policy. NodePorts answer on loopback only (nodeport-addresses=127.0.0.1/32): Docker-style DNAT traffic to them would pass the forward chain, which accepts by default. Reach Traefik or Gitea from another machine with SSH port forwarding, e.g. ssh -L 30443:127.0.0.1:30443 -L 3001:127.0.0.1:3001 dev@<server>.

To open the sandbox's HTTPS entry to your own subnet instead, limit it in the forward chain first, then let k3s answer on the server's address too:

# /etc/nftables.conf, forward chain (and the same with `sudo nft add rule inet filter forward ...` to apply it now,
# without reloading the file: that would drop Docker's tables)
iifname "eth0" ct original proto-dst 30443 ip saddr != $LAB drop
iifname "eth0" ct original proto-dst 30443 meta nfproto ipv6 drop
# /etc/rancher/k3s-lab/config.yaml, then: sudo systemctl restart k3s-lab
kube-proxy-arg:
  - "nodeport-addresses=127.0.0.1/32,<server address>/32"

docs.title: Pointing a scan or a runner at it
docs.text:
. ~/lab-sandbox/env.sh
Setting Value Registry (image prefix) localhost/lab ($LAB_REGISTRY): images localhost/lab/<app>/<component>:<tag>, built and tagged locally, not pushed Output repository --output-repo $LAB_OUTPUT_REPO --output-username lab-admin, write token in OUTPUT_GIT_TOKEN sandbox.env equivalents CZ_SANDBOX_GIT_URL, CZ_SANDBOX_GIT_USERNAME, CZ_SANDBOX_GIT_TOKEN (read-only); sync.sh puts them in the store Sandbox verification --verify-sandbox --kubeconfig $LAB_VERIFIER_KUBECONFIG (or containerizer sandbox verify --kubeconfig ...) Ingress --ingress-domain sandbox.lab.test; verify with --ingress-address 127.0.0.1:30443 --ingress-ca $LAB_CA Secrets the apps need secret.sh <namespace>--<name> '{"key": "value"}'

Two things the lab does not cover yet: containerizer org has no Gitea provider (scan sources from GitHub, GitLab or Azure DevOps and write the output to the lab), and --no-push-images does not tag the gate's image as <registry>/<app>/<component>:<tag>, so for local images that tag has to be added (docker tag) by whatever replaces the push.

docs.title: The smoke test
docs.text:
smoke.sh checks the whole path without a scan: it builds localhost/lab/smoke:1 (nginx answering 200 on 8080) with docker build, writes an app smoke into a clone of the output repository in the layout containerizer org writes, generated by containerizer from examples/ci-demo with that image (smoke_app.py: lab/_/smoke/, its gitops/flux tenant, ExternalSecret, GitRepository and Kustomization, containerizer.json, and sandbox/ from write_sandbox), and pushes it. Then Flux syncs the root Kustomization, sync.sh puts smoke--cz-git in the store, the app's own Kustomization deploys it as smoke-reconciler, the pods become Ready with no Pulling event, and containerizer sandbox verify reads the result back as the verifier:

smoke/Demo.Web: healthy - 2/2 ready
sandbox health: healthy=1

smoke.sh --remove takes the app out of the repository again, and Flux prunes it.

docs.title: How Containerizer works
docs.text: Containerizer tells you whether an application can run as a Linux container on Kubernetes, explains why, and generates hardened container builds and Kubernetes manifests for the parts that can. This page explains how the assessment works and what it generates. To install and use it, start with Getting started.

docs.title: Design principles
docs.text:
• Rules first, AI last. Classification is done by a data-driven rule set (rules/*.yaml). An LLM is consulted only for components the rules are unsure about, and what it says is validated before it is used or learned.
  • Learns by doing. When unsure, the tool builds and runs the generated container, matches failures against failure rules, patches the build plan and retries. Fixes that work are proposed as rules with their evidence; once a person approves them (rule review), the next run needs no retries and no AI.
  • No application changes. Dockerfiles use the application folder as build context with their own Dockerfile.dockerignore; configuration is overridden with environment variables and volumes.
  • Secure by default. Multi-stage builds, chiseled (distroless) .NET images, non-root user, read-only application files, read-only root filesystem, all capabilities dropped, seccomp, secrets only as Kubernetes Secret references, base images pinned to a version line.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
scan ──► roles ──► facts ──► findings ──► reachability ──► confidence ──► rating
  │        rules     rules     rules        (type graph)      unknowns         │
  │                                                              │ low          ▼
  │                                                     verify (build+run) ──► report / generate
  │                                                              │ unexplained
  │                                                     Claude (validated) ──► rules/learned/
  1. Scan reads project files (.csproj/.vbproj incl. old-style and imported .props, package.json, requirements.txt/pyproject, go.mod, pom.xml/gradle, BizTalk/SQL/SSIS projects, ASP.NET Web Site projects listed in a .sln), source and configuration. Nothing from the scanned repository is executed. Java and Node.js have their own parsers (see Java and Node.js): Maven parents, profiles and modules, Gradle version catalogs and subprojects {}, npm/yarn/pnpm workspaces, and the lockfile's Windows-only and native packages.
  2. Role rules (rules/00-roles.yaml) decide what each project is: web, worker, console, spa, desktop, library, test, tool, BizTalk, SharePoint, Sitecore XP, SQL CLR, SSIS.
  3. Fact rules (rules/05-facts.yaml) extract ports, health endpoints, run-once arguments, connection strings, folders the app writes to, Kestrel endpoints.
  4. Finding rules (rules/10-runtime.yaml, 20-platform.yaml, 30-integration.yaml) detect blockers and work items with a severity: info < config < refactor < rewrite < blocker, an explanation, a fix, and whether a Windows container would be a workable stop-gap.
  5. Reachability: findings in shared libraries only count for components whose code actually reaches the offending types (a type/extension-method mention graph) and that it compiles for its target framework, and Windows-only calls guarded by OperatingSystem.IsWindows() (directly, through a helper, or at every caller) are ignored.
  6. Confidence: packages and references unknown to rules/packages*.yaml, and uncertain rules, lower a component's confidence. Low confidence triggers verification and, optionally, Claude.
  7. Rating per application: A container-ready (built on a modern stack and libraries, runs in containers with configuration only, no code changes), B minor refactoring, C major refactoring (framework port), D partial (some components must stay on Windows), E not feasible. A also requires every server component to be stateless: persistent data may live in services that are available as managed cloud services (SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, Redis, blob storage, queues), but not on the component's own disk or in its process memory. Rules that find such data carry state: local or state: memory (rules/36-state.yaml, sqlite-local, lucene-local-index): a local SQLite/LiteDB file with no server database wired up, a local Lucene/Examine index, uploads or data files written under the content root or App_Data, ASP.NET Core session without a distributed cache, and Hangfire in-memory storage. An app that is otherwise ready but keeps such data is rated B, and the report lists what keeps it stateful. Not counted: SQLite next to a server database provider (sqlite-optional), a read-only SQLite file shipped with the app, Lucene used only for text analysis, temp files and logs, and the ASP.NET Core Data Protection key ring (one PersistKeysTo* line; reported separately).

docs.title: Rules are data
docs.text:
- id: com-office-automation
  when:
    any:
      - code: 'GetTypeFromProgID\("(Word|Excel|Outlook)\.Application'
      - reference: 'Microsoft\.Office\.Interop\..*'
  severity: blocker
  category: com
  windows_container: false
  title: Microsoft Office automation (COM)
  why: Drives Word/Excel through COM ...
  fix: Replace with a document library (OpenXML SDK, ClosedXML, ...)
  refs:
    - https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/porting/

Every finding is explained without AI: why says what breaks in a Linux container, fix what to do, and refs link to the documentation or upstream issue behind it. All three are shown with the finding in the web UI and in the generated MIGRATION.md. Findings observed at run time carry the explanation and links of the failure rule that recognised them, and every non-default build decision (a plan rule, a config override, a fix learned while verifying) is listed with its reason and links at the top of the generated Dockerfile and in plan.json.

Condition primitives: sdk, tfm, package, reference, framework_ref, property, output_type, kind, role, name, path (regex on the project file's path relative to the repository root), file (glob), code / config / text (regex with optional in: glob and unguarded), readme, closure (a condition that holds for the project or any project it references, e.g. a file-system class elsewhere in the solution), references (a condition that holds for a project this one references directly), combined with any / all / not. unguarded: true skips Windows-only hits the code already keeps off Linux: a few lines after an OperatingSystem.IsWindows()/IsOSPlatform(...) check or after a call of a project helper whose body is one (bool IsWindows { get; } = RuntimeInformation.IsOSPlatform(OSPlatform.Windows), static bool IsModuleLoaded() => OperatingSystem.IsWindows() && ..., also from referenced projects), inside if (<OS check> && ...) { } or the else of if (!<OS check>), after if (!<OS check>) return/throw, inside a method/type marked [SupportedOSPlatform("windows")], or in a member/type whose every caller is guarded. Callers are searched in the project and the projects that reference it (test projects excluded), two levels deep: calls of a static member or a P/Invoke, constructions (new T(...)) and static accesses of the type for instance members. A virtual/override member, a method group, a type created through typeof/a generic method argument (DI) or subclassed has callers that cannot be followed, so the hit counts. unguarded: callers applies only the caller check (for an annotation on the type itself, as supported-os-windows does). same_file: true next to an all requires its code/config/text conditions to match in the same file (e.g. an assembly loader and an install path probe, not two unrelated files).

The scanner evaluates the target-framework part of MSBuild conditions: an item under Condition="'$(TargetFramework)' == 'net472'" (also TargetFrameworkIdentifier, GetTargetPlatformIdentifier(...), $(TargetFramework.StartsWith(...)), properties whose value is a TFM such as $(SAMPLES_TFM)) is dropped when no TFM of the project gets it, and recorded per TFM otherwise; conditions on anything else (Configuration, Exists(), OS) count as possibly true. The same holds for <Compile Remove/Include> in SDK-style projects. A consumer follows a multi-targeted library along the TFM it compiles against (NuGet's nearest framework), so a net8.0 app does not inherit the net472-only references, project references or source files of a net472;net8.0 library. C# #if branches that none of the project's TFMs compile are blanked before code rules run (NETFRAMEWORK, NETCOREAPP, NETSTANDARD, NETx_y[_OR_GREATER], NET4xx, platform symbols such as WINDOWS, and legacy platforms NETCF, MONO, SSCLI, SILVERLIGHT that no current SDK defines); symbols the project defines in any configuration (DefineConstants), #defined in the file, or unknown stay possibly active.

Properties the scanner sets on projects (usable with property:):

Property Meaning RunByBuild an MSBuild <Exec> elsewhere in the repository runs this executable (dotnet Name.dll, Name.exe, dotnet run --project ...): a build-time helper; the value is that build file RunFromSourceBy a repository script starts it with dotnet run (compiled from the checkout): a developer utility; the value is the script ReferencedBy the first project that references this one (ProjectReference): it is compiled into something else HostedBy a front-end (Node) or Blazor WebAssembly project served by a .NET project: nested in its folder, referenced by it, or writing its bundles into its folder (webpack output.path: "../Web/Scripts", "destination": "../Web/Styles", a copyfiles ... ../Web/... script; Visual Studio .esproj projects) SpaRoot on the .NET host: the folder of the nested front-end project WebSiteProject an ASP.NET Web Site project (no project file) found in this solution

ASP.NET Web Site projects (Visual Studio "New Web Site", solution entries with project type {E24C65DC-7377-472B-9ABA-BC803B73C61A} and no .csproj) are read from the .sln: the folder becomes a .NET project named after the entry, with the target framework from TargetFrameworkMoniker and the solution's ProjectReferences/ProjectDependencies of the entry as project references. Its project path is shown as <folder>/<name>.website (there is no such file).

Next to title / why / fix, a finding rule takes refs:, a list of verified https links (docs page, upstream issue, vendor statement) shown with each finding; tests/test_rule_docs.py enforces that every refactor/rewrite/blocker rule has one or is on its commented allowlist. Later files override earlier rules with the same id; rules/learned/ is loaded last.

docs.title: Migration assistant
docs.text:
For every component that is not ready (verdict refactor, rewrite or blocker), each blocking finding is mapped to a concrete Linux-compatible replacement from rules/migrations.yaml: System.Drawing → SkiaSharp/ImageSharp, WCF → CoreWCF, Windows Service → worker service, Office automation → Open XML SDK/ClosedXML, registry → configuration, Event Log → ILogger, MSMQ → a broker, and so on, with packages to add and remove, steps, checks and references. Parts with no Linux replacement (desktop UI, hardware, vendor COM SDKs, BizTalk) are marked "keep on Windows" instead of being forced into a code change.

- id: replace-system-drawing
  for: [system-drawing-core, pkg-mschart, pkg-qrcoder-gdi]
  kind: replace                    # replace | port | externalize | isolate
  replace: System.Drawing (GDI+)
  with: SkiaSharp or ImageSharp for images, QuestPDF for documents
  packages: {add: [SkiaSharp, SkiaSharp.NativeAssets.Linux.NoDependencies], remove: [System.Drawing.Common]}
  steps: [...]
  verify: [...]

The plan is also rendered as a self-contained prompt for AI coding agents (Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, ...): the findings with their evidence, the replacements in order, constraints (minimal changes, no secrets in code, non-root and read-only file system) and how to verify. The web UI shows it on the component's migration assistant with a copy button.

For a B-rated application Containerizer can also make the changes: a refactoring patch has the LLM change the code for its refactor findings, one file at a time with structured edits, then applies the patch to the assessed commit, runs the rules on it again and builds and runs the changed components. The patch is offered for download as verified (applies, builds and runs) or applies only, with how to apply it with git am; one that does not apply cleanly is never offered.

docs.title: Self-learning loop
docs.text:
For each component that can be containerized the scan:

  1. builds the generated Dockerfile (application folder as context);
  2. runs it hardened (read-only root filesystem, all capabilities dropped, no new privileges, non-root, only the writable folders mounted) and probes the health endpoint. Writable folders are host directories during the test, so apps that log only to files can still be diagnosed;
  3. matches the log against rules/50-failures.yaml:
  4. retry: patch the build plan (e.g. remove a pinned global.json, retarget an out-of-support TFM to net10.0, add Kerberos libraries, make a folder writable) and try again;
  5. external: the container works, it only lacks a database/broker/directory/identity provider — then the tool retries in a dependency-free smoke mode (Development environment, which many apps map to SQLite and simulators) to prove the app actually serves requests. For the smoke run only, appsettings.Development.json is mounted read-only (the image never contains it), relative SQLite paths are made absolute and writable, and sample input files are mounted from the repo. An app that never answers HTTP gets the same smoke retry;
  6. platform / code: a runtime finding the static rules missed;
  7. if nothing matches and the scan has Ask the LLM on, the LLM proposes a diagnosis, a regex and a plan patch; it is applied only if the regex matches the log and the patch uses whitelisted plan keys;
  8. learns what worked: plan patches → plan rules, confirmed AI failure rules → failure rules, runtime findings → finding rules, and packages of components that ran → Linux-safe packages (raising confidence next time). The run uses them right away; for everything else they wait as candidates with their evidence until an administrator approves or rejects them under Admin → Rule review. Approved rules go to your internal (private) rules repository, never into this public one (rule review).

docs.title: AI fallback (Claude or a self-hosted LLM)
docs.text: The LLM is set once under Admin → Source control & LLM (the LLM): the Claude API, or any self-hosted OpenAI-compatible server such as Ollama, vLLM, LM Studio or llama.cpp. It is asked only about components the rules are unsure of and failures no failure rule explains. Every answer is validated against its schema before it is used or learned, responses are cached, and usage and cost are tracked.

docs.title: Generated output
docs.text:
Per component: Dockerfile (+ Dockerfile.dockerignore), k8s.yaml (Deployment or CronJob, Service, NetworkPolicy, PVCs where state must persist, ExternalSecrets for every credential), plan.json (the build plan). For .NET Framework components that could work in Windows Server containers, a Dockerfile.windows stop-gap. Per app: kustomization.yaml and MIGRATION.md. Java (Maven/Gradle; Spring Boot, Quarkus, plain JVM programs, WARs on Tomcat) and Node.js (npm/pnpm/yarn; Express, NestJS, Next.js and others) components get distroless, non-root images built on the runtime line they declare; see Java and Node.js.

GitOps: every app also gets gitops/ with Argo CD and Flux configuration built from the same data:

Argo CD Flux Scope AppProject pinned to the repo, the app namespace and the generated kinds tenant.yaml: namespace, ServiceAccount, admin RoleBinding in that namespace only; Kustomization applies as that ServiceAccount Namespace CreateNamespace with the Pod Security "restricted" labels created by tenant.yaml with the same labels Sync automated, prune, self-heal, server-side apply, retries GitRepository (read-only key, optional signed-commit check) or cosign-verified OCIRepository; prune, wait Image updates Argo CD Image Updater annotations (semver, Git write-back) ImageRepository, ImagePolicy, ImageUpdateAutomation with $imagepolicy markers in kustomization.yaml

Techniques used to avoid application changes:

  • out-of-support .NET (Core 3.1, 5, 6, 7): build with the .NET 10 SDK and run on the supported .NET 10 runtime with DOTNET_ROLL_FORWARD=Major; if the old target can't be built, retarget with net10.0 in the build stage's copy of the entry project (its netstandard libraries keep their targets);
  • global.json SDK pins are removed inside the build stage only;
  • Kestrel endpoints from appsettings.json are re-pointed with Kestrel__Endpoints__X__Url;
  • connection strings and secret settings become ConnectionStrings__X env vars from a Secret;
  • folders the app writes to (logs, App_Data, Data Protection keys) become volumes;
  • Windows paths in configuration (D:\\Archive, \\\\fs01\\share) are re-pointed to /data/... volumes with Section__Key env vars; key and certificate files go to /secrets from a Kubernetes Secret;
  • Serilog file-only sinks are switched to the console (logs to stdout) with Serilog__WriteTo__N__Name;
  • custom listen-address settings ("WebhookUrls": "http://*:8085") are re-pointed to port 8080;
  • NLog folders from ${configsetting:...} / ${environment:...} with Windows defaults are re-pointed by env var, and ${basedir}/logs becomes a writable folder;
  • installed Windows tools (C:\\Program Files\\wkhtmltopdf\\bin\\wkhtmltopdf.exe) map to the Linux binary on PATH;
  • console tools with sub-commands (usage text, verb arrays, case "x":) get one CronJob per command;
  • workers that use the ASP.NET Core shared framework get the aspnet base image;
  • old netstandard1.x packages that break a linux-x64 restore (NU1605) get a portable publish;
  • corporate TLS-inspecting proxies: an optional ca build secret is honoured.

docs.title: Security gate
docs.text:
Everything here is data in rules/60-security.yaml.

Hardened manifests. Every generated pod gets the baseline: runs as the image's own non-root UID (runAsUser/runAsGroup/fsGroup: 1654 for .NET, 101 for nginx), read-only root filesystem, all capabilities dropped, no privilege escalation, seccomp RuntimeDefault, no service account token, no service links, CPU/memory/ephemeral-storage requests and limits, and a sizeLimit on every emptyDir. namespace.yaml enforces Pod Security restricted for the whole app.

Exceptions only when the app needs them, decided by rule conditions and recorded on the pod as containerizer.io/exception.<id> annotations with the reason:

Exception When What changes nginx-writable-dirs single-page app /tmp and /var/cache/nginx writable kerberos-keytab Negotiate (Windows) authentication keytab from a Secret at /etc/krb5/keytab, credential cache in /tmp native-rendering-memory PDF/image libraries (DinkToPdf, QuestPDF, ImageSharp, ...) in the component or a library it references 1 GiB memory limit, writable font cache file-uploads IFormFile / MultipartReader 1 GiB /tmp, 2 GiB ephemeral storage icmp-ping System.Net.NetworkInformation.Ping net.ipv4.ping_group_range sysctl (no NET_RAW) kubernetes-api-client KubernetesClient and similar service account token mounted, sa-token check waived privileged-port plan port below 1024 NET_BIND_SERVICE

Lint. The gate checks the manifests against Pod Security restricted (host namespaces, privileged, capabilities, volume types, host ports, privilege escalation, non-root, seccomp, sysctls) plus read-only root FS, resources, secret literals (in env, ENV and Secrets), the service account token, emptyDir limits, image tags and NetworkPolicies, and the Dockerfiles for a non-root final stage, tagged base images, ADD <url>/curl | sh and base image end of support. Errors fail the gate. A pod annotation containerizer.io/waives: "check,check" relaxes named checks for hand-made exceptions.

The gate favours accuracy over speed: it builds every image, scans it with every available scanner and merges the results, and starts it with the docker equivalent of its pod spec (user, read-only root, dropped capabilities, sysctls, emptyDir mounts) to prove the exceptions are enough; read-only or permission errors in the log fail the gate. A lock older than 14 days is refreshed first.

Vulnerability scan. The gate scans the final base image of every component and the built image; findings missing from the base are attributed to the application's own packages (upgrade them) rather than the base (bump it). It fails on vulnerabilities at or above scan.fail_on (default CRITICAL) that have a fix; accepted risks go in scan.allowlist with a reason and an expiry date. Trivy and Grype both scan, and their results are merged. When even the newest base tag still ships a vulnerable OS package with a fix, the gate upgrades just that package in the final stage (apk upgrade / apt-get --only-upgrade; chiseled images have no package manager and need a newer tag). Results go to SECURITY.md and security.json next to the generated files.

SBOM and licences. Every built image gets a CycloneDX SBOM from Syft, with NuGet licences looked up from the feed, each package checked against the licence policy (deny fails the gate, warn is reported; GPL/AGPL warn by default) and the scan's CVEs attached to the package they are in. The SBOM is stored with the results and committed next to the generated files; the web UI shows the packages of each component and a portfolio page of licences and CVEs. See SBOMs, licences and CVEs.

docs.title: NSA/CISA hardening
docs.text:
The manifests follow the NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guide and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark section 5 as far as an application repository can. Every generated app gets a HARDENING.md that lists each control as applied, applied with an exception, not applicable, or an action for the cluster operator, with the guide section and CIS number.

  • Pods: on top of the baseline above, AppArmor RuntimeDefault and a ServiceAccount per component (token not mounted). A component that needs the API gets an empty Role + RoleBinding to fill in with least privilege.
  • Network: security.yaml holds a default-deny policy for the namespace. Each component has its own policy: ingress only on its port, egress to DNS, sibling components, and the external ports the code needs. Those ports are inferred from packages, code and configuration, for example SQL Server 1433, SMTP, LDAP/Kerberos, message brokers, or a port in a connection string. Cloud metadata endpoints are always blocked, and single-page apps get no external egress. The inferred list is recorded in a containerizer.io/egress annotation and in the report.
  • Namespace: a LimitRange (defaults without a CPU limit, so pods are not throttled) and a ResourceQuota sized from the workloads with 50 % headroom.
  • Secrets: no generated file is a Secret or holds a value. Component settings, Flux source and registry credentials and the sandbox's Git token are External Secrets ExternalSecrets from the ClusterSecretStore app-secrets (remote keys <namespace>--<name>). Each namespace reads the store as its own ServiceAccount and only gets its own keys. cluster/secret-store.yaml defines the store (kubernetes provider by default; Vault, Azure Key Vault or AWS Secrets Manager by setting), and the gate fails on any plain Secret or Secret reference that no ExternalSecret produces. See Secrets (External Secrets).
  • Cluster kit (cluster/): an API server audit policy (metadata only for Secrets, full requests and responses for RBAC, every write and every exec) and a Kyverno verifyImages policy that only admits images signed with your cosign key. These are for the cluster operator to apply. The report also lists the cluster controls the generator can't set, such as etcd encryption, kubelet authentication and control plane TLS.
  • GitOps: Argo CD's AppProject allows only the Namespace cluster kind, no plain Secrets and no other source namespaces, and warns on orphaned resources. Applications sync with ServerSideApply, PruneLast and FailOnSharedResource. On Flux, the quota, LimitRange and default-deny policy move into the platform-owned flux/tenant.yaml. The synced Kustomization deletes them from its set with $patch: delete and doesn't force, so the app repository can't loosen them under the tenant's impersonated ServiceAccount.

Patched base images. rules/images.yaml lists the base image lines and rules/images.lock.yaml the newest patch tag of each line that passed the vulnerability policy, with its digest; the generator uses the exact tag. The bump policy is per image: patch releases of the same line by default, newer stable lines for nginx, and the successor line for toolchains past end of support (node, golang). .NET majors are never moved automatically. A lock older than 14 days is refreshed before the gate runs.

docs.title: Results on the challenge
docs.text: See bench/RESULTS.md for the current numbers (rule accuracy, verification results and the model comparison). The labels used for scoring are in bench/labels.yaml, written from each scenario's README and code.

docs.title: Platform migrations
docs.text: Organization scans skip repositories that already have a Dockerfile: the team containerizes them already. Many of those applications still run on Docker Swarm, HashiCorp Nomad, Azure Container Apps or a similar platform. When an administrator enables such a repository, the scan moves it to Kubernetes instead of skipping it, with the same output as for applications it containerizes itself: hardened manifests, External Secrets, an HTTPS Ingress, sandbox identity provider registration, GitOps files, and a health check in the sandbox cluster.

docs.title: Turning it on for a repository
docs.text:
1. Open Admin → Repositories and pick a repository the scan skipped with Has a Dockerfile.
  2. Choose Enabled and save, with a note if you like. The next run of the scan migrates it.

A repository that has a Dockerfile but no deployment descriptor the scan can read is containerized from its source code, as before. The repository page shows Platform migration with the platform and the files it was read from once a run has migrated it.

From the command line, containerizer org --migrate-containerized migrates every repository with a Dockerfile, and containerizer replatform <checkout> --out <folder> migrates one checkout without a scan (--build builds the images and runs the security gate).

docs.title: What is read
docs.text:
Platform Files Docker Swarm, Docker Compose docker-compose*.yml, compose*.yaml, *stack*.yml with services: HashiCorp Nomad *.nomad, *.nomad.hcl, *.hcl with a job block, Nomad job JSON ({"Job": ...}) Azure Container Apps az containerapp --yaml files, ARM templates and Bicep files with Microsoft.App/containerApps or Microsoft.App/jobs Amazon ECS task definitions (containerDefinitions) Fly.io, Cloud Foundry, Google App Engine, Render, Marathon, Heroku, Kamal recognised; translated only in LLM-heavy mode

From each service or task: the image or the Dockerfile and build context it is built from, command and arguments, settings, secrets and secret files, ports and whether they are published, replicas, CPU and memory, the health check, volumes, the schedule of batch and periodic jobs, and depends_on.

Becomes From Deployment, or a CronJob for scheduled jobs (Nomad periodic batch jobs, Container Apps jobs; a batch job without a schedule gets a placeholder one) the service or task Service, and an HTTPS Ingress when the app was reachable from outside (published port, external ingress, Traefik or Fabio tags) the ports ExternalSecret, remote key <namespace>--<component> settings whose name or value is a secret (passwords, tokens, keys, connection strings, URLs with a password), Swarm secrets and configs, Container Apps secret references, Nomad Vault templates, ECS secrets PersistentVolumeClaim (and one replica) named volumes, Nomad volume mounts, Azure Files mounts, ECS mount points emptyDir anonymous volumes, tmpfs, bind mounts (noted), /tmp Probes the health check: an HTTP probe when it calls curl/wget on localhost or is an HTTP check, else TCP or exec NetworkPolicy the ports in the settings' URLs and connection strings, HTTPS, the app's own namespace Sandbox IdP client sign-in settings in the environment, e.g. OpenIdConnect__Authority and OpenIdConnect__ClientId

Databases, caches and brokers in a compose file or Nomad job (PostgreSQL, Redis, RabbitMQ, ...) are not migrated as apps: use a managed service or the appliance's lab services. What cannot be carried over (placement constraints, scale rules, Dapr, privileged mode, the Docker socket, variables set where the stack is deployed) is listed in the app's MIGRATION.md.

docs.title: Images and the security gate
docs.text:
The image is the application's own. A service with a build section, or whose image name matches a folder with a Dockerfile, is built from the repository's Dockerfile; any other is pulled from where the platform runs it and mirrored to the scan's registry (the worker needs access to that registry; allow its host on the Firewall page). Then the same gate as for generated images runs: manifest lint, image vulnerability scan, SBOM, and a run with the hardened security context (non-root user, read-only root file system, all capabilities dropped). Findings in the repository's own Dockerfile are reported as warnings to fix there.

When the hardened run fails because the app writes to a folder, the folder the error names becomes a writable emptyDir and the run is repeated. A component that still fails is not deployed, with the reason on the repository page.

docs.title: LLM-heavy mode
docs.text:
Off by default. When it is on, platform migrations and the sandbox tester ask the LLM as often as they need:

  • descriptors the rules cannot read (other platforms, files that do not parse) are translated by the LLM;
  • every service is reviewed by the LLM before the manifests are generated: settings that are secrets, health check paths, ports, writable folders;
  • a container that fails the hardened run gets an LLM fix, for up to CONTAINERIZER_LLM_HEAVY_ROUNDS rounds (default 3);
