  • with sandbox verification (containerizer org --verify-sandbox --llm-heavy), a component that is failing in the cluster gets an LLM diagnosis in sandbox/HEALTH.md. For migrated apps its fix is applied, committed and checked again, and kept in the app's sandbox-fixes.json so later scans generate it too.

Every answer is validated before use: unknown keys, names and paths that do not fit, and secret values in settings are dropped, and what the LLM changed is marked in MIGRATION.md. It needs three switches:

  1. CZ_LLM_HEAVY=true in /etc/containerizer/appliance.env (then reboot). Outside the appliance, set CONTAINERIZER_LLM_HEAVY=true for the worker.
  2. Ask the LLM on the organization scan, and an LLM under Admin → Source control & LLM.
  3. LLM-heavy mode on the organization scan.

docs.title: LLM usage
docs.text:
Every LLM call is counted, by scan, repository, feature (assessment, build-diagnosis, dev-database, platform-migration, sandbox-tester) and model, and shown in the LLM usage row of the Grafana dashboard: calls, tokens in and out, the estimated cost, which scans have LLM-heavy mode on, and the repositories that cost the most. The repository page shows the calls of its latest scan.

Metric Labels containerizer_llm_calls_total scan, repository, feature, backend, model, result (answered, cached, failed) containerizer_llm_input_tokens_total, containerizer_llm_output_tokens_total scan, repository, feature, model containerizer_llm_cost_usd_total scan, repository, feature, model containerizer_llm_seconds_total scan, feature, model containerizer_llm_heavy_mode scan containerizer_llm_heavy_allowed

The cost is an estimate from the list prices of the Claude models. For a self-hosted LLM set CONTAINERIZER_LLM_PRICE_INPUT and CONTAINERIZER_LLM_PRICE_OUTPUT (US dollars per million tokens) in worker.env to count what it costs you; without them its cost shows as 0. Cached answers use no tokens.

docs.title: Refactoring patches
docs.text:
An application rated B needs targeted code changes: findings of severity refactor such as a certificate read from the Windows certificate store, Windows authentication, the Event Log, Win32 calls or hard-coded Windows paths. Every such rule says in plain text how to fix it (its fix:), and the migration assistant turns that into guidance. A refactoring patch goes one step further: the LLM makes the changes, and Containerizer applies the patch, checks it with the rules and builds and runs the changed components before it offers the patch as a download, with how to apply it.

Containerizer never writes to your repository: no branches, no pull requests, and the source control credentials stay read only. You review the patch, apply it yourself and open the pull request.

docs.title: Who can order one
docs.text:
Role On the application's results page Admin → Refactoring Admin, Operator The Refactoring box: the orders and their status, and Request a refactoring patch Every order: the patch, the coloured diff, Download .patch Product owner, Viewer, anyone without sign-in The orders and their status only No access

Patches contain the application's source code, so only operators and administrators see them, like the other pages that act on the source (organization scans, the LLM queue). The order button posts to the admin pages (/admin/refactoring/new), which check the role and the form's CSRF token; on a results page served without sign-in the button does not show.

The box shows on applications rated B. Choose All components that need changes or one component, and whether to also change code for configuration findings (below). The order needs the assessment's commit and the repository's clone on this machine: it works for applications that an organization scan assessed here. For anything else, use the command line on a checkout.

docs.title: What is sent to the LLM
docs.text:
• Refactor findings of the chosen components, and configuration findings in the same files (they often go with them: the LocalMachine store finding and the certificate store finding are one change). With also change code for configuration findings, configuration findings in other files too (drive paths as defaults, credentials, local folders): many of these are better solved in the deployment, and the LLM may say so instead of changing code.
  • Never blocker or rewrite findings (a port, or a part that stays on Windows), findings whose fix is to keep the part on Windows, findings in library code the component never reaches, and findings whose evidence names no file. The order's page lists them under Findings not sent to the LLM.
  • One LLM call per file, with every finding in that file, never the whole application, and at most 8 calls per order (--max-calls on the command line). A call has the rules' why and fix, the evidence lines, the file (or, when it is large, the part around the evidence lines), the component's appsettings.json, its target framework and packages, and strict instructions. Each call is kept under about 12,000 tokens so that it fits a slot of the built-in CPU LLM.

The LLM answers with structured edits, not with a diff (diffs written by LLMs are often malformed):

{"edits": [{"file": "src/Jobs/Bank/BankGatewayClient.cs",
            "search": "using var store = new X509Store(StoreName.My, StoreLocation.LocalMachine);",
            "replace": "..."}],
 "new_files": [], "package_changes": [{"action": "add", "package": "...", "version": "..."}],
 "fixed": ["cert-store-localmachine-code"], "not_fixed": [{"rule": "...", "reason": "..."}],
 "notes": "Mount the certificate from a Secret and set Bank__CertificatePath."}

Containerizer applies the edits itself: each search text must occur exactly once in the file, and only the files shown may be edited (new files stay inside the application folder). An answer that does not apply is sent back once with the errors ("not found", "occurs 3 times: include more lines"); if it still does not apply, that file is left unchanged and its findings are not fixed. The errors name the first line of the search text that is not in the file and the file's closest line. One slip is forgiven: models often get backslashes wrong when they write code into JSON ("LocalMachine\\My" in C# comes back with one backslash), so a search text that matches exactly once with every run of backslashes scaled the same way applies, with the replacement's backslashes scaled alike. Each answer may be at most 4,096 tokens plus half of the question's (8,192 at most), so a model that rambles cannot hold a CPU slot for an hour. Line endings, the byte order mark and the encoding of each file are kept. Package changes go into the component's .csproj; for other project types they are listed in the notes to make by hand.

The changes become one commit in a scratch copy ("Containerizer: <app>: <findings fixed>", author Containerizer <containerizer@localhost>), and the patch is git format-patch of it, so git am applies it as a commit with that message.

docs.title: How it is verified
docs.text:
The patch is applied to a second, clean copy at the assessed commit: git apply --check, then git am. Then:

  1. The rules run again on the patched copy. Each finding shows whether it is gone from this file, in fewer places or still found, and any new finding of the changed components is listed: check whether the patch caused it.
  2. Each changed component is built and run with the same build-and-run step as the scans (verify): the generated Dockerfile, a hardened container, an HTTP probe.
Status Meaning Queued Waiting in the LLM queue Generating The LLM is writing the changes (the page says which file) Verifying Applying the patch, running the rules, building and running Verified The patch applies cleanly, and every changed component builds and runs Applies only The patch applies cleanly, but a build or a run failed, or could not be done (no Docker, a component that is not built in a Linux container as it is): the log tail says why Failed No patch: the LLM made no usable edits, or the patch did not apply cleanly (never offered) Cancelled Skipped on the LLM queue page

A failure to reach the LLM, or a source that is gone, is a failed attempt of the queue job: it is tried again up to three times (the LLM queue page shows the error), then the order fails. A commit that is no longer in the clone (the repository moved on, and the scan worker keeps shallow clones) fails with a message: scan the repository again and order a new refactoring.

The page shows every change as a coloured diff per file, here a real patch the dev server's CPU LLM wrote for the challenge app expense-claims:

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
The order's page has Download .patch (<app>-<component>-containerizer.patch, or -all- for every component) and the steps:

git checkout -b containerizer-refactor <assessed commit>
git am --keep-cr < expense-claims-ExpenseClaims.Jobs-containerizer.patch
# or, if your branch has moved on since the assessed commit:
git apply --3way expense-claims-ExpenseClaims.Jobs-containerizer.patch

--keep-cr keeps Windows line endings in files that have them (without it git am drops them and the patch does not apply). Then review every change, build and run your tests, set the configuration the notes mention (paths, certificates, credentials as Kubernetes Secrets), push the branch and open a pull request yourself.

docs.title: Make it A
docs.text:
Make it A is one order for everything that keeps a B-rated application from A: its refactor findings, its configuration findings that name a file, and, for the server components that keep their own data, the move of that data to SQL Server (the same guidance as Make it stateless). It runs on request only: Make it A in the Refactoring box of the results page (operators, administrators and the application's product owners, with the queue's estimate), or Make all B apps A for administrators (below). A scan never orders one by itself.

Where an order of the same kind is already waiting, running or has a patch, the box offers that order (its status, Open the patch, Download .patch and the commit it was made for) instead of a new one; Request a new one is for code that has changed since.

The order is one refactor job (goal rating-a) that loops in the queue runner:

  1. Generate. The LLM is asked about every file with findings, as for a refactoring patch; the files of a stateful component that open its embedded database get the stateless guidance.
  2. Apply and verify. Everything changed so far becomes one commit for the assessed commit; it is applied to a clean copy, and the changed components are built and run.
  3. Repair. When a build or run fails, a repair round in the same job gives the LLM the compiler errors (or the run log), the files they are in and the patch, and the combined patch is verified again: at most 2 repair rounds a pass.
  4. Assess again. The patched copy is assessed with every rule. A is reached when it rates A and builds and runs.
  5. Second pass. Still B with findings left (still found by the rules, or a component that still keeps its data) and LLM calls left: one more pass on what remains, then steps 2 to 4 again. At most 2 passes.

Every LLM call of the job, retries and repair rounds included, counts against its limit of 16 calls; files beyond it are not attempted. The order page shows each pass and round (files, calls, changes, the build and run, the rating), the rating before and after (B → A: Rating A reached, or B → B: 4 of 6 fixed; still keeps data in Api (Embedded file database)), the result per finding as the rules see the final patched copy, and the one patch to download, as for any refactoring patch. Its statuses are the same (verified, does not build, does not start, ...).

Estimates. The button and the bulk page show the queue's estimate of the first pass (the size of what it sends, a typical file for each stateful component, at the speed the queue learned); repair rounds and a second pass, when needed, take more, up to the limit of 16 calls.

Make all B apps A (Admin → Refactoring, administrators): a confirmation page lists every B-rated application with what changes, its estimate, and whether it will wait for approval under the LLM queue's approval policy (Admin → LLM queue), with the total; Queue places one order per application (an application that already has the same order waiting is left alone). Nothing is queued by opening the page.

docs.title: The sandbox variant
docs.text:
A Make it A order whose patched copy rates A and is verified is deployed to the sandbox beside the original, never in its place, the way an organization scan deploys (the same code):

  • Its own name. The patched copy's folder is <app>-refactor-<job> (a DNS label of at most 63 characters), and everything that an organization scan derives from an application's name derives from it: the namespace <app>-refactor-<job>, the images <registry>/<app>-refactor-<job>/<component>, the Ingress hosts, the sandbox IdP clients and the lab services, so the variant shares nothing with the original or with another order. The image tag is 1.<yyyymmdd>.<hhmm>-refactor.<job>, a semver pre-release that the original's image automation never picks up.
  • Where. A sibling folder of the original in the output repository of the organization scan that assessed the application, <Organization>/<Project>/<Repository>-refactor-<job>/, with sandbox/ regenerated, in one commit; Flux (or Argo CD) deploys it from there. The registry, output repository and branch, image pull secret, security gate and Push images are that scan's; the output repository's write token is its registered credential. An application that no organization scan with an output repository assessed here is not deployed, and the order page says so (no output repository: ...).
  • Data. Only the components that rate A are deployed, with no uploaded dev database: the variant gets a new, empty lab database of its own (when the lab services are on), as a new application would.
  • Health. The runner reads the variant's namespace back with a read-only kubeconfig (CONTAINERIZER_SANDBOX_KUBECONFIG, optional CONTAINERIZER_SANDBOX_CONTEXT; on the appliance the verifier account of sandbox/verify-rbac.yaml, below) and records it in the order: running in the sandbox, failing in the sandbox, or deployed, health not checked without a kubeconfig. The original's sandbox results on its results page stay as they are: the variant is not a sandbox check of the application and teaches the learning loop nothing.
  • Expiry and removal. A variant expires after 7 days (CONTAINERIZER_SANDBOX_VARIANT_DAYS). Remove from the sandbox on the order page (administrators, operators, the application's product owners) asks for its removal; the queue runner takes expired and requested variants out of the output repository within a few minutes (the folder deleted, sandbox/ regenerated, one commit: the cluster removes the namespace) and records it: removed or expired. The patch stays available.

The results page shows the variant's state next to the order, with its URL (open ↗) while it runs.

Images without a registry. When the organization scan's Push images is off and the sandbox cluster shares the image builder's Docker image store (a lab: k3s with --docker on the machine that builds), set CONTAINERIZER_LOCAL_IMAGES=1 for the scan worker and the LLM queue runner: each image is then tagged with its deploy reference (docker tag, no push) and the manifests run it with imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent. Such images have no digest, signature or SBOM attestation (they need a registry). Without the setting, nothing changes: with Push images on the images are pushed (the appliance pushes to its own registry).

docs.title: The command line
docs.text:
containerizer refactor path/to/app [--component NAME] [--out DIR] [--include-config] [--max-calls 8] [--no-verify]
containerizer refactor path/to/app --queue [--sql ...]

Without --queue it runs at once with the LLM of the environment (CONTAINERIZER_LLM_BASE_URL and CONTAINERIZER_MODEL for a self-hosted one; the LLM), and writes the patch and a summary (<app>-<component>-containerizer.json: every finding's result, the verification, the payload) to --out. The application folder must be a git checkout for git am to work: the patch is made for its HEAD commit, and uncommitted changes are not in it. A folder without git gets a patch for git apply -p1 in that folder. With --queue the order goes to the LLM queue in SQL Server (--sql or CONTAINERIZER_SQL), or to llm-queue.json in --out, which containerizer llm-queue --file works through.

--goal rating-a runs Make it A on the checkout (the loop, the repair rounds and the second pass; --max-calls is then the limit of the whole order, 16 by default); the command line never deploys a sandbox variant.

docs.title: On the appliance
docs.text:
The LLM queue runner (containerizer-llm-queue) carries out the orders. For them it

  • reads the scan worker's clones (/var/lib/containerizer/worker/scan-<id>/repos/<app>) read only, and makes its scratch copies with git clone --shared in /var/lib/containerizer/refactor, the only folder it may write to besides the LLM answer cache. It reads no other folder: a job that names another source is refused (CONTAINERIZER_REFACTOR_SOURCES), so a row in the database cannot make it read the machine's files;
  • is in the docker group, like the scan worker, to build and run the patched components. The docker group is root-equivalent: the runner builds the same repositories' code in the same hardened containers as the scan worker, which is why the appliance is a dedicated machine with an egress allow-list (appliance). Without Docker the patches are applies only.
  • for sandbox variants: clones the scan's output repository into its scratch space with the registered write token, pushes the variant's images to the appliance's registry, reads the lab services that are on, and reads the variant's health with the kubeconfig of the read-only verifier account, /run/containerizer/sandbox-verifier.kubeconfig. cz-sandbox (root, every 2 minutes) gives that account its Role in every namespace Containerizer generated (sandbox/verify-rbac.yaml: workloads, pods, their logs and events, the namespace's Flux Kustomization; no Secrets, nothing cluster-wide) and writes the kubeconfig with a 24-hour token (root:containerizer, 0640). A new variant's namespace gets its Role at the next run of cz-sandbox; the runner waits for it within its health check (15 minutes, CONTAINERIZER_SANDBOX_VARIANT_TIMEOUT).

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The LLM can be wrong. A patch that builds and runs is not a patch that is correct: the build and a start-up probe do not run your tests. Review every change.
  • APIs the component cannot use. Models suggest APIs of newer frameworks than the component targets (on a net6.0 component, Qwen3-Coder used X509CertificateLoader, which is .NET 9 and later). The build catches it: such a patch is applies only, with the compiler error in the log tail. Fix it with the LLM on the order page asks again with the errors; Make it A does so by itself (at most 2 rounds a pass).
  • Speed. On the built-in CPU LLM each file takes five minutes or more, and the verification build takes minutes too; an order of a few files takes most of an hour. The queue runs it when its settings allow.
  • Small context. The LLM sees one file (or part of a large one) and the component's settings, not the whole application: changes that span several files (a new option class wired up in Program.cs) may be left as not fixed with a reason, or made in one file only.
  • What is verified is the component's container as Containerizer generates it, with the production services it needs missing (a smoke test in Development mode when they are), not the application in its real environment.
  • Make it A stops at its limits (16 LLM calls, 2 passes, 2 repair rounds a pass): an application whose findings need more stays B, and the order says what is left. The rating after is the rules' rating of the patched copy and the build and run of its components, not a test of the application.
  • A sandbox variant runs the patched code with a new, empty lab database: it shows that the application starts and answers as a stateless container, not that its data or its integrations work.

docs.title: Rule review
docs.text:
The learning loop of a scan builds and runs applications, matches failures against the failure rules, patches the build plan and retries (how it works). Nothing it learns enters the ruleset until an administrator approves it under Admin → Rule review:

  1. The run uses what it learns, and nothing else does. A learning run works on a staging copy of the learned rules, so its own result is as good as it can be while the rules other runs read stay unchanged.
  2. What it learned waits as a candidate with its evidence: every new finding or plan rule, failure rule and Linux-safe package.
  3. A person decides: approve (after editing the rule in the text box, if needed) or reject with a reason. Rejected rules are not proposed again. Every decision is in the change history.
  4. Approved rules go into your internal rules repository, never into this tool's public rules/ folder: what your applications taught the tool stays inside your organization.

docs.title: What a candidate shows
docs.text:
Kind A finding or plan rule (70-reviewed.yaml), a failure rule of the build-and-run loop (55-reviewed-failures.yaml), or a package proven to work on Linux (packages-reviewed.yaml) Source learned (from a build and run) or ai (proposed by the LLM, with the model's name) Confidence The rule's own confidence if it has one (0.7 for LLM rules), else 0.9 when the container built and ran with it, 0.8 for a failure observed at runtime, 0.6 otherwise Seen How many runs learned the same rule. The same condition and effect learned again adds evidence to the existing candidate, whatever its id or wording Evidence For each run (the latest 20): repository and commit, application and component, every attempt (which failure rule matched, its outcome, the exit code, the diagnosis), and the tail of the failing log

Logs are stored with credentials masked (passwords and keys in connection strings, Authorization headers, user:password in URLs, JSON web tokens, private keys). The masking catches the common forms, not every secret an application can print, so rule review is for administrators only.

docs.title: What approval checks
docs.text:
A learned rule has to meet the same bar as the curated ones:

  • a unique id (lower-case letters, digits, ., -, _), not already used by a curated or approved rule;
  • every regular expression in when compiles; the condition is not empty;
  • finding rules: a title, a why of at least 60 characters, a fix, and at least one https reference for refactor, rewrite and blocker findings;
  • plan rules and failure-rule fixes only use known build-plan keys;
  • failure rules: stage, outcome and a match that does not match an empty log;
  • packages: a valid expression that does not match (almost) any package name.

docs.title: Setting up the internal rules repository
docs.text:
1. Create a private or internal Git repository for the approved rules. It needs one commit (a README is enough); the rules folder is created by the first approval.
  2. Under Admin → Source control, add a write token for that repository's URL. It must be able to push a branch and open a pull request in that one repository: GitHub fine-grained token with Contents and Pull requests: Read and write, GitLab project access token with the role Developer and the scopes api and write_repository, or Azure DevOps Code: Read & write.
  3. Under Admin → Rule review → Internal rules repository, enter the repository URL, the branch the pull requests target (default main) and the folder of the rules in it (default rules). The provider is worked out from the URL for github.com, gitlab.com and gitlab.* hosts, dev.azure.com and *.visualstudio.com; choose it for other servers, and give the API URL of a self-hosted GitHub Enterprise Server or GitLab if it is not at the usual address.
  4. Allow the Git server on Admin → Firewall.

Until all of this is in place, the Rule review page says what is missing, and candidates keep waiting. The settings are in the change history.

Like every source control token, the write token is sealed for the scan worker: the web UI cannot use it. So approving hands the rule to the scan worker, which opens the pull request within a minute, also while a scan is running. The candidate shows the pull request is being opened until then, and approved with the pull request's link after. If it fails (a token without the permission, a repository the token cannot see), the page shows why and the rule waits for a new decision.

The worker clones the internal repository, appends the rule to the right file on a branch containerizer/rule-review-<candidate>, pushes it and opens a pull request that names the reviewer and their note. It contains the rule, not the evidence logs. Safeguards:

  • The repository's visibility is read with the token first: only private or internal repositories (Azure DevOps: a private project) are accepted. A public repository, or one whose visibility the token cannot read, is refused and the rule stays pending.
  • Approved rules are never written into this tool's rules/ folder.
  • Approving the same candidate again after a failure reuses the branch and the open pull request.

Before every scan the worker fetches the repository again, so scans use an approved rule as soon as its pull request is merged. If the Git server cannot be reached, the scan uses the rules it fetched last.

Approved rules are loaded after the curated ones and carry reviewed: {candidate, by, at}. Editing or deleting them by hand in the internal repository later is fine.

docs.title: Sandbox HTTPS
docs.text: Publish the apps that the organization scans deploy to the sandbox cluster over HTTPS, under one wildcard domain that an administrator sets up. Each component that serves HTTP gets its own address, recorded on its generated Ingress (containerizer.io/url).

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A domain for the sandbox apps, for example sandbox.example.com. Give the sandbox a domain of its own: not the domain the admin pages are under. The appliance refuses a domain that contains its own host name, so an app can never share a name with the admin pages. A separate registrable domain (example-sandbox.net) isolates the apps from your other sites best.
  • A wildcard certificate for *.<domain> with its private key, both in PEM:
    • the server certificate first, then its intermediates (the root is optional);
    • RSA with at least 2048 bits, or ECDSA P-256 or P-384;
    • the key without a password (openssl pkey -in key.pem -out plain.pem);
    • valid now. The page warns when it expires within 30 days. Renew it before then and paste the new one.
  • A DNS record that points the wildcard name at the appliance (see DNS).

A certificate from a public CA works in every browser. A certificate from your internal CA works where that CA is trusted.

docs.title: Set it up
docs.text:
Admin → Sandbox HTTPS (administrators only): enter the domain as *.sandbox.example.com, paste the certificate chain and the private key, and save. The page checks that the certificate names *.<domain>, matches the key, is valid now, comes with its chain in order and is a server certificate, and says which check failed. The system agent (root) then checks it all again and:

  • writes the certificate and key to /var/lib/containerizer/system/sandbox-https.{crt,key}, the key readable only by root and Caddy;
  • adds a site for *.<domain> to Caddy. Caddy validates the site before it is restarted, so a broken site never takes the admin pages down; if anything fails, every file goes back to what it was;
  • installs the certificate in k3s as Traefik's default certificate (see How it works).

The key is never shown again, and the change history records the domain and the certificate's fingerprint and expiry, never the key or the certificate text. Turn off deletes the certificate and key from the appliance, Caddy and k3s; generated Ingresses stay in the output repository until the next scan. Every organization scan after setup generates the Ingresses.

docs.title: Names
docs.text:
Each component that serves HTTP gets exactly one DNS label under the domain:

Component App (namespace) URL web shop https://web-shop.sandbox.example.com/ shop shop https://shop.sandbox.example.com/ api expense-claims https://api-expense-claims.sandbox.example.com/

The rule is <component>-<app>.<domain>, or just <app>.<domain> when the component has the app's name. Both parts are the Kubernetes names (lower case, letters, digits and hyphens). A name longer than 63 characters is cut and gets 8 hex characters of a SHA-256 of <app>/<component>, so it stays unique and does not change between scans. The names containerizer-edge and containerizer-idp are the appliance's own (Caddy's check of Traefik, the sandbox identity provider): a component that would get one of them gets the hash suffix instead. The name has one label because a wildcard certificate covers exactly one label: *.sandbox.example.com covers web-shop.sandbox.example.com but not web.shop.sandbox.example.com.

Two different apps can end up with the same name, for example component a of app b-c and component a-b of app c. That is rare but possible. The health check then marks the one that does not answer as failing. Rename a component or an app to fix it.

docs.title: DNS
docs.text:
Point the wildcard at the appliance, in the zone of the domain:

*.sandbox.example.com.   300  IN  A      192.0.2.10                 ; the appliance's address
; or, when the appliance has a DNS name:
*.sandbox.example.com.   300  IN  CNAME  containerizer.example.com.
  • Use an AAAA record as well if the appliance has an IPv6 address that clients use.
  • An internal-only sandbox needs the record only in your internal DNS zone. The certificate can still be from a public CA if the domain is one you own publicly.
  • Check it with dig +short web-shop.sandbox.example.com (any name under the domain must return the appliance), then curl -I https://web-shop.sandbox.example.com/.
  • The record is for your users: the appliance itself never needs to resolve these names, and nothing needs to be allowed on the Firewall page.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
browser ──https://web-shop.<domain>──► :443 Caddy (appliance) ──TLS──► Traefik (k3s, 10.43.0.80) ──► Service web ──► pods
             wildcard certificate          *.<domain> site            same certificate, Host routing      namespace shop
  • Port 443 is not opened for this: it is already open. Caddy answers on 443 for the admin pages and picks the site by the name the browser asks for. *.<domain> is a second site next to the admin pages' own name. The firewall's inbound rules stay the same: TCP 22 and 443, nothing else. Port 80 stays closed, so the apps are never reachable over plain HTTP from outside.
  • Caddy terminates TLS with the wildcard certificate and adds Strict-Transport-Security. It removes its Server header and passes the request to Traefik over TLS. It checks Traefik's certificate against the same certificate chain, so the hop from the host into the cluster is encrypted and authenticated too.
  • Traefik, the ingress controller that k3s ships, runs again on the appliance. It is configured by /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests/containerizer-traefik.yaml, which lives in the OS image. Its Service has the fixed cluster address 10.43.0.80 and no load balancer or host ports, so nothing outside the appliance reaches it directly. Its HTTP entry point only redirects to HTTPS. Its default certificate is the wildcard: TLSStore default points to the TLS Secret containerizer-sandbox-tls in kube-system. It trusts X-Forwarded-For only from the node's bridge address (Caddy), so apps see the client's address.
  • The certificate in k3s goes through External Secrets when External Secrets Operator is installed on the sandbox:
    • The value goes into the sandbox's secret store (Secret containerizer-sandbox-tls in namespace containerizer-secrets, read by ClusterSecretStore app-secrets).
    • kube-system may read that one key only (ServiceAccount app-secrets-reader, a Role with resourceNames).
    • An ExternalSecret in kube-system creates the TLS Secret from it.

Before ESO is installed, the system agent writes the TLS Secret directly. Either way, k3s encrypts Secrets at rest (secrets-encryption: true). containerizer-sandbox runs python -m containerizer.sysagent sandbox-https sync every 2 minutes. That brings k3s in line with the setting, including right after a restart, before Traefik is up. - No key in the apps' namespaces or in Git. The generated Ingress names its host under spec.tls without a secretName, so the ingress controller's default certificate serves it. The private key is never copied into an app's namespace, where the app's own reconciler could read it. The output repository never contains a Secret for it.

docs.title: The generated Ingress
docs.text:
For each component with a Service (web and spa components), <component>/k8s.yaml gets:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: web
  annotations:
    containerizer.io/url: https://web-shop.sandbox.example.com/
    traefik.ingress.kubernetes.io/router.entrypoints: websecure   # HTTPS only on Traefik
    traefik.ingress.kubernetes.io/router.tls: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"              # HTTP -> HTTPS on ingress-nginx
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/force-ssl-redirect: "true"
spec:
  tls:
    - hosts: [web-shop.sandbox.example.com]                        # default certificate: no secretName
  rules:
    - host: web-shop.sandbox.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - {path: /, pathType: Prefix, backend: {service: {name: web, port: {name: http}}}}
  • No ingressClassName is set, so the cluster's default class applies. On k3s that is Traefik.
  • The component's NetworkPolicy already admits its port from other namespaces, so the ingress controller can reach it. The default-deny policy stays.
  • The Argo CD AppProject allows Ingress because it is one of the generated kinds. The Flux tenant's admin role covers it in the namespace.
  • On another cluster, give the ingress controller the wildcard certificate as its default. For ingress-nginx, use --default-ssl-certificate. For Traefik, use a default TLSStore. Redirect HTTP to HTTPS at the entry point: the Traefik annotations above put the route on websecure only.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: What you see Where to look "Not saved: …" on the page The sentence says which check failed: name, key, order, validity "The last change was not applied" Caddy or the agent refused it: journalctl -u containerizer-sysagent Browser: certificate error The chain is incomplete (paste the intermediates) or the CA is not trusted on that machine 404 at a URL No Ingress with that host: was the app scanned after the domain was set? kubectl get ingress -A 502 at a URL Traefik is not up or does not have the certificate yet: kubectl -n kube-system get pods,tlsstore, journalctl -u containerizer-sandbox

docs.title: Sandbox identity provider
docs.text:
Apps that sign users in usually point at a corporate identity provider: Entra ID, AD FS or an Okta tenant. They can't use it in a sandbox, because nobody will register a lab URL there. So containerizer org deploys its own identity provider into the sandbox cluster. Every component that signs users in with OpenID Connect, SAML 2.0 or WS-Federation is registered there and pointed at it, through configuration only. The app's code is never changed. Test users and groups are created too.

Everything is declarative and lives in the output repository under sandbox/idp/, next to the apps. Flux applies it with the apps; the secrets come from the secret store (External Secrets).

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
IdP WSO2 Identity Server 7.3 at https://containerizer-idp.<sandbox domain>/ (console: /console) OpenID Connect issuer https://containerizer-idp.<domain>/oauth2/token, discovery …/oauth2/token/.well-known/openid-configuration SAML 2.0 entity ID https://containerizer-idp.<domain>, metadata …/identity/metadata/saml2 WS-Federation metadata …/wsfed-metadata/FederationMetadata/2007-06/FederationMetadata.xml, passive endpoint …/wsfed Test users alice (group sandbox-admins), bob and carol (sandbox-users), e-mail <user>@<domain> Where the details are shown application page of the results UI (Sign-in in the sandbox), sandbox/idp/README.md, each component's idp.json

On the appliance, containerizer idp users on the console prints the test users' passwords.

The IdP needs a sandbox domain (--ingress-domain, or the appliance's Sandbox HTTPS setting): issuer, metadata and redirect URLs have to be the same for the browser and for the apps. Without a domain, or with --no-sandbox-idp, nothing changes.

docs.title: Why WSO2 Identity Server
docs.text:
The IdP had to speak all three protocols that .NET line-of-business apps use, with the least to run. That means one process, an embedded database, no licence key, and an open-source licence that lets us ship it.

OIDC SAML 2.0 WS-Federation Licence Notes WSO2 Identity Server 7.3 yes yes yes (passive STS, built in) Apache 2.0 one JVM container, embedded H2, about 1 GiB RAM, REST APIs for everything Keycloak + keycloak-wsfed yes yes extension Apache 2.0 + AGPL-3.0 the WS-Fed extension's last release targets Keycloak 8 (WildFly); it does not load in current Keycloak authentik yes yes Enterprise edition only MIT / commercial the WS-Federation provider is not in the open-source edition Shibboleth IdP (plugin) yes no Apache 2.0 SAML-first; no WS-Federation A .NET IdP (Duende IdentityServer + WS-Fed plugin) yes plugin plugin commercial needs a licence and code we would have to write and maintain

WSO2 is the only option that covers all three protocols out of the box under a permissive licence. It also configures entirely over documented REST APIs (applications, SCIM 2.0 users and groups, claims), which is what makes a declarative, Git-driven setup possible.

docs.title: How a component is detected and configured
docs.text:
Detection rules (rules/38-sandbox-idp.yaml) set facts from packages and code:

Protocol Detected from Settings section looked for in appsettings.json (+ appsettings.Production.json) OpenID Connect Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.OpenIdConnect, .AddOpenIdConnect(; Entra ID (Microsoft.Identity.Web) is reported a section with ClientId and Authority or MetadataAddress WS-Federation Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.WsFederation, .AddWsFederation( a section with Wtrealm, or MetadataAddress and Realm SAML 2.0 Sustainsys.Saml2.AspNetCore2, ITfoxtec.Identity.Saml2, .AddSaml2( a section named like Saml* with an IdP metadata key

For each section found, the generator:

  1. registers the component at the IdP as <app>--<component>, with its sandbox URL (https://<component>-<app>.<domain>/) as redirect URI, realm or SP entity ID;
  2. overrides the keys of that section with environment variables in the component's k8s.yaml, for example OpenIdConnect__Authority, OpenIdConnect__ClientId, WsFederation__MetadataAddress, WsFederation__Wtrealm, Saml2__IdpMetadata, Saml2__IdpEntityId, Saml2__EntityId. It also sets ASPNETCORE_FORWARDEDHEADERS_ENABLED=true, so the app builds https:// redirect URLs behind Traefik;
  3. gives an OIDC client a secret when the section has a ClientSecret key. The value is made once and kept in the secret store, and the component reads it through its existing <component>-secrets ExternalSecret (remote key <namespace>--<component>, property e.g. OpenIdConnect__ClientSecret). Without a ClientSecret key the client is public with PKCE;
  4. lets the component's pods reach the IdP's public name: a CoreDNS override sends containerizer-idp.<domain> to Traefik in the cluster, and the component's egress policy allows Traefik.

The key names it matches are listed under idp.protocols in the rules file. A component whose sign-in settings are only in code (no section found) is not changed; its idp.json and the application page say so.

Claims, as the apps expect them from Entra ID or AD FS:

  • OIDC: sub, name, given_name, family_name, email, preferred_username, groups;
  • WS-Federation and SAML: the AD FS claim types (…/claims/name, …/emailaddress, …/givenname, …/surname, …/role from groups). The name identifier is the user name.

docs.title: What is in Git
docs.text:
sandbox/idp/
  kustomization.yaml     ConfigMaps from the files below, all resources
  namespace.yaml         containerizer-idp, Pod Security "restricted"
  secrets.yaml           ExternalSecret cz-idp (remote key containerizer-idp--cz-idp) and its store access
  server.yaml            WSO2 (PVC on the data partition, init container, Deployment, Service, Ingress, /wsfed redirect)
  sync.yaml              CronJob cz-idp-sync, every 5 minutes
  network.yaml           default deny; Traefik in, DNS + Traefik out
  dns.yaml               coredns-custom key containerizer-idp.override
  config/                deployment.toml, init.sh, FederationMetadata.xml.in
  sync/                  idp.json (claims, groups, users), apps__<app>--<component>.json, idp_sync.py
  README.md              the IdP's URLs and every registered client

cz-idp-sync applies sync/ through WSO2's REST APIs and can run as often as you like. It creates missing groups and users, creates or updates applications, and deletes the applications it created that are no longer in Git. Applications someone added by hand in the console stay. It uses only the Python standard library, talks to the IdP's public HTTPS URL and never prints a secret.

With Argo CD the app-of-apps may only create Applications, so apply the IdP once yourself: kubectl apply -k sandbox/idp.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
Nothing secret is in Git. The remote key containerizer-idp--cz-idp in the secret store holds:

Property admin-password the IdP's admin user (console and the sync job) keystore-password the IdP's own key store; the key is generated on first start and never leaves the volume user-<name> test users' passwords client-<app>--<component> OIDC client secrets; the same value is put under the component's own remote key

On the appliance, cz-sandbox runs containerizer idp secrets every 2 minutes. Once Flux has deployed sandbox/idp, it creates the values that are missing and keeps the ones that exist, through server-side apply with field manager containerizer-idp. With another store (Vault, a cloud secret manager), create these properties there yourself.

docs.title: Limitations and quirks
docs.text:
• One IdP host name per repository. When the domain changes, the IdP starts afresh: new key, empty database, everything rebuilt by the sync job.
  • WS-Federation tokens are SAML 2.0. WSO2's SAML 1.1 tokens use an xsi:type that the .NET SAML 1.1 reader rejects. The metadata therefore advertises /wsfed, which Traefik redirects to WSO2's /passivests with a request for a SAML 2.0 token.
  • WS-Federation: one role value. WSO2 sends a user's groups as one comma-separated role value, so each test user is in one group.
  • .NET 8 and WS-Federation. ASP.NET Core 8's WS-Federation handler depends on Microsoft.IdentityModel 7.1.2, which rejects every token (IDX10204, dotnet/aspnetcore#52099), with AD FS as with this IdP. Rule wsfed-identitymodel-issuer-bug reports it; the fix is a package reference to 7.4.1 or later.
  • OIDC Identity.Name. Like Entra ID, the token has a name claim, not unique_name. An app that reads User.Identity.Name needs TokenValidationParameters.NameClaimType = "name", as it would with Entra ID.
  • Trust of the wildcard certificate. Apps call the IdP's metadata over HTTPS. A certificate from a private CA must be trusted by the app's image too (see the sandbox HTTPS settings).
  • The console is exposed at /console on the sandbox domain, protected by the admin password. The sandbox should only be reachable from your network.
  • Entra ID-only apps (Microsoft.Identity.Web) are reported, not changed: the library expects Entra ID's endpoints.

docs.title: How it was verified
docs.text: The generated sandbox/idp/ files were run in Docker: the WSO2 container with the same mounts, the init script under a read-only root file system, a TLS proxy in front, and the sync job. Then three unmodified ASP.NET Core 8 apps (examples/sandbox-idp/) signed in as alice in a real browser, configured only with the generated environment variables. OIDC, WS-Federation and SAML 2.0 (Sustainsys) all returned the expected claims. The Traefik redirect middleware and the CoreDNS override are standard k3s resources but have not yet been run in a k3s cluster: they wait for the sandbox cluster CI job.

docs.title: SBOMs, licences and CVEs per package
docs.text:
Every image a scan builds gets a software bill of materials (SBOM) in CycloneDX JSON. Each package in it is checked against a licence policy and gets the vulnerabilities the security gate's image scan found in it. The SBOM is written next to the component's generated files in the output repository (sbom.cdx.json), stored with the results, and shown in the web UI and the API. A denied licence fails the gate, so the component is not deployed.

The web UI shows a Packages column per component on the application page, every package with its licence, policy status and CVEs on the component page (with Download CycloneDX JSON), and licences and CVEs across the portfolio under Dependencies and licences.

docs.title: How an SBOM is made
docs.text:
Image SBOM. Syft reads the built image from the local Docker daemon: OS packages (dpkg, apk, rpm) with the licences from their copyright files, .NET packages from the *.deps.json files of the application and the runtime, npm, Python, Java and Go packages.

NuGet licences. Syft does not read NuGet licences, so Containerizer looks them up in each package's .nuspec on the NuGet feed (sbom.nuget_feed, the v3 service index; nuget.org by default): the licence expression when there is one, else the licence URL of older packages, mapped to an SPDX identifier where the URL names one licence unambiguously (licenses.nuget.org/MIT, the Apache and Open Source Initiative pages, the old .NET Library licence). Answers are cached under .work/ so a package version is looked up once. The licence found is also written into the SBOM file. nuget_licenses: false turns this off for runners without access to the feed; private feeds that need credentials are not queried (those packages show as unknown).

Source SBOM. For components that are not built, the scan stores the packages the component's project files declare, including those of the projects it references:

  • a lock file gives every runtime package with its exact version: package-lock.json (npm, lockfile v2/v3 also carry the licence; development packages are left out) or packages.lock.json (NuGet, when the project restores with a lock file);
  • otherwise the declared references (PackageReference, packages.config, package.json dependencies, requirements.txt, ...). A version range or floating version (8.0.*, ^1.2.0) is kept as written and left out of the package URL; transitive packages appear only in the image SBOM.

Nothing from the repository is executed. Source SBOMs have no CVE data: nothing was scanned. Turn them off with sbom.source: false. On the component page and in the API, the image SBOM wins when both exist for the latest assessment.

docs.title: Licence policy
docs.text:
The policy is in rules/60-security.yaml under sbom:.

Each package's licence is normalised to an SPDX expression where the data allows it. Several licences listed on one package all apply (A AND B): a Debian package lists the licence of every file it ships. An expression is judged as written: A OR B passes when either passes, A AND B needs both, and WITH <exception> is judged by the licence it modifies.

sbom:
  os_packages: report         # report | evaluate
  licenses:
    deny: []                  # fail the gate
    warn: ['AGPL(-.*)?', 'GPL(-.*)?', 'SSPL(-.*)?', 'CC-BY-NC(-.*)?', 'BUSL(-.*)?|Elastic-2\.0|Commons-Clause']
    allow: ['LicenseRef-public-domain', 'LicenseRef-Microsoft-NET-Library']
    unknown: report           # report | warn | deny
    accepted:                 # exceptions with a reason and an optional expiry
      - {package: 'Ghostscript\.NET', reason: 'separate commercial licence, contract 2026-114', expires: 2027-06-30}

The lists hold regular expressions matched against each whole SPDX identifier (case-insensitive), so GPL(-.*)? matches GPL-2.0-only and GPL-3.0-or-later but not LGPL-2.1-only. The result per package is one of:

Status Meaning Allowed an SPDX licence the lists do not deny or flag, or one on allow Review (warn) the policy asks for a decision, for example a copyleft licence Denied the policy does not allow it: the security gate fails Unknown no licence found, only a link to a licence page, or a name that is not an SPDX identifier (unknown: decides whether that warns or fails)

Shown but not counted: OS packages of the base image (unless os_packages: evaluate; the copyright files make glibc read "GPL AND LGPL", which says little about an application that runs on it), the application's own assembly, and packages with an accepted exception (until it expires). SPDX identifiers are recognised from rules/spdx-licenses.yaml, a copy of the SPDX License List.

docs.title: CVEs per package
docs.text: The gate's image scan (Trivy and Grype, merged; see Security gate) reports each finding with its package URL. Findings are matched to SBOM packages by package URL (ignoring qualifiers such as distro=), else by name and version. A vulnerable package the SBOM does not list is added as its own row (found by the vulnerability scan), so no CVE is dropped. The SBOM does not change what fails the gate on vulnerabilities: that is still scan.fail_on and scan.allowlist.

docs.title: In the registry
docs.text: A scan attaches the SBOM to each image it pushes with ORAS, which the appliance includes: an OCI referrer artifact of type application/vnd.cyclonedx+json, addressed by the image digest (list it with oras discover <image>@<digest>, fetch it with oras pull). The component page shows whether it was attached, or why not (for example a registry that does not accept referrers).

docs.title: Organization scans
docs.text: An organization scan reads every Git repository of one Azure DevOps organization (or Azure DevOps Server collection), GitHub organization or GitLab group, assesses them, and deploys the ones that are ready to the sandbox cluster. Administrators and operators define scans under Admin → Organization scans: the organization, filters, where images and generated files go, and the days and time (UTC) to run, or Run full scan. The scan worker on the appliance runs them. Before the first scan, an administrator registers a read-only token for the organization and a write token for the output repository (source control tokens), and allows the hosts on Admin → Firewall.

docs.title: Discover first, then scan
docs.text:
A scan runs in two phases, so time is not spent on repositories nobody uses any more:

  1. Discover (on the scan's page) lists the projects, every Git repository in them and each repository's latest commit on its default branch, through the provider's API only. Nothing is cloned, assessed, built or pushed, and the output repository is not touched, so even a large organization is listed in minutes. Discovery also marks the automatic skips the API alone shows (archived, empty, fork, not updated recently, left out by the filter).
  2. An administrator or operator reviews the result and disables what is deprecated:
  3. Admin → Repositories shows each repository's latest commit. No commit for a year and Oldest commit first bring the old ones to the top; select them and Disable, with a note.
  4. Admin → Repositories → Projects lists the projects (Azure DevOps projects, GitLab subgroups) with their number of repositories and latest commit. Disabling a project disables all its repositories, including ones added to it later. GitHub organizations have no project level: disable the repositories, or pause the scan.

  1. Run full scan (or the schedule) then processes only the enabled repositories. Disabled ones are never cloned, and one that was deployed before leaves the sandbox at that run.

Disabled repositories and projects are also hidden from the results pages: the overview, the trends, the SBOM pages and the application pages leave out the applications that come from them (they stay on the admin pages). Enabling them again brings their results back at once. Repositories the scan skips automatically are not hidden. Every change to a project or repository, with who made it and the note, is in Admin → Change history (Projects, Repositories) and on the project's or repository's own page.

Scan now, on a project's or repository's page or for the ones selected in the lists, runs a full scan of only those, outside the schedule, for example after a fix was pushed. The other repositories keep their results from the last full run. Disabled ones stay disabled; a run of the scan that is already queued or running has to finish first.

Discovery can be run again at any time, for example before a scheduled run, to see the new projects and repositories first. Scheduled runs are always full scans; new repositories found by them are processed in that run unless their project is disabled.

docs.title: What happens to each repository
docs.text:
1. Listed through the provider's API, including private and internal repositories the token can read. Every run (discovery or full) lists the organization again: new projects and repositories are added (a full run processes the new repositories in that run), renamed ones are followed by the provider's id, and ones that are gone are marked removed. Repositories an administrator disabled, or whose project is disabled, stop here.
  2. Skipped automatically when there is nothing to do, with the reason shown on Admin → Repositories (automatic skips).
  3. Cloned shallow (default branch only, no tags, submodules, symlinks or LFS objects). Clones are kept on the appliance, and later runs only fetch the newest commit and reset the work tree to it.
  4. Assessed, built and run: every feasible component is built and run hardened, failures are matched and fixed where a rule knows how, and the application is assessed again (how it works). With Ask the LLM on, the LLM is consulted about what the rules are unsure of. Every assessment is stored, A or not, so the results pages and trends cover the whole organization.
  5. Selected: a component is deployed only when it is a server component (web, worker, console, SPA) rated A on its own (including the stateless requirement), a Linux image can be generated for it, and it built and ran in the verification (or ran and only lacked its database or broker).
  6. Security gate: lint, image build, vulnerability scan, licence policy and a run with the pod's security context (security gate). A component that fails is dropped, and the rest are gated again so the namespace, network policies and GitOps files cover only what is deployed.
  7. Images pushed as <registry>/<app>/<component>:<tag> and :git-<commit>. The tag is 1.<yyyymmdd>.<hhmm> of the run (semver, so Flux image automation can follow it). With the registry set to localhost:5000/<path>, images go to the appliance's own registry and need no credentials; an external registry needs push credentials in worker.env.
  8. Committed to the output repository after every repository, so a long run can be followed and survives interruptions.

A repository that is skipped or has no A component loses its folder in the output repository, so the sandbox stops deploying it. A repository that fails keeps its previous folder and is reported as failed.

A scan runs at most once at a time, and a paused scan does not run at all. If the worker was down at the scheduled time, the scan runs once when it is back. Cancel stops a running scan after the repository it is on. A scan that has run cannot be deleted (its history is kept): pause it.

docs.title: Automatic skips
docs.text:
Automatic skip Reason shown, for example Has a Dockerfile found src/Api/Dockerfile: the team already containerizes it. Enabled, it is moved from Docker Swarm, Compose, Nomad, Azure Container Apps or ECS to Kubernetes (platform migrations) No application code 14 files (.md 9, .yml 3, .json 2), no source code: documentation, configuration, pipelines, SQL or scripts Language not supported Ruby (32 files), but no project the tool can build (...) Nothing to deploy only library, test: 3 projects, nothing that runs on its own Not updated recently no update since 2026-01-07: no commit on the default branch for the scan's skip repositories not updated for days (default 183) Archived, Empty, Fork as the provider reports (forks only with skip forks) Left out by the filter the scan's include/exclude regular expressions on project/repository

Automatic skips are checked again at every run, so a repository that gets new commits or loses its Dockerfile is processed again by itself. Archived, empty, filtered and stale repositories are decided from the provider's API without fetching anything. An administrator can Enable a repository (process it even though a skip applies), Disable it (never fetch it; it also leaves the sandbox at the next run and its results are hidden from the results pages) or set it back to Automatic, with a note in the change history. A disabled project overrides the settings of its repositories.

docs.title: Output repository layout
docs.text:
<Organization>/
  README.md                  every repository: status, rating, deployed and excluded components with reasons
  org-run.json               the same as data (merged across runs)
  <Project>/<Repository>/    one application (namespace <app>)
    kustomization.yaml       namespace, security policies, components, image tags
    namespace.yaml security.yaml HARDENING.md SECURITY.md MIGRATION.md cluster/
    containerizer.json       source URL, commit, images, digests, verification
    gitops/argocd/           AppProject + Application for this app
    gitops/flux/             tenant.yaml, git/sync.yaml, oci/, image automation
    <component>/             Dockerfile, Dockerfile.dockerignore, k8s.yaml, plan.json, sbom.cdx.json
    pipeline/<provider>/     the image build pipeline for the application's own repository (build-pipelines.md)
sandbox/
  README.md namespaces.txt
  argocd/bootstrap.yaml      app-of-apps
  flux/bootstrap.yaml        GitRepository + root Kustomization
  idp/                       sandbox identity provider, when a component signs users in

The project folder is the Azure DevOps project, _ for GitHub (no projects), or the GitLab subgroup path with -- for /. The app name (Kubernetes namespace and image path) is <project>-<repository> in DNS form, prefixed with app- when it would be a system namespace, shortened with a hash past 63 characters, and given a hash suffix when two repositories would map to the same name.

docs.title: The sandbox cluster
docs.text:
The appliance's k3s cluster deploys what the scans commit. Fill in /etc/containerizer/sandbox.env (output repository URL, branch and a read-only token for it, separate from the scan's write token) and allow the Git server on Admin → Firewall. Every 2 minutes the appliance then:

  • puts the read-only token in the secret store for Flux's root sync and for every app namespace listed in sandbox/namespaces.txt;
  • creates the root GitRepository and Kustomization of sandbox/flux/. The root creates each tenant (namespace with Pod Security "restricted", ServiceAccounts, a namespace-only RoleBinding, read access to its own secret store keys), and each app then reconciles as its own ServiceAccount.

Nothing in the output repository is a Secret: credentials are ExternalSecrets (secrets). Apps that need a database, cache or object storage get one from the lab services, or a restored copy of their development database. Apps that sign users in with OpenID Connect, SAML 2.0 or WS-Federation are pointed at the sandbox identity provider. kubectl as root on the appliance shows the result. To deploy the same output repository to another cluster, follow sandbox/README.md in it (Argo CD or Flux).

docs.title: The LLM queue
docs.text:
With Ask the LLM on, LLM reviews chooses when the LLM is asked:

  • Inline (the default): during the scan, as before.
  • Queued: the scan asks the LLM nothing and the rules decide; the component reviews wait in the LLM queue and their answers are used by the next scan of each repository (queued LLM reviews: what is queued, in what order, and how an answer takes effect). Use it with a slow self-hosted LLM. LLM-heavy mode needs inline reviews.

Admin → LLM queue (administrators and operators) shows:

  • the jobs waiting, in the order the runner takes them: the repository and component, why it is queued (uncertain, or a second opinion on the rules' blocker or rewrite verdict) and the estimated tokens and time. Top, Up, Down and Bottom move a job; new jobs still go in by their priority. Skip takes one out of the queue;
  • at the top, the totals: jobs waiting and being asked, by kind (uncertain, second opinion); their estimated tokens in and out; the LLM time they need at the measured speed with the parallel requests set, for example ~7 h 20 min of LLM time (3 in parallel), and when they would all be done if the queue ran without a pause; what the estimate is learned from; and, outside the hours, when they next start;
  • the finished jobs: each answer (verdict and confidence, the reasoning and the question on the job's page), with the tokens and time it really took, failures (a job is tried three times, five minutes apart and more, before it fails) and skipped jobs. Requeue puts a failed or skipped one back;
  • repositories whose reviews are all answered since their last scan, with Re-scan now: a full scan of only that repository, so the answers apply without waiting for the schedule;
  • the settings: Paused; the days and hours (UTC) the runner may start jobs (no day selected: every day; From and To empty: all day; 22:00 to 06:00 runs past midnight, and the night belongs to the day it started); Only when idle: no organization scan running and the machine's 1-minute load average per CPU below the limit (0: the load is not looked at); and Parallel requests, as many as the LLM server answers at once (1 for a CPU server). The runner looks at them before each job; a job it has started finishes.

Every change to a job (queued, moved, skipped, requeued, answered, failed) and to the settings is in Admin → Change history.

Estimates. Each queued job's input tokens are estimated from the length of its question (3.5 characters a token to begin with) and its output from the answers before it (1,500 tokens to begin with). From every answer the runner learns, separately for each LLM (server and model): the characters per token of its tokenizer, the answer length of each kind of job, and its speed (prompt and generation tokens per second when the server reports its timings, as llama.cpp does, otherwise tokens per second from the time each answer took). Each figure is a moving average that gives the newest answer a weight of 0.2. The queue's time is the sum of the jobs' times divided by the parallel requests; the speeds are as measured with the parallel requests of the time, so this is a rough estimate. It does not include waiting for the hours or for the machine to be idle. Until an LLM has answered once, the page says time: learning.

The runner is containerizer llm-queue, a process of its own next to the scan worker (containerizer-llm-queue on the appliance). It uses the worker's database login, opens the LLM registered under Source control & LLM with the worker's key (or uses the worker's environment settings), writes into the worker's answer cache, and serves its metrics on port 9465: the jobs by status, kind and reason, the oldest waiting job, the estimated tokens and LLM time waiting, jobs finished, and the LLM usage of its answers (feature assessment-queued). On another machine, give it the worker's settings and the same CONTAINERIZER_AI_CACHE (shared), or rely on the next scan finding the answer in the queue; monitoring/systemd/containerizer-llm-queue.service is a unit for it. A job it is asking when it stops goes back to the queue.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Each token is only sent where it belongs: the read-only token to its own server's API and its own organization's clone URLs, the write token only to push the output repository, which is never scanned (how the tokens are protected). Git gets each token scoped to one repository URL, not in .git/config, the process list or clone URLs.
  • Clones are made with symlinks off, no submodules, and the file/ext transports disabled. The scanner never executes scanned code, but building and running the images does execute the repositories' build steps. That is why the appliance is a dedicated machine with an outbound allow-list for every build.
  • Registry credentials are written only to a temporary Docker config (mode 700) for the run.
  • Nothing secret is written to the output repository, and build logs are not copied there.

docs.title: Metrics and Grafana
docs.text:
The worker exports Prometheus metrics about the scans, the worker process and the machine, and the appliance's Grafana (https://<appliance>/grafana/, linked as Grafana ↗ on the admin pages) has a dashboard of them: scans running and waiting, time since the last successful run, progress of the current run, repositories by state (disabled_admin counts repositories disabled directly or through their project) and latest result, time per repository, clones and pulls, pushed images, LLM usage (calls, tokens and estimated cost by repository and feature, platform migrations), the LLM queue (jobs waiting, the oldest one, the runner open or waiting, jobs answered and failed), and the machine's CPU, memory, disk and network.

Alert rules are included (monitoring/prometheus/containerizer-alerts.yml): worker down, run failed, no successful run for 8 days, runs not starting, repositories failing, disk over 90 %, memory low. The metric names are listed in containerizer/metrics.py.

docs.title: Sign-in and roles
docs.text:
The web UI signs people in with your identity provider over OpenID Connect (Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, Keycloak, Google Workspace, ...). The admin pages, the System and Firewall pages and the API appear only once sign-in is set up. Sign-in and roles are the only web UI settings that are not on the admin pages: they are in /etc/containerizer/web.env on the appliance (mode 600), because they decide who may use the admin pages in the first place. Restart the web UI after a change (systemctl restart containerizer-web).

For development without an identity provider (never on the appliance, where it is refused), see admin pages without sign-in.

docs.title: Register the app at your identity provider
docs.text:
The redirect URI is https://<CZ_HOSTNAME>/auth/callback, where CZ_HOSTNAME is the name set in appliance.env (first boot). Then fill in:

Variable Meaning CONTAINERIZER_OIDC_ISSUER Issuer URL, e.g. https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant id>/v2.0 (Entra ID), https://<org>.okta.com, https://<keycloak>/realms/<realm> CONTAINERIZER_OIDC_CLIENT_ID / CONTAINERIZER_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET The app registration. The secret is optional (PKCE is always used); prefer a confidential client. CONTAINERIZER_ADMINS Who is an administrator (see the rules below). CONTAINERIZER_OIDC_SCOPES Optional. Default openid profile email. CONTAINERIZER_PUBLIC_URL Optional. Default https://<CZ_HOSTNAME>.

Allow the identity provider's host on Admin → Firewall (or in egress.json before the first sign-in, e.g. login.microsoftonline.com): the web UI fetches its signing keys.

Microsoft Entra ID: register a web application with the redirect URI above and add a client secret. Create one app role per role below (for example Containerizer.Admin, Containerizer.Operator, Containerizer.Read, and one per owned business unit such as Finance.Owner) and assign them to groups under Enterprise applications. Entra ID does not send email_verified, so use role: or group: rules there, not email: or domain:.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
Each role is an allow-list of rules, comma separated:

Rule Matches group:<id> a group claim (Entra ID: the group's object id) role:<name> an app role email:<address>, domain:<e-mail domain> the e-mail address, only when the provider marks it verified (email_verified) sub:<subject id> one user Role Variable Can Admin CONTAINERIZER_ADMINS Everything, including business units, Source control & LLM, Rule review, Lab services, Firewall, System and the access log. Operator CONTAINERIZER_OPERATORS Read everything, including the change history. Run and schedule organization scans (discovery and full scans), enable and disable projects and repositories, order and pause the LLM queue and set when it runs, order refactoring patches of B-rated applications and download them (Admin → Refactoring), upload dev database backups. Cannot change the mapping. Product owner CONTAINERIZER_PRODUCT_OWNERS Read everything, including the change history. Map applications and change their display name, owner, description and hidden flag, and change their products, but only within their scope (below). Viewer CONTAINERIZER_VIEWERS Read the results pages. Only matters when sign-in for the results pages is on.

Refactoring patches contain source code: product owners and viewers see an order's status on the application's results page, but not the patch, and only administrators and operators see the Request a refactoring patch button (who can order one).

Nobody outside these lists gets into /admin. One person can have several roles; admin includes all of them. The roles are enforced by the web UI and the API, and every change in the change history records the role it was made in.

Product owner scopes. Each entry is <rules>=<scopes>; entries are separated by ;, rules and scopes within an entry by ,:

CONTAINERIZER_PRODUCT_OWNERS="role:Finance.Owner=bu:Finance; group:6f1c...=product:Billing,product:#12"
  • bu:<name>: a business unit and every product in it, now and later. With a business unit in scope, the owner can also add products to it and delete empty ones.
  • product:<name>: one product and its applications.
  • bu:#<id> / product:#<id>: the same by id (the number in the admin page address). An id keeps working after a rename; a name scope does not. Names are matched without regard to case.

A product owner can take over unmapped applications by mapping them to one of their products, and move their applications between their products. Everything outside their scope shows as view only. Scopes are checked on every request, so a product moved to another business unit leaves (or joins) that owner's scope at once.

docs.title: Sign-in for the results pages (optional)
docs.text:
By default anyone who reaches the web UI over HTTPS can read the results. Set CONTAINERIZER_VIEWERS to limit that to named people; admins, operators and product owners can always read. Opening a results page without a session then goes straight to the identity provider and back. People who match no list get a "not allowed" page, and the database is not read for them.

CONTAINERIZER_VIEW_AUDIT=true (needs CONTAINERIZER_VIEWERS) records every sign-in, refused sign-in, results page opened and sign-out in the access log, which admins see on the admin pages. If a row cannot be written, the page is not shown, so a view is never left unrecorded. The access log is personal data: tell users their access is recorded, and keep it only as long as your policy says (deleting old rows needs the database owner).

docs.title: Session security
docs.text:
• Authorization code flow with PKCE (S256), state and nonce. The ID token's signature is verified with the provider's published keys, as are issuer, audience and expiry; unsigned and HMAC tokens are refused.
  • The session is a random id in an HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, Secure, __Host- cookie, new at every sign-in, ending after 8 hours, 1 hour idle, or at sign-out. Sessions are kept in memory, so a restart signs everyone out.
  • Every form carries a per-session CSRF token and cross-site posts are refused by Origin. Responses carry a strict Content-Security-Policy (no inline script), X-Frame-Options: DENY, HSTS and no-store; errors are logged on the server and never shown.
  • The change history (business units, products, application mapping, scans, repositories, tokens, lab services, rule decisions) is written by database triggers, so even direct SQL changes are recorded. No database role of the web UI can update or delete audit or access log rows; forward them to your SIEM if they must be tamper-proof.

Grafana has its own sign-in: user admin with the password in /etc/containerizer/secrets/grafana-admin, or your identity provider through GF_AUTH_GENERIC_OAUTH_* settings in /etc/containerizer/grafana.env.

docs.title: Source control tokens and the LLM
docs.text:
Organization scans (scheduled-scans.md) read Azure DevOps, GitHub and GitLab organizations and push the generated files to an output Git repository. The tokens for both are registered by administrators under Admin → Source control & LLM, together with the LLM the scans ask (see The LLM below):

  • Organizations (read-only): one token for each Azure DevOps organization (or Azure DevOps Server collection), GitHub organization or GitLab group the scans may read, on the cloud service or a self-hosted server. This is the allow-list: a scan of an organization without a registered, enabled token does not run, and nothing is ever read anonymously.
  • Output repositories (write): one token for each repository the generated Dockerfiles, manifests and GitOps files are pushed to, matched by the repository's URL. The internal rules repository of the rule review gets its write token here too.

docs.title: How the tokens are protected
docs.text:
• Sealed for the worker. The moment a token is saved, the web UI seals it for the scan worker's public key (X25519 key agreement, HKDF-SHA256, AES-256-GCM). The web UI has only the public key, so it cannot open what it stored; only the worker, with the private key, opens a token, just before a run. The sealed token is bound to its purpose, provider, server and organization or repository: it does not open if it is moved to another row or another purpose in the database.
  • Never shown again. The page has a password field to enter a token and a button to replace it, nothing that shows it. The admin database role may write the sealed token but is not granted SELECT on it.
  • Audited, without the token. Adding, replacing (Token saved changes), enabling, disabling and removing a token are in the change history with who did it. The token itself is never copied there.
  • Only sent where it belongs.
  • The read-only token goes to its own server's API, and with the clone URLs of its own organization only (https://github.com/<org>/…, https://gitlab.com/<group>/…, https://dev.azure.com/<org>/… or https://<org>.visualstudio.com/…, or the self-hosted server's equivalent). A repository whose clone URL is elsewhere is refused. An API redirect or pagination link to another host does not get the token, and https is never followed down to http.
  • The write token is chosen by the output repository's URL, never by host or organization, and is only used to clone and push that repository. The output repository can therefore be in a scanned organization: it is never scanned itself, and the read-only token is never used to push.
  • Git gets each token as an http.<repository URL>.extraHeader in its environment, so it is valid for that one repository URL only, is not written to disk or the process list, and no credential helper sees it. Errors and logs are redacted.
  • Least privilege is checked where the provider allows it. The worker records on the page when a token last worked, and warns when a GitHub classic token has scopes that can write or a GitLab token has more than read_api / read_repository. Registering the same token as both an organization's read-only token and its output repository's write token is refused.
  • Admins only. The Source control page is for administrators; operators can schedule scans, but only of organizations an administrator registered.

docs.title: The sealing key
docs.text: The appliance makes the key pair at first boot: /etc/containerizer/secrets/credential-key for the worker and credential-key.pub for the web UI. Back up credential-key with the database: the registered tokens open only with it. A new key pair means entering every token again (the page marks tokens sealed for another key). Also allow each Git server's host on Admin → Firewall.

docs.title: Making the tokens
docs.text: Give every token an expiration date and enter the same date on the page: it warns 14 days before, and an expired token stops its scans with a clear message. Revoke a token where it was made when you replace or remove it here.

docs.title: Read-only token for an organization
docs.text:
Provider Token Permissions Server (self-hosted) GitHub Fine-grained personal access token: resource owner the organization, repository access All repositories Contents: Read-only and Metadata: Read-only, nothing else https://ghe.example.com/api/v3 GitLab Group access token on the group, role Reporter (on GitLab.com group tokens need Premium or Ultimate; otherwise a personal access token of a Reporter in the group) scopes read_api and read_repository https://gitlab.example.com Azure DevOps Personal access token for this organization only Custom defined: Code: Read and Project and Team: Read (scopes) https://tfs.example.com/tfs, the collection as the organization

Notes:

  • GitHub organizations can require approval of fine-grained tokens, or forbid them (token policy). A classic token needs the repo scope for private repositories, which can also write: avoid it.
  • GitLab: the organization is the group path; subgroups are included (acme covers acme/platform/*), or register a subgroup alone (acme/platform).
  • Azure DevOps is retiring PATs for All accessible organizations: make one per organization. Use a dedicated account that can read the repositories but not change them.
